text: WheelZoom WheelZoom ( parent : QObject | None = None ) [Source] Bases: QObject Zoom when the mouse wheel turns with Ctrl held, wherever the pointer is. A touchpad that sends small steps is added up, so that a whole notch is needed to move one step. Examples >>> WheelZoom (). eventFilter ( ... QObject (), QEvent ( QEvent . Type . None_ ) ... ) False Constructor Start with no wheel turned. Parameters parent ( QObject or None, default None ): The object that owns the filter. Constructor examples >>> WheelZoom (). _turned 0

title: alto.ui.zoom
text: WheelZoom.follow def follow ( app : QGuiApplication ) -> None [Source] Watch the window that has the focus, and each window that gains it later, such as a dialog that opens. The filter goes on the windows, not on the application. A window is handed each wheel turn before the widget under the pointer is, so a turn anywhere in it is seen, while the many events that pass between the widgets inside it are not: a filter on the application runs for every one of those, which made building a page half as slow again. Parameters app ( QGuiApplication ): The application whose windows to watch. Examples >>> handler = WheelZoom () >>> handler . follow ( app )

title: alto.ui.zoom
text: WheelZoom.watch def watch ( window : QWindow | None ) -> None [Source] Zoom when the wheel turns with Ctrl held over a window. Parameters window ( QWindow or None ): The window. None, which is what Qt passes when no window has the focus, does nothing. Examples >>> from PySide6.QtWidgets import QWidget >>> widget = QWidget () >>> widget . show () >>> handler = WheelZoom () >>> handler . watch ( widget . windowHandle ()) >>> handler . watch ( None )

title: alto.ui.zoom
text: WheelZoom.eventFilter def eventFilter ( watched : QObject , event : QEvent , ) -> bool [Source] Take a wheel event with Ctrl held as a zoom, and let every other event through. Parameters watched ( QObject ): The object the event is for. event ( QEvent ): The event. Returns bool : True when the event was a zoom, so that nothing under the pointer scrolls. Examples >>> WheelZoom (). eventFilter ( ... QObject (), QEvent ( QEvent . Type . None_ ) ... ) False

title: alto.updates
text: alto.updates What kind of copy of Alto is running, how it can be updated, and the commands and answers that checking involves. A copy installed with scripts/alto-install.sh is a uv tool install from a git address. The installed package records that address and the commit it was built from, so it can follow the newest release (a tag) or the newest commit on the main branch. A packaged copy (a PyInstaller build) cannot replace itself, so it can only be told that a newer release exists. This module decides and describes; alto.ui.update_flow runs the commands and asks the questions. A packaged copy replaces itself with a downloaded release. What makes that safe is here: a release carries SHA256SUMS and a signature of it ( SHA256SUMS.sig , Ed25519, made with a private key that only the release workflow has), and a copy of Alto trusts only the public keys in UPDATE_PUBLIC_KEYS . It installs a file only if the signature verifies, the signed list names the file, and the file’s hash is the one listed. Examples >>> short ( ... "b6e2091ba08f6b79dcf293d1a77d86f7a812d4fe" ... ) 'b6e2091'

title: alto.updates
text: Source Source ( url : str , commit : str , ref : str = 'HEAD' , ) [Source] Where an installed copy of Alto came from. Attributes url ( str ): The git address it was installed from. commit ( str ): The commit it was built from. ref ( str ): The branch or tag it follows; “HEAD”, the address’s default branch, unless the install named one. Examples >>> Source ( ... "https://github.com/altosaurus/alto.git" , ... commit = "b6e2091" , ... ). ref 'HEAD'

title: alto.updates
text: short def short ( commit : str ) -> str [Source] Shorten a commit id to the seven characters people use for it. Parameters commit ( str ): The full commit id. Returns str : Its first seven characters. Examples >>> short ( ... "b6e2091ba08f6b79dcf293d1a77d86f7a812d4fe" ... ) 'b6e2091'

title: alto.updates
text: parse_direct_url def parse_direct_url ( text : str ) -> Source | None [Source] Read where a package was installed from, out of the direct_url.json that the installer leaves with it. Parameters text ( str ): The contents of the file. Returns Source or None : The git address, the commit and the ref, or None if the package was not installed from a git address (a copy that runs from a source folder has a folder there instead). Examples >>> parse_direct_url ( ... '{"url": "https://example.org/a.git", "vcs_info": {"vcs": ' ... '"git", "commit_id": "abc1234"}}' ... ) Source(url='https://example.org/a.git', commit='abc1234', ref='HEAD') >>> named = ( ... '{"url": "https://x.org/a.git", "vcs_info": {"vcs": ' ... '"git", "commit_id": "abc1234", "requested_revision": ' ... '"dev"}}' ... ) >>> # noinspection PyUnresolvedReferences >>> parse_direct_url ( named ). ref 'dev' >>> parse_direct_url ( ... '{"url": "file:///home/me/alto", "dir_info": {"editable": ' ... 'true}}' ... ) is None True >>> parse_direct_url ( "not json" ) is None True

title: alto.updates
text: installed_source def installed_source () -> Source | None [Source] Say where the Alto that is running was installed from. Returns Source or None : Its git address and commit, or None if it was not installed from a git address. Examples >>> source = installed_source () >>> source is None or len ( ... source . commit ... ) == COMMIT_LENGTH True

title: alto.updates
text: is_tool_install def is_tool_install ( * , prefix : Path | None = None , ) -> bool [Source] Say whether Alto is running from an environment that uv tool made, which is what the install script makes. Parameters prefix ( Path or None, default None ): The environment to look at; the one that is running if None. Keyword-only. Returns bool : True if the environment has the receipt that uv tool install leaves in it. Examples >>> is_tool_install ( prefix = Path ( "/nowhere" )) False

title: alto.updates
text: InstallKind class InstallKind ( Enum ) [Source] How the running copy of Alto got where it is, which decides how it can be updated. Attributes SCRIPT ( InstallKind ): Installed with scripts/alto-install.sh : it can replace itself, from a release or from the main branch. PACKAGE ( InstallKind ): A packaged build (a tarball or the Windows installer): it can only be told that a newer release exists. OTHER ( InstallKind ): Installed from a git address some other way, so there is no uv tool to update it with. SOURCE ( InstallKind ): Run from a source folder, which is updated with git. Examples >>> InstallKind . SCRIPT . name 'SCRIPT'

title: alto.updates
text: is_frozen def is_frozen () -> bool [Source] Say whether Alto is running as a packaged build, made with PyInstaller, rather than from Python. Returns bool : True for a packaged build. Examples >>> is_frozen () False

title: alto.updates
text: install_kind def install_kind ( source : Source | None , * , tool : bool , frozen : bool , ) -> InstallKind [Source] Decide what kind of copy of Alto this is. Parameters source ( Source or None ): Where it was installed from, if it was installed from a git address. tool ( bool ): Whether it runs from an environment that uv tool made. Keyword-only. frozen ( bool ): Whether it is a packaged build. Keyword-only. Returns InstallKind : The kind. Examples >>> here = Source ( ... "https://example.org/a.git" , ... commit = "abc1234" , ... ) >>> install_kind ( ... here , tool = True , frozen = False ... ). name 'SCRIPT' >>> ( ... install_kind ( ... here , tool = False , frozen = False ... ). name , ... install_kind ( ... None , tool = False , frozen = False ... ). name , ... ) ('OTHER', 'SOURCE') >>> install_kind ( ... None , tool = False , frozen = True ... ). name 'PACKAGE'

title: alto.updates
text: cannot_update def cannot_update ( kind : InstallKind ) -> str | None [Source] Say why a kind of copy cannot update itself at all, if it cannot. Parameters kind ( InstallKind ): The kind of copy. Returns str or None : A sentence for a copy run from a source folder or installed some other way; None for one that can be told about updates. Examples >>> ( ... cannot_update ( InstallKind . SOURCE ) ... == SOURCE_FOLDER , ... cannot_update ( InstallKind . OTHER ) ... == NOT_BY_SCRIPT , ... ) (True, True) >>> cannot_update ( ... InstallKind . SCRIPT ... ) is None and cannot_update ( ... InstallKind . PACKAGE ... ) is None True

title: alto.updates
text: find_program def find_program ( name : str , * , home : Path | None = None , ) -> str | None [Source] Find a program to run, also in the places the installers put them, which a program started from the dock may not search. Parameters name ( str ): The program’s name, such as “git” or “uv”. home ( Path or None, default None ): The home folder to look in besides the search path; the user’s own if None. Keyword-only. Returns str or None : Its path, or None if it is nowhere to be found. Examples >>> find_program ( ... "no-such-program-anywhere" ... ) is None True

title: alto.updates
text: check_command def check_command ( source : Source , * , git : str , ) -> tuple [ str , list [ str ]] [Source] Give the command that asks the address Alto came from for the commit at the end of a branch or tag. Parameters source ( Source ): Where the running copy came from. git ( str ): The path of the git program. Keyword-only. Returns tuple of str and list of str : The program and its arguments. Examples >>> check_command ( ... Source ( ... "https://example.org/a.git" , ... commit = "abc1234" , ... ), ... git = "git" , ... ) ('git', ['ls-remote', 'https://example.org/a.git', 'HEAD'])

title: alto.updates
text: install_command def install_command ( source : Source , * , uv : str , tag : str | None = None , ) -> tuple [ str , list [ str ]] [Source] Give the command that installs Alto over the installed copy: a release, or the newest commit of the address. uv tool install --force is used rather than uv tool upgrade , because an upgrade stays on the tag or branch the copy was installed from, and a copy that follows a release must be able to move to the main branch and back. Parameters source ( Source ): Where the running copy came from. uv ( str ): The path of the uv program. Keyword-only. tag ( str or None, default None ): The release to install, such as “v0.1.0”; the address’s default branch if None. Keyword-only. Returns tuple of str and list of str : The program and its arguments. Examples >>> here = Source ( ... "https://example.org/alto.git" , ... commit = "abc1234" , ... ) >>> install_command ( here , uv = "uv" , tag = "v0.1.0" ) ('uv', ['tool', 'install', '--force', 'git+https://example.org/alto.git@v0.1.0']) >>> install_command ( here , uv = "uv" ) ('uv', ['tool', 'install', '--force', 'git+https://example.org/alto.git'])

title: alto.updates
text: parse_ls_remote def parse_ls_remote ( text : str ) -> str | None [Source] Read the commit id out of what git ls-remote printed. Parameters text ( str ): The output: a line for each ref, each a commit id, a tab and the ref’s name. Returns str or None : The commit id on the first line, or None if there is none (the ref does not exist, or git printed an error). Examples >>> parse_ls_remote ( ... "b6e2091ba08f6b79dcf293d1a77d86f7a812d4fe \t HEAD \n " ... ) 'b6e2091ba08f6b79dcf293d1a77d86f7a812d4fe' >>> ( ... parse_ls_remote ( "" ) is None , ... parse_ls_remote ( ... "fatal: repository not found" ... ) ... is None , ... ) (True, True)

title: alto.updates
text: Asset Asset ( name : str , url : str , size : int = 0 , ) [Source] A file of a release: the installer, the tarball, the checksums or their signature. Attributes name ( str ): Its name, such as “alto-0.1.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz”. url ( str ): The address it is downloaded from. size ( int ): Its size in bytes, as GitHub states it; 0 if it does not. Examples >>> Asset ( ... "SHA256SUMS" , ... url = "https://example.org/s" , ... size = 300 , ... ). size 300

title: alto.updates
text: Release Release ( version : str , tag : str , url : str , assets : tuple [ Asset , ...] = field ( default = ()), ) [Source] A release of Alto, as published on GitHub. Attributes version ( str ): Its version, such as “0.1.0”. tag ( str ): The tag it is made from, such as “v0.1.0”. url ( str ): The page where it and its downloads are. assets ( tuple of Asset ): Its files. Examples >>> Release ( ... "0.1.0" , ... tag = "v0.1.0" , ... url = "https://example.org/r" , ... ). version '0.1.0'

title: alto.updates
text: version_key def version_key ( text : str ) -> tuple [ int , ...] | None [Source] Turn a version, with or without the “v” of a tag, into numbers that can be compared. Parameters text ( str ): The version, such as “0.10.2” or “v1.0”. Returns tuple of int or None : Its numbers; None if it is not made only of numbers and dots, as a pre-release such as “1.0.0rc1” is not. Examples >>> version_key ( "v0.10.2" ), version_key ( "1.0" ) ((0, 10, 2), (1, 0)) >>> ( ... version_key ( "1.0.0rc1" ) is None , ... version_key ( "" ) is None , ... version_key ( "unknown" ) is None , ... ) (True, True, True)

title: alto.updates
text: is_newer def is_newer ( candidate : str , * , installed : str , ) -> bool [Source] Say whether one version is newer than another, comparing numbers and not text, so 0.10.0 is newer than 0.9.0. Parameters candidate ( str ): The version that may be newer. installed ( str ): The version to compare it with. Keyword-only. Returns bool : True if the candidate is newer. False if it is the same or older, or if either is not a plain version. Examples >>> ( ... is_newer ( "0.10.0" , installed = "0.9.0" ), ... is_newer ( "v0.1.0" , installed = "0.0.0" ), ... ) (True, True) >>> ( ... is_newer ( "1.0" , installed = "1.0.0" ), ... is_newer ( "0.0.0" , installed = "0.1.0" ), ... ) (False, False) >>> is_newer ( "1.0.0" , installed = "unknown" ) False

title: alto.updates
text: installed_version def installed_version () -> str [Source] Give the version of Alto that is running. Returns str : The installed version, or “unknown” if Alto was not installed as a package. Examples >>> installed_version (). count ( "." ) >= 1 True

title: alto.updates
text: parse_latest_release def parse_latest_release ( text : str ) -> Release | None [Source] Read GitHub’s answer about the latest release. Parameters text ( str ): The JSON that releases/latest answers with. Returns Release or None : The release, or None if the answer is not one, is a draft or a pre-release, or has a tag that is not a plain version. Examples >>> answer = ( ... '{"tag_name": "v0.1.0", "html_url": ' ... '"https://example.org/r", "draft": false, "prerelease": ' ... 'false}' ... ) >>> parse_latest_release ( answer ) Release(version='0.1.0', tag='v0.1.0', url='https://example.org/r', assets=()) >>> parse_latest_release ( ... answer . replace ( ... '"prerelease": false' , ... '"prerelease": true' , ... ) ... ) is None True >>> parse_latest_release ( "not json" ) is None True

title: alto.updates
text: release_answer def release_answer ( status : int , * , text : str , ) -> Release | str [Source] Make sense of what came back when the latest release was asked for. Parameters status ( int ): The HTTP status, or 0 if no answer came at all. text ( str ): The body of the answer, or the reason there was none. Keyword-only. Returns Release or str : The release, or a sentence that says why there is none to offer. Examples >>> release_answer ( 404 , text = "" ) == NO_RELEASE True >>> release_answer ( ... 0 , text = "Name or service not known" ... ) 'Alto could not reach GitHub: Name or service not known' >>> release_answer ( ... 403 , text = "rate limit exceeded" ... ) 'GitHub answered with an error (403): rate limit exceeded'

title: alto.updates
text: fetch_text def fetch_text ( url : str , * , seconds : int , ) -> tuple [ int , str ] [Source] Fetch a web address, waiting at most a number of seconds. It blocks, so the interface runs it on another thread. Parameters url ( str ): The address. seconds ( int ): How long to wait for the server. Keyword-only. Returns tuple of int and str : The HTTP status and the body. If the server was not reached, 0 and the reason. Examples >>> fetch_text ( ... "http://127.0.0.1:9/" , seconds = 2 ... )[ 0 ] # nothing listens there 0

title: alto.updates
text: ssl_context def ssl_context () -> ssl . SSLContext [Source] Make the settings for a secure connection, trusting the certificate authorities that come with Alto. A packaged copy cannot count on the system’s: the Python inside it may look for them where the computer it was built on keeps them, and a connection would then fail on a distribution that keeps them somewhere else. Returns ssl.SSLContext : A context that checks the server’s certificate and name against certifi’s list. Examples >>> ( ... ssl_context (). verify_mode ... == ssl . CERT_REQUIRED , ... len ( ssl_context (). get_ca_certs ()) > 100 , ... ) (True, True)

title: alto.updates
text: platform_asset_name def platform_asset_name ( version : str , * , system : str , machine : str , ) -> str | None [Source] Give the name of the file that updates a packaged copy on this system, as the release workflow names it. Parameters version ( str ): The version, such as “0.1.0”. Keyword-only after the first. system ( str ): The operating system, as platform.system() says it (“Linux”, “Windows”). Keyword-only. machine ( str ): The processor, as platform.machine() says it (“x86_64”, “AMD64”). Keyword-only. Returns str or None : The name, or None if there is no package for this system. Examples >>> platform_asset_name ( ... "0.1.0" , ... system = "Linux" , ... machine = "x86_64" , ... ) 'alto-0.1.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz' >>> platform_asset_name ( ... "0.1.0" , ... system = "Windows" , ... machine = "AMD64" , ... ) 'alto-0.1.0-windows-x64-setup.exe' >>> platform_asset_name ( ... "0.1.0" , ... system = "Linux" , ... machine = "aarch64" , ... ) is None True

title: alto.updates
text: find_asset def find_asset ( release : Release , * , name : str , base : str = DOWNLOAD_BASE , ) -> Asset | None [Source] Find a file of a release by its name, if it is at the address where a release keeps its files. Parameters release ( Release ): The release. name ( str ): The file’s name. Keyword-only. base ( str, default DOWNLOAD_BASE ): What the address must start with. Keyword-only. Returns Asset or None : The file, or None if the release has none by that name or it is somewhere else. Examples >>> files = ( ... Asset ( "a" , url = DOWNLOAD_BASE + "v1/a" ), ... Asset ( "b" , url = "https://example.org/b" ), ... ) >>> found = find_asset ( ... Release ( ... "1" , tag = "v1" , url = "" , assets = files ... ), ... name = "a" , ... ) >>> found . name if found else None 'a' >>> find_asset ( ... Release ( ... "1" , tag = "v1" , url = "" , assets = files ... ), ... name = "b" , ... ) is None True

title: alto.updates
text: parse_checksums def parse_checksums ( text : str ) -> dict [ str , str ] [Source] Read a SHA256SUMS file: a line for each file, with its SHA-256 hash and its name. Parameters text ( str ): The file’s contents, as sha256sum writes them. Returns dict of str to str : The hash of each named file, in lower case. Lines that are not a hash and a plain file name are left out. Examples >>> entry = ( ... "ab" * 32 ... + " alto-0.1.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz" ... ) >>> parse_checksums ( ... entry ... + " \n not a line \n " ... + "cd" * 32 ... + " ../evil" ... ) {'alto-0.1.0-linux-x86_64.tar.gz': 'abababababababababababababababababababababababababababababababab'}

title: alto.updates
text: verify_signature def verify_signature ( data : bytes , * , signature : str , keys : tuple [ str , ...], ) -> bool [Source] Say whether an Ed25519 signature of some data was made with one of the keys. Parameters data ( bytes ): What was signed. signature ( str ): The signature, base64. Keyword-only. keys ( tuple of str ): The public keys (base64) that are trusted. Keyword-only. Returns bool : True only if the signature is well formed and one of the keys made it. No key, a key that is not a key, and a signature that is not one all give False. Examples >>> from nacl.signing import SigningKey >>> pair = SigningKey . generate () >>> public = base64 . b64encode ( ... bytes ( pair . verify_key ) ... ). decode () >>> signed = base64 . b64encode ( ... pair . sign ( b "the list" ). signature ... ). decode () >>> verify_signature ( ... b "the list" , ... signature = signed , ... keys = ( public ,), ... ) True >>> verify_signature ( ... b "another list" , ... signature = signed , ... keys = ( public ,), ... ) False >>> verify_signature ( ... b "the list" , signature = signed , keys = () ... ) False

title: alto.updates
text: self_check def self_check () -> list [ str ] [Source] Check, without any network, that what a copy needs to check an update is there and works. It is what alto --self-test runs, so that the build can tell that a packaged copy carries the certificate list and the signature library (which PyInstaller must be told about), and that the keys in the code are keys. Returns list of str : What is wrong, one sentence each; empty if all is well. Examples >>> self_check () []

title: API reference
text: API reference Every public module, class and function in Alto, with its signature and docstring. Names that begin with an underscore are internal and are left out. The pages are written from the docstrings by scripts/api_docs.py , so they match the code.

title: API reference
text: alto Alto: a music theory trainer that learns what you find hard and asks it more often. Module What it is alto.anki_export Write portable Anki decks from Alto questions and optional calendar review dates. alto.audio Note playback: recorded instrument samples (University of Iowa), with pitch-shifting for missing notes. alto.circle_schemes The color schemes of the circle of fifths: the presets, and the schemes a user makes. alto.instrument_info What is known about each instrument’s recordings, for the summary shown in the instrument settings. alto.instrument_packs Media and fingerboard geometry supplied by third-party instrument packs. alto.location Where Alto keeps its practice history and its settings, and how to keep them somewhere else with ALTO_HOME . alto.notation_excerpts Public-domain piano excerpts available for offline notation practice. alto.notation_terms Notation Identification terms, grouped by subject with their score placement and SMuFL code points. alto.plugin_registry Install registered instrument packs from the latest release in their public GitHub repositories. alto.selfupdate Replacing a packaged copy of Alto with a newer release: whether it can, getting the update, checking it, and handing over. alto.settings User settings. Pure Python (no Qt); persistence lives in ui/exercise_settings.py. alto.terms Glossary entries that an installed plugin supplies, kept apart from the built-in ones. alto.updates What kind of copy of Alto is running, how it can be updated, and the commands and answers that checking involves.

title: API reference
text: alto.exercises The exercises and the framework they are built on. Module What it is alto.exercises.base Exercise framework. Register a ChoiceExercise for button answers or an Exercise for construction tasks. alto.exercises.library The exercises: note names, intervals, key signatures, scales, chords, arpeggios, keyboard keys and note construction. alto.exercises.packs Load third-party instrument packs from ZIP archives and authoring folders. alto.exercises.rhythm_equations Build balanced rhythm equations with exact operator counts.

title: API reference
text: alto.learning Spaced repetition: who is learning (profiles), what they answered (a database) and what to ask next. Module What it is alto.learning.backup Backup files: everything Alto keeps, in one file that can be read back into a clean install. Pure Python (no Qt). alto.learning.calendar Daily exercise queues for SM-2 and FSRS. alto.learning.database The SQLite store: profiles, every answer given, and what is known about each question. Pure Python (no Qt). alto.learning.grading Answer-button intervals for Anki’s default SM-2 and FSRS-6 deck settings. alto.learning.learner Ties the profile, the database and the scheduler together for the exercise screen. alto.learning.response_times Rolling response times for one learner and exercise. alto.learning.scheduler How a question’s history turns into how soon it comes back. Pure Python, no database and no Qt. alto.learning.stats Numbers and series for the statistics screen, worked out from the answers in the database. Pure Python, no Qt.

title: API reference
text: alto.lessons The lessons: guided walks through a topic, with small exercises along the way. Module What it is alto.lessons.base What a lesson is made of: steps, and the small tasks inside them. alto.lessons.circle_of_fifths The lesson on the circle of fifths, taught from nothing. alto.lessons.clef_basics The lesson on clefs, taught from nothing. alto.lessons.duration A first rhythm lesson on counting the length of sound and silence. alto.lessons.intervals A guided introduction to naming intervals on the staff and keyboard. alto.lessons.key_signatures A guided lesson on reading and writing key signatures. alto.lessons.packs Turn the lessons that an instrument plugin declares into Lesson s that Alto lists and shows. alto.lessons.pitches_and_notes A first lesson connecting a sound, a piano key, and a written note. alto.lessons.scale_identification Reading scales and recognizing their interval patterns.

Module What it is alto.theory.fifths The circle of fifths: the twelve keys in order, each major with its relative minor. alto.theory.key_signatures Staff positions for written key signatures. alto.theory.pitch Pitches and intervals, spelled correctly (C# is not Db). alto.theory.scales Scales, modes, key signatures and chords, built from spelled intervals.

Module What it is alto.ui.anki_exporter Modeless Anki deck exporter using Alto’s exercise controls and music engraving. alto.ui.answer_bank A responsive, scrollable grid for large banks of answer buttons. alto.ui.app_settings The application-wide settings dialog. alto.ui.background Run slow work, such as a download, on another thread, and hear how it went on the window’s thread. alto.ui.backup_flow Exporting a backup and importing one: the file dialogs, the questions asked, and the safety copy made before anything is replaced. alto.ui.charts Small charts drawn with QPainter, in the application’s theme colors. alto.ui.circle The circle of fifths: twelve wedges, the major keys on the outside and their relative minors on the inside. alto.ui.circle_colors The pages of the circle of fifths settings that choose its colors: a grid of schemes to pick from, and an editor to make one. alto.ui.colors Mixing colors. title: Your data
text: Your data Everything Alto stores is on your own computer. Alto has no accounts, no sync and no analytics. Your name is only a label for a profile in a local file. On supported installations Alto contacts GitHub to check for releases. You can turn off daily checks in Settings → Updates .

title: Your data
text: Where it is Your practice history, profiles included, is one SQLite file named alto.db : System Location Linux ~/.local/share/Alto/alto.db macOS ~/Library/Application Support/Alto/alto.db Windows C:\Users\<you>\AppData\Roaming\Alto\alto.db To keep a second copy of Alto apart, for example one you are changing while you use the installed one to practice, set ALTO_HOME to a folder. Alto then keeps its history in data/alto.db there and its settings in config/ , and leaves the usual places alone. scripts/dev.sh starts Alto from a clone this way, in ~/.alto-dev . Your settings (theme, notation style, keyboard style, instrument, exercise options and the last profile you used) are stored separately by Qt, in your usual configuration location.

title: Your data
text: What the file contains Table Holds profiles Each profile’s name, creation time, scheduler, self-grading preference, and response-time grading thresholds. attempts One row for every answer: the profile, exercise, question, your answer, whether it was right, the attempt number, how long it took and when. items What is known about each question: its strain, how often it was answered and missed, its typical time, when it was last seen, and the question itself so it can be asked again. practice_cards Introduced card identities, the questions themselves, and the local date each was introduced in scheduled practice. review_schedules The next review time and algorithm state for each card studied with SM-2 or FSRS. practice_limits Daily allowances for each profile and exercise. daily_reviews Completed calendar reviews by profile, exercise, and day. Because it is a normal SQLite file, you can open it with any SQLite tool if you want to run your own queries. Close Alto first. Alto’s own database browser is read-only.

title: Your data
text: Anki decks Open ☰ → Tools → Anki Exporter to turn Alto exercises into flashcards you can study in Anki. You can keep practicing in Alto while the exporter is open.

title: Your data
text: Deck selection and preview Check the exercises you want to export. Checking a category selects every exercise in it. Choose All exercises to select the whole list. Clicking an exercise name displays a sample card, even if its box is unchecked. Front shows the question and its illustration, when there is one. Back adds the answer and explanation. The settings button in the upper right opens the highlighted exercise’s options. These start with your current practice settings. Changes you make here apply only to the export. For example, you can narrow an Interval Identification deck to thirds and sixths and keep practicing all intervals in Alto. Exercises with a fixed set of cards export every matching card. Exercises that generate a sample of questions export each distinct card in that sample.

title: Your data
text: Review scheduling By default, exported cards start as new in Anki. If your Alto profile uses SM-2 or FSRS, check Include scheduling to carry over due dates and intervals for matching cards you’ve already reviewed. The exporter uses the schedule from when you opened the window. Cards you haven’t studied start as new.

title: Your data
text: Export summary and file Choose Export… to see how many cards match. The table groups decks by exercise type. Each group starts expanded. A row marked No cards is skipped. The total below the table is the number of cards in the package. Use Browse… to choose a destination or enter a path in File name . A filename alone saves to your home directory. The suggested name is alto.apkg for multiple exercises or, for a single exercise, a name such as alto - Interval Identification.apkg . Click Export to save. A spinner marks the deck being prepared and a green check marks each finished deck. The progress bar tracks the whole package, including the final save. To stop, click Cancel and confirm. Canceling preserves any existing file at the destination. When the status reads Export successful , click Close to return to the exporter.

title: Your data
text: Import into Anki Open the saved .apkg file in Anki. If you exported schedules, enable Import any learning progress during import to keep the review dates and intervals. Anki schedules subsequent reviews independently of Alto. A package containing one nonempty deck places it directly under Alto . With several nonempty decks, Anki groups them by Alto’s exercise categories, for example Alto → Intervals → Interval Identification and Alto → Notation → Note Identification . Exporting the same question again preserves its card identity.

title: Your data
text: Backing up and restoring Open the ☰ menu and choose Tools → Export backup… to save everything Alto keeps to one file: all the profiles, every answer and the record of each question, and every setting (the theme, the notation and keyboard styles, the instrument, each exercise’s options and the profile you used last). Choose Tools → Import backup… to read one back. Importing replaces everything with the backup, so on a clean install, or on another computer, Alto comes up exactly as it was when the backup was made: same profiles, same history, same settings, and the same profile open. Nothing is merged. What is there before the import is gone from the app, so Alto saves a backup of it first, next to alto.db in a file named alto-before-import-<date and time>.altobackup . If you imported the wrong file, import that one to put everything back. A backup file ends in .altobackup . It is a zip file holding the database, the settings and a note of which version of Alto made it, with a checksum of each part. Before anything is changed, Alto checks the file all the way through. A file that is damaged, is not an Alto backup, or was made by a newer version of Alto is refused with an explanation, and nothing changes. A backup from an older version is brought up to date as it is imported. A backup contains your whole practice history, so keep it as private as the history itself. To move to another computer: install Alto there, start it once (it asks for a first profile), then import the backup.

title: Your data
text: Copying the files by hand Back up the history only: close Alto and copy alto.db somewhere safe. Copy it back to restore it. This leaves out the settings; Export backup… includes them. Move the history to another computer: copy the file to the same location there. Start over: close Alto and delete alto.db . The next launch asks for a new profile and starts with an empty history.

title: Application launch
text: Application launch The first window you see depends on who has used Alto before. On a new installation, Alto asks for a name. On the next launch, it can open directly to the exercise catalog. To see where those paths diverge, open alto/__main__.py in your editor and follow one launch through main() . Module source on GitHub

title: Application launch
section: A first run from the terminal
text: A first run from the terminal From the repository root, with Alto’s Python environment active, run these commands in a Linux shell. Keep the terminal open for the second launch later in the tutorial. practice_dir = $( mktemp -d ) ALTO_HOME = " $practice_dir " python -m alto ALTO_HOME gives this run its own settings and practice history. Leave the Welcome to Alto dialog open for a moment. Python has already executed much of main() , but it hasn’t reached the line that creates the main window.

title: Application launch
text: The entry point Start reading at the bottom of alto/__main__.py . With python -m alto , Python finds the package’s __main__.py and executes it under the name __main__ . That makes this condition true: if __name__ == "__main__" : raise SystemExit ( main ()) Python calls main() first. When it returns, SystemExit passes its result back to the operating system as the process exit code. Importing alto.__main__ from a test skips this block, so the test can decide when to call main() . The other launchers lead to the same function. The installed alto command gets its entry point from alto = "alto.__main__:main" in pyproject.toml . The packaged desktop application starts in packaging/launcher.py , which imports and calls main() .

title: Application launch
text: The Qt application At the top of main() , two command-line options can finish the run early. python -m alto --version reports the installed version. --self-test checks the update prerequisites and returns 0 on success or 1 on failure. Both branches return before the first Qt application object is created. For the interactive run, follow these lines: app = QApplication ( sys . argv ) app . setApplicationName ( "Alto" ) app . setApplicationDisplayName ( "Alto - Music Theory" if alto_home () is None else "Alto (dev) - Music Theory" ) apply_theme ( saved_theme ()) app is the Qt object shared by all of Alto’s windows. Applying the theme here lets even the first profile dialog use the saved colors. The next two calls set the desktop file name and load the window icon from alto/assets/icon.svg . At this point Qt is configured, but Alto still needs a profile.

title: Application launch
text: The profile decision db = Database ( database_path ()) profile = startup_profile ( db ) if profile is None : return 0 For this run, database_path() resolves to data/alto.db inside the temporary directory. Database opens SQLite and creates the tables for a new database. startup_profile(db) looks up the available profiles. An empty table leads to the welcome dialog you left open. Database API · Profile selection code 1 Name field and Create profile button · ProfileDialog Type Ada and select Create profile . ProfileDialog saves the name and accepts the dialog. startup_profile() remembers the selection and returns the profile to main() . Had you selected Close , it would have returned None and the return 0 above would have ended the run. With existing profiles, Alto first tries the remembered profile, then uses the sole profile if there is only one. When several profiles exist and there is no remembered match, the same dialog class displays a list. Its modal exec() processes clicks while main() waits for a selection. 1 Saved profile list · ProfileDialog

title: Application launch
text: Construction of the main window learner = Learner ( db , profile = profile ) window = MainWindow ( learner ) The first line pairs Ada’s profile with the open database. An exercise can now ask the learner for a question or record an answer against that profile. The second line passes the same learner into the window. To find the code behind the screen you now see, step into MainWindow.__init__() in alto/ui/main_window.py . It stores the learner, sets the starting size, restores saved window geometry if available, and calls _build() . Learner API · MainWindow API Inside _build() , look for these lines: self . stack = QStackedWidget () self . home = HomePage ( REGISTRY ) # start screen with a button for every exercise self . home . exercise_chosen . connect ( self . open_exercise ) self . home . lesson_chosen . connect ( self . open_lessons ) self . home . resume_button . clicked . connect ( self . _back_from_topbar ) self . stack . addWidget ( self . home ) The stack holds pages that share the same area of the window. Its first page is the catalog. In the screenshot, select the Note Identification tile to inspect ExerciseCard , or select the catalog region to inspect HomePage , which arranges those cards. The toolbar and search field belong to the surrounding MainWindow . 1 2 3 4 Exercise and lesson switch · SegmentedControl Search field · MainWindow Note Identification tile · ExerciseCard Exercise catalog · HomePage

title: Application launch
section: The event loop and the first click
text: The event loop and the first click Back in __main__.py , the last four statements of main() are: app . learner = learner app . main_window = window window . show () return app . exec () The first two assignments keep references to the active learner and window on the application. window.show() makes the constructed window visible. app.exec() runs Qt’s main event loop, which delivers input and paint events. main() stays at that call while you use Alto. In the running app, click Note Identification . The catalog emits exercise_chosen with the exercise class. The connection you saw in _build() sends it to MainWindow.open_exercise() , which opens an ExerciseView in the stack. The toolbar stays in place as the catalog gives way to the staff and answer buttons. ExerciseView API 1 2 3 Exercise list · MainWindow Notated question · StaffWidget Answer buttons · ExerciseView Close the window. Qt’s event loop returns, and its exit code travels back through main() to the terminal. In the same shell, run ALTO_HOME="$practice_dir" python -m alto again. This time you should go straight to the catalog. To watch the difference in a debugger, set a breakpoint on profile = startup_profile(db) and step over it. On the second launch, the call returns Ada’s profile without waiting for a dialog.

title: Database
text: Database Alto keeps practice history for all local profiles in one SQLite file. At launch, Database(database_path()) opens alto.db in the application data directory, or $ALTO_HOME/data/alto.db when a development directory is set. A new database uses schema version 7, recorded in SQLite’s PRAGMA user_version . Application launch A single question can produce several answers. Suppose Ada answers a note question incorrectly after three seconds, then correctly one second later. Alto appends two rows to attempts , with durations of 3,000 and 1,000 milliseconds. It maintains one row in items for Ada and that question. After this first showing, the row records one showing, one wrong attempt, zero first-try successes, and 3,000 milliseconds of first-answer time. The attempt log preserves the sequence. The item row gives the scheduler a summary it can use the next time Ada practices.

title: Database
text: Database access Connection and SQL. alto.learning.database.Database uses Python’s standard sqlite3 module. It opens a connection, enables foreign keys, and issues SQL with bound parameters. Its row factory, sqlite3.Row , lets callers read columns by name. Some methods return Profile or ItemRecord dataclasses. Calling Database() without a path creates an in-memory database, which is useful for trying queries in a Python shell. Database API Practice and replay. Learner.record() appends the attempt, reads the old item summary, and inserts or updates the item under its composite key. Learner.pick() reads summaries and uses the scheduler to choose among fresh questions and saved questions that match the exercise settings. Python’s json module encodes and decodes the saved question. Learner API The database browser. The Answers , Questions , and Profiles tabs present rows from attempts , items , and profiles , respectively. DatabasePage requests rows through Database . Its Qt table model, RowsModel , supplies display values, and a QSortFilterProxyModel handles sorting and filtering. Database browser API

title: Database
text: Entity–relationship diagram Each attempt and each item belongs to exactly one profile. A profile may have zero or more of either, and deleting it cascades to both tables. The solid lines show those foreign keys. The dashed line shows how Alto looks up an item summary for an attempt. Many attempts can match the same summary, but an attempt can match at most one because the join uses the item’s full primary key. Select a table to jump to its dictionary. PK = primary key. FK = foreign key. 0..* = zero or more rows.

title: Database
text: Data dictionary The tables below follow the column order in alto/learning/database.py . The introduction date is optional for cards first practiced with ASRS. SQLite supplies the integer primary keys when Alto inserts a profile or an attempt. The four item counters have explicit defaults of zero. Times ending in _at , along with last_seen , are Unix timestamps in seconds. Durations use milliseconds.

title: Database
text: Profiles One row per local practice profile. Column SQLite type Key or default Meaning id INTEGER Primary key Profile identifier used by both history tables. name TEXT Unique, COLLATE NOCASE Display name. Alto trims and collapses whitespace before insertion. SQLite’s case-insensitive comparison treats names such as Ada and ada as duplicates. created_at REAL   Time the profile was created. scheduler TEXT Default Alto The profile’s selected question scheduler. ASRS retains its original database identifier, Alto . self_grading INTEGER Default 0 Whether this profile rates correct answers in SM-2 and FSRS. easy_percent INTEGER Default 15 Fastest share of correct first answers graded Easy, in percent. hard_percent INTEGER Default 15 Slowest share graded Hard, in percent.

title: Database
text: Attempts One row per submitted answer, including each retry. The attempts_by_item index covers (profile_id, exercise, item_key) . The browser uses these three columns in a left join to obtain the question payload when an item summary exists. The attempts_by_time index covers (profile_id, answered_at) , for a profile’s answers since a date, which the statistics read. It is created when the database opens rather than in a schema version, since an index changes no data and an older Alto can still open the file. Column SQLite type Key or default Meaning id INTEGER Primary key Identifier for this submission. profile_id INTEGER Foreign key → profiles.id Profile that submitted the answer. exercise TEXT   Python class name of the exercise, such as NoteNames . item_key TEXT   Stable 20-character hexadecimal identifier returned by Question.item_key() . Reordering the answer buttons preserves this identifier. attempt_no INTEGER   Submission number within this showing of the question, starting at 1. answer TEXT   The answer the learner submitted. correct INTEGER   Alto writes 1 for a correct answer and 0 for an incorrect answer. duration_ms INTEGER   Elapsed time from presentation to the first answer, or from the preceding answer to a retry. answered_at REAL   Time the answer was submitted. timing_valid INTEGER Default 1 Set to zero when the exercise was hidden or Alto lost focus during the question. Older attempts retain their recorded times.

title: Database
text: Items One row per distinct question practiced by a particular profile within an exercise. The first three columns together form the primary key. They also identify the submissions contributing to this summary. SQLite enforces the foreign key to profiles . Alto maintains the correspondence with attempts when it records an answer. Column SQLite type Key or default Meaning profile_id INTEGER Primary key (1), foreign key → profiles.id Profile whose history this row summarizes. exercise TEXT Primary key (2) Exercise class name, as in attempts.exercise . item_key TEXT Primary key (3) Question identifier, as in attempts.item_key . strain REAL   Scheduler score updated after each submission. A higher value gives the question more weight in later practice. seen INTEGER Default 0 Showings for which a first answer was submitted. A retry leaves this count unchanged. first_try_right INTEGER Default 0 Showings answered correctly on the first attempt. wrong_attempts INTEGER Default 0 Incorrect submissions across all showings, including retries. total_first_ms INTEGER Default 0 Sum of first-answer durations across showings, in milliseconds. last_seen REAL   Time of the most recent submission for this item, including a retry. signature TEXT   Identifier returned by settings_signature() for the most recently recorded exercise settings. Used to find eligible replay candidates. payload TEXT   JSON from Question.to_dict() for the most recently recorded question. Alto uses it for replay and answer previews.

title: Database
text: Practice cards Each row identifies a calendar practice card. Version 6 removes adaptive-only entries from this table and retains their answer history in items and attempts . Column SQLite type Meaning profile_id , exercise , item_key INTEGER, TEXT, TEXT Composite primary key. Deleting the profile removes its cards. signature , payload TEXT, TEXT Exercise settings and playable question at introduction. introduced_on TEXT Local date of a calendar introduction. May be empty for scheduled cards imported by older versions. pending_new INTEGER 1 until the first answer to a new introduction, then 0.

title: Database
text: Review schedules A practice card can have a separate schedule for SM-2 and FSRS. On entry to a calendar scheduler, missing schedules are initialized from the other calendar scheduler for that profile. The inherited row preserves the due timestamp and last grade, with the state translated for its new scheduler. Existing schedules resume independently. Column SQLite type Meaning profile_id , exercise , item_key INTEGER, TEXT, TEXT Composite foreign key referencing the practice card, with cascading deletion. scheduler TEXT Together with the card identity, this forms the primary key. due REAL Unix timestamp of the next review. state TEXT Automatic SM-2 stores repetitions, interval and ease. Self-graded SM-2 also stores the learning phase, step and scheduled delay. FSRS stores its serialized card. last_rating INTEGER The most recent grade (1 Again, 2 Hard, 3 Good, 4 Easy). Again marks a missed card for the red counter.

title: Database
text: Practice limits Column Type Meaning profile_id INTEGER Owning profile. Part of the primary key with exercise . exercise TEXT Exercise class name, or an empty string for the profile defaults. new_cards INTEGER Daily new-card allowance. Zero pauses introductions, −1 allows unlimited introductions, and NULL inherits the default. reviews INTEGER Daily review allowance. Zero pauses reviews, −1 allows unlimited reviews, and NULL inherits the default.

title: Database
text: Daily reviews Column Type Meaning profile_id INTEGER Owning profile. exercise TEXT Exercise class name. day TEXT Local date. Together with profile and exercise, identifies the row. completed INTEGER Reviews graded that day across SM-2 and FSRS.

title: Development environment
text: Development environment Use uv to create a Python environment for your checkout of Alto. It installs Alto in editable mode, so the next time you run it, your Python changes take effect.

title: Development environment
text: Source checkout You’ll need Git and uv. If you’re installing uv for the first time, follow the instructions for your operating system, then open a new terminal and run uv --version . uv installation instructions Clone Alto and enter the repository. If you already have a checkout, open a terminal in the folder that contains pyproject.toml . git clone https://github.com/altosaurus/alto.git cd alto

title: Development environment
text: Project environment From the repository root, create .venv and install Alto with its development tools, including pytest, Ruff, and pre-commit. uv sync --locked --extra dev --python 3.14 Alto requires Python 3.11 or newer. This command uses Python 3.14 and lets uv download it if needed. The --locked flag checks that uv.lock matches pyproject.toml and installs the recorded versions. Run the same command after pulling dependency changes.

title: Development environment
text: Shell activation Activate the environment so that python and the developer tools in this terminal use Alto’s .venv . Repeat this step when you open a new terminal. Linux or macOS (Bash or Zsh) source .venv/bin/activate Windows (PowerShell) . \.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

title: Development environment
text: Setup check Print Alto’s version and run the music theory tests. The first command prints Alto followed by its version and exits. The second should report passing tests. python -m alto --version python -m pytest -q tests/test_theory.py If you’ll be contributing changes, run pre-commit install once in this checkout to enable the repository’s Git hooks. Keep the environment active for the Application launch walkthrough .

title: Exercise view
text: Exercise view Open Note Identification from the exercise catalog. You’ll follow one written note from the exercise that chooses it to the button that grades it. Then you’ll turn on Octave and watch the same view switch to a two-part answer. For the first pass, open the Exercise settings gear, choose Note names → Letters (C D E) , and leave Octave off. 1 2 3 Exercise list · MainWindow Notated question · StaffWidget Answer buttons · ExerciseView

title: Exercise view
text: The first question Start in MainWindow.open_exercise() . On the first visit, the selected tile supplies the exercise class, NoteNames . The window constructs ExerciseView(cls(), learner=self.learner) . The view builds its staff, controls, and settings pane, then calls next_question() . MainWindow.open_exercise · ExerciseView.next_question Inside next_question() , follow q = self._pick_question() . With a profile open, this calls Learner.pick() . The profile’s scheduler decides which eligible question to show, so a question can be a review of a note the learner has seen before. To trace a freshly generated note, follow ChoiceExercise.generate() into NoteNames.make_question() . It chooses a clef, key signature, and note value from the enabled settings, then draws a pitch within that clef’s range. NoteNames._question_for() turns that pitch into a Question with both the notation and the accepted answer. Learner.pick · NoteNames.make_question To see how that one object drives the screen, put a breakpoint on self.question = q in alto/ui/exercise_view.py . Inspect these expressions in your debugger: str ( q . staff [ 0 ][ 0 ]) # The written pitch, for example "C4" q . clef , q . key # How to draw and read the staff q . choices , q . answer # The button labels and the expected answer q . octaves # None while Octave is off For middle C with letter names, q.answer is "C" . Continue through next_question() to self.staff.show_notes(...) , which draws the question, then to the loop over q.choices , which creates the buttons. The view also clears the previous attempt count and starts the response timer. Question fields

title: Exercise view
section: An answer from click to feedback
text: An answer from click to feedback Set a breakpoint in ExerciseView.submit() and click the name of the note you see. The button passes its choice string to submit() , which calls q.check(choice) . For the middle C example, clicking C succeeds. The staff drawing has already done its job by this point. The comparison uses the answer stored in the question. ExerciseView.submit · Question.check Step into _record() . It increments the attempt number and passes the question, submitted answer, correctness, and elapsed time to Learner.record() for the active profile. Every graded attempt goes into the history. Only the first attempt on this showing counts toward the view’s score and streak. Learner.record A correct answer reaches _finish_answer() , which marks it answered and plays the note when sound is on. Try a wrong button on another question. It flashes red, and _after_miss() consults the practice mode. In ordinary ASRS or ARTS practice you can try another button on the same note. With SM-2 or FSRS, the scheduler brings the missed card back for review. Practice modes

title: Exercise view
text: A two-part answer Open the gear and turn on Octave while a note is on screen. Watch for a new question and a second row of buttons. Here’s what happens between the switch and the next answer: NoteNameSettingsPanel receives the toggle. Its inherited _octave_toggled() in alto/ui/settings_menu.py sets cfg.require_octave , saves the settings, and emits changed . The view connected this signal to next_question() when it built the pane. Inspect q.answer and q.octaves at the same breakpoint as before. For a question showing middle C, the expected answer is now "C4" . The exercise fills q.octaves from the enabled clefs’ pitch ranges. The view sees that second set of choices and wires both rows to _pick() . Select the octave first. The button stays selected and the score stays put. Now select the note name. Once both parts are present, _submit_pair() combines them in name–octave order and checks the result. A correct pair goes through submit() . A wrong pair records one failed attempt and flashes both selections. NoteNameSettingsPanel

title: Exercise view
text: Question material and feedback settings Change in Exercise settings What to observe Under Clefs , leave only Bass selected. The replacement question uses the bass clef. New pitches come from its configured Range . With Octave on, the offered octaves come from that range too. Under Buttons , choose Limited and reduce Button count . ChoiceExercise.limit_buttons() samples the other choices while keeping the correct answer available. With Octave on, the limit applies separately to names and octaves. Under Next Question , choose Wait before answering. The current question stays in place when you change this setting. On a correct answer, _finish_answer() reads the saved mode. Wait leaves Next for you to press, After Animation advances when feedback finishes, and Immediately advances while the answer audio can continue. With calendar self-grading enabled, you choose a rating to advance. If the wrong notes are being asked, inspect the settings and the Question returned by _pick_question() . If that object is right but the wrong controls appear, follow next_question() . If the view accepts an unexpected answer, inspect the choice passed to q.check() . ChoiceExercise.limit_buttons

title: UI style guide
text: Release comparison Open the same screen at the same window size, theme, and display scale. Select a reference image to view it at its original dimensions. Compare solid pixels inside a surface or along a straight border. Rounded corners and glyph edges contain intermediate colors. For a quick check, use the 1100 × 720 exercise catalog . Measured from the top-left of either PNG, pixel (10, 10) is the window and (85, 65) is the search fill. Sample the top tile outline and the face just below it at (200, 109) and (200, 110) in Light, or (200, 106) and (200, 107) in Dark. Match these to the component table. With Alto set to System , switch the desktop from light to dark and back while a lesson tile and the search field are visible. Check the tile face, border, musical glyph, toolbar icons, and search outline after each switch. Repeat with search focused and text entered. Its accent outline, text, and focus should survive the switch. Keep release-candidate captures in a separate directory. On a GNOME Wayland session, run QT_QPA_PLATFORM=wayland .venv/bin/python scripts/screenshots.py --require-native-theme --only home lesson-tiles stats --out /tmp/alto-candidate . This option stops the capture if Qt cannot supply the requested mode. The reference PNGs live in docs/assets/ui-reference/v0.0.2/ , outside the regular screenshot refresh. title: For developers
text: For developers Alto is a Python application using PySide6. The source is at github.com/altosaurus/alto . This page is the quick reference: commands, tooling and the short recipes. Resources explains how the program works and the ideas underneath it (audio, notation, spaced repetition, styling, animation), with reading lists.

title: For developers
text: Layout Folder What is in it alto/theory/ The music theory engine: spelled notes, intervals, scales and chords. Pure Python, no Qt. alto/exercises/ The exercises, the Question and Exercise base classes, and registration of installed instrument packs. alto/learning/ Profiles, the SQLite database, the scheduler and the statistics calculations. No Qt. alto/ui/ The Qt widgets: main window, staff drawing, exercise screen, charts, settings and the database page. alto/assets/ Bundled music fonts and instrument recordings. tests/ The test suite. The theory, exercise generation, and learning code can be tested without a display. The pack loader uses Qt’s image reader to check each supplied picture against its original dimensions. Plugin API

title: For developers
text: Running the tests pip install -e ".[dev]" pytest -n auto # the whole suite, on every core at once pytest tests/test_audio.py # one file, in one process -n auto (from pytest-xdist) runs the tests in one process per core, which takes the suite from minutes to under a minute. Leave it out when running a few tests, where starting the processes would take longer than the tests. sh scripts/run-tests.sh runs the suite the way the pre-push hook and GitHub do: everything but the performance budgets, on every core. The budgets time real operations, so they run in the Budgets workflow instead (see below). Set ALTO_TEST_WORKERS to use a different number of processes. Two checks keep the suite fast as it grows. A test that takes longer than 8 seconds fails ( TEST_TIME_LIMIT in tests/conftest.py ) unless it is marked @pytest.mark.slow , for a thorough check that is worth the time. And tests/test_test_speed.py fails when a test file gains a fixed wait ( QTest.qWait or time.sleep ) outside tests marked motion or slow : let animations and feedback finish with motion.settle() instead, which takes no time (see the Animation guide). When a file loses a wait, lower its number in that test’s BASELINE . The tests that touch widgets run with Qt’s offscreen platform, so no display is needed. The tests never read or change your own settings, profile or history. tests/conftest.py points them at a throwaway folder, closes every window and database a test leaves open, and turns the sound off. Coverage measures executable statements under alto/ . The pre-push hook and the pytest job that collects coverage require tests to execute every added or modified statement in that package. The Codecov project percentage tracks historical gaps. For code pull requests and pushes to main , the oldest Python version in the pytest matrix (currently 3.11) runs the suite with coverage and checks the patch. Download the pytest-coverage artifact from the Tests run to inspect coverage.xml . The Codecov workflow reads that same artifact. To measure coverage locally: sh scripts/run-tests.sh --patch-coverage

title: For developers
section: Which checks run for which change
text: Which checks run for which change The pre-push hook runs the full pytest suite once and checks the resulting coverage against the branch diff from origin/main . Fetch the target branch first and set ALTO_COVERAGE_BASE when targeting another branch. On pull requests, GitHub selects pytest and coverage using the changes since the branch diverged from its base. Pull request changes Pytest Coverage Only local previews ( work/** ), .gitignore , or .git-blame-ignore-revs Skip Skip Documentation under docs/ or top-level Markdown, optionally mixed with the housekeeping files above Run the documentation tests on Python 3.14 Skip Anything else, including application assets, dependencies, packaging, tests, or workflows Run the full suite on the oldest and newest supported Python Measure coverage and enforce patch coverage Ruff and Pyright run on pull requests that change Python source, type stubs, or inputs to the respective tool. For example, a Ruff configuration change runs Ruff, a change to scripts/typecheck.sh runs Pyright, and a change to pyproject.toml runs both. The Docs check builds the site for changes under docs/ , to CHANGELOG.md , or to its workflow. Pushes to main run the full suite on every supported Python version, along with Ruff, Pyright, and coverage. A new push to a pull request cancels its previous run.

title: For developers
text: Keeping Alto fast Three things watch how fast Alto is, each for a different kind of slowdown. The operations they time are in benchmarks/operations.py : opening every page (and going between a lesson and an exercise), asking and answering a question, painting each screen, drawing the circle of fifths at new sizes, and reading and writing the data of a profile with a year of practice behind it. Budgets, after each merge. tests/test_performance.py (marked perf ) fails when an operation takes longer than its budget in benchmarks/budgets.py . A budget is four or five times what the operation takes on a development machine, so that a slow build machine does not fail a test but a change that makes something many times slower does. The first use of something in a new process (starting the app, the first look at a page, the circle at sizes not used before) is measured in a process of its own, because Qt makes fonts and layouts on first use and later runs hide that cost. The budgets time real operations, so they are left out of the pull request’s tests, where other test processes share the cores. The Budgets workflow ( .github/workflows/budgets.yml ) runs them on a machine of their own after each merge into main that touches the app, the benchmarks or the budgets, and by hand. A missed budget opens an issue labeled performance , or adds the run to the one that is open, and does not fail the run. Run them yourself with pytest -m perf . A history, from release to release. benchmarks/suite.py is an ASV suite, and the Performance workflow ( .github/workflows/performance.yml ) measures main daily at 09:37 UTC and keeps the results on the branch asv-results . A change of more than 30% against the previous release is written in the run’s summary. That is advice and not a failure, because a shared build machine is too noisy for a strict gate; it is there to show a slow creep that no single budget would catch. First visits. The first time a page shows text with ♯, ♭ or ♮ in a new size, Qt spends about 40 ms looking for a font that has the signs, because the interface font does not. alto/ui/warmup.py does that once for each size the interface uses, and loads the music font, a step at a time while the app is idle after it opens, so the first visit to a page is nearly as quick as the second. A new style sheet size belongs in its SIZES . By hand, before a release. The run takes a minute or two, and the feel of animations on a real screen is not something a test can judge, so look at the lesson, the circle of fifths and the statistics page on a real display as well. python -m benchmarks.survey # every operation once, slowest first, in milliseconds python -m benchmarks.operations page:lesson --profile # where the time goes in one operation, the first time pytest -m perf # the budgets asv run -E existing: $( which python ) --set-commit-hash $( git rev-parse HEAD ) # record this commit asv compare v0.0.0 HEAD # what changed since a release, once both have been recorded When an operation is made faster or slower on purpose, change its budget in the same commit. A new page or exercise needs a line in benchmarks/budgets.py (a prefix such as page: covers it) and, if it is a new kind of operation, an entry in benchmarks/operations.py ; the tests fail until it has a budget, so nothing goes unwatched. The first release to be measured is the one that has benchmarks/ . To record a release baseline, run the Performance workflow by hand with ref set to its tag.

title: For developers
text: Type checking Pyright checks the types of alto , tests and scripts , in basic mode, as if for Python 3.11: sh scripts/typecheck.sh It must report no errors. It runs on every pull request ( .github/workflows/pyright.yml ) and before each push. Two things to know when writing Qt code: Write Qt enums in their full form , such as Qt.AlignmentFlag.AlignLeft , not the short Qt.AlignLeft . The short form works when the program runs, but Pyright cannot see it. Qt functions that may return nothing ( layout() , widget() , QApplication.instance() ) have to be checked for None before use, with an if or an assert . If Pyright is wrong about one line, silence just that line with # pyright: ignore[ruleName] and a short reason.

title: For developers
section: Running your copy apart from the installed one
text: Running your copy apart from the installed one Alto’s history and settings are kept by name, so a clone run with python -m alto shares them with an installed Alto. To keep them apart, run the clone with sh scripts/dev.sh . It sets ALTO_HOME to ~/.alto-dev (or to a folder you choose), where the clone has its own database and settings. The first run also adds “Alto (dev)” to the application menu, with the clone’s icon, so the dock shows the development copy on its own and not grouped with the installed one. See Your data .

title: For developers
text: Pre-commit A pre-commit configuration runs the checks automatically before each commit. Set it up once: pip install -e ".[dev]" pre-commit install It then trims trailing whitespace, makes sure files end with a newline, checks YAML and TOML files, refuses very large files (the bundled recordings and fonts are exempt) and runs Ruff, applying its safe fixes. If a hook changes a file, the commit stops so you can review the change, then commit again. On push , the hooks run the test suite, Pyright, and Pylint’s duplicate-code check ( R0801 ). Pylint compares all modules in alto/ so it can find matches in unchanged files. A failure in any of these checks stops the push. Run the duplicate check alone with pre-commit run pylint-duplicates --hook-stage pre-push --all-files , the commit checks with pre-commit run --all-files , the push checks with pre-commit run --all-files --hook-stage pre-push , and update the pinned hook versions with pre-commit autoupdate .

title: For developers
text: Merged local branches Run pre-commit install again in an existing clone to install the post-merge hook. When a merge or fast-forward pull updates your checked-out main , the hook deletes local branches whose tips are in both main and origin/main . Each deletion prints the branch name and its previous commit. Branches with new local commits or commits incorporated only by a squash merge stay available for review. The hook skips every branch checked out in a worktree and always keeps main , gh-pages , and asv-results . To keep another long-running branch in this clone, add its exact name before pulling. Repeat the command for each branch you want to keep. git config --local --add alto.keepBranch gd_dev sh scripts/prune-branches.sh --dry-run The preview refreshes origin and lists eligible local branches. The automatic hook uses the references already in your clone and only deletes local branches.

title: For developers
text: Linting Alto uses Ruff for linting and formatting. It is installed with the dev extra and configured in pyproject.toml . Ruff checks code at 79 characters and docstrings and standalone comments at 72 characters throughout the repository. Docstring summaries can wrap or start on their own line. ruff format alto tests scripts # format the code ruff check --fix alto tests scripts # report problems and apply the safe fixes Run them in that order. Anything that does not fit on a line, whether a list, a dictionary, a call or a signature, is put one element per line with a trailing comma, and a trailing comma you write yourself keeps a short one exploded. The ruff-format pre-commit hook does this on every commit. Ruff warns that the trailing-comma rule can conflict with the formatter. Run in this order, it does not: the formatter leaves out a comma after a lone long argument, the check adds it, and the formatter keeps it. Imports follow these rules: Absolute only. from alto.ui.store import store , never from .store import store ( TID252 ). At the top of the file. None inside a function ( PLC0415 ), except in the >>> examples of a docstring, which have to import what they use. Two modules that need each other do not import each other: notation.py and keyboard_styles.py call hooks that staff.py and keyboard.py register with on_redraw . The conftest.py files set the settings folders before importing anything from Alto, so their imports are marked # noqa: E402 . One name per line when a from import has two or more names, in parentheses with a trailing comma. Ruff cannot enforce this, but it keeps an import you have already written that way. Sorted like isort ( I ): the standard library, then third-party packages (PySide6, numpy, pytest), then alto as its own section ( known-first-party ), each section sorted alphabetically.

title: For developers
text: PyCharm The code is kept free of PyCharm warnings as well as Ruff and Pyright errors. PyCharm’s settings live in .idea/ , which is not in the repository, so a fresh clone needs the three changes below. Without them PyCharm shows many warnings that are not real problems. 1. Use a project inspection profile that ignores the alto imports. PyCharm analyses the >>> examples in docstrings, which is useful, but it resolves alto.exercises and the like only when the file itself imports them, so every example that imports from another package gets a false “Cannot find reference” warning. Settings, Editor, Inspections : choose the Project Default profile (the one saved in the project, not the IDE one). Under Python, Unresolved references , add these to Ignore references : alto.exercises.* , alto.learning.* , alto.theory.* , alto.ui.* , alto.audio.* and alto.__main__ . The result is this in .idea/inspectionProfiles/Project_Default.xml , with USE_PROJECT_PROFILE set to true in profiles_settings.xml next to it: <inspection_tool class= "PyUnresolvedReferencesInspection" enabled= "true" level= "WARNING" enabled_by_default= "true" > <option name= "ignoredIdentifiers" > <list> <option value= "alto.exercises.*" /> <option value= "alto.learning.*" /> <option value= "alto.theory.*" /> <option value= "alto.ui.*" /> <option value= "alto.audio.*" /> <option value= "alto.__main__" /> </list> </option> </inspection_tool> Names that really are unresolved are still reported, in code and in examples. 2. Add a database connection, so the SQL in alto/learning/database.py is checked. Without one, PyCharm warns about every SQL string. Make a file with the real schema, which Database creates when it opens a new file: python -c "from alto.learning import Database; Database('.idea/alto-schema.db').close()" Delete the file and run this again whenever the schema in database.py changes. In the Database tool window, add a SQLite data source named alto (schema) for that file ( jdbc:sqlite:<path to the clone>/.idea/alto-schema.db ). In Settings, Languages & Frameworks, SQL Dialects , set the Project SQL Dialect to SQLite ( .idea/sqldialects.xml ). 3. Leave “Analyze Python code in docstrings” switched on. The examples are real code, so PyCharm should keep checking them. A few habits keep them quiet: Name example variables so they do not shadow a parameter or a module-level name; a trailing underscore is fine ( database_ , cfg_ ). Where PyCharm cannot tell a value is not None , or the example deliberately uses a private member, put a comment line before that statement: >>> # noinspection PyUnresolvedReferences or >>> # noinspection PyProtectedMember . It covers only the next statement. In code, suppress a false positive narrowly, with # noinspection <Inspection> on the line above the statement or the function, and say why when it is not obvious. A few things that are not obvious: PyUnusedLocal is not honored for the parameters of a fake that has to match what it replaces; delete them explicitly ( del volume, kwargs ) instead. Read saved text with text_value in alto/ui/store.py , not str(settings.value(...)) , which PyCharm flags and Pyright needs. Declare every attribute in __init__ , not in the method that first sets it.

title: For developers
text: Designing lessons and exercises A lesson teaches a musical idea that a learner can apply in several situations. An exercise gives repeated practice in one specific technique. In an identification exercise, the learner reads or hears an example and names what it is. In a construction exercise, the learner starts with a specification and supplies the notes or symbols that satisfy it. Plan the relationship by learning goal. One lesson can prepare a learner for several exercises, and an exercise can reinforce ideas introduced in several lessons. Reuse an existing lesson when it already explains the idea a new exercise depends on. An instrument plugin follows the same guidance for the lessons in its manifest, which Alto appends to alto.lessons.LESSONS with register_lesson when the plugin loads. Order the lesson tiles by prerequisite in alto.lessons.LESSONS . Start with a lesson that assumes no music theory knowledge. When adding a lesson, place it after the ideas it uses and before lessons that build on it. Choose the lesson outcome. Write one sentence describing what a first-time learner should understand by the end. Use that sentence to decide which examples belong and where the lesson should stop. Map the practice. For each related exercise, describe what the learner is given, what they do, and what makes the answer correct. Check the exercise catalog for a match before proposing a new drill. Check the vocabulary in teaching order. Read the lesson as a learner who has completed only the preceding lessons. For each musical term, find where its meaning was taught. If it is new, give a plain-language definition where the learner first needs it, before a diagram or question asks them to use it. A mention in a title or a glossary entry alone does not teach the term. For example, introduce the tonic as the note that feels like home, then ask the learner to find it. Repeat this check when reordering lessons. Build a short guided sequence. Introduce the idea with an example the learner can read or hear. When the concept is visual, consider annotating the first example to show where to look. On a keyboard, bracket the pair of black keys and label the neighboring C. On a staff, an arrow from “notehead” to the oval shows which part of the note to read. Then change one feature and ask the learner to predict or explain the result. Give feedback that points back to the example. Use the closing step to name the skills the learner can practice next. Choose the primary practice target with Lesson.exercise and list additional practice targets in Lesson.related_exercises . Time a first pass. Aim for 20 minutes or less , including reading, listening, guided questions, and time to use a hint. Count independent exercise practice separately. If the lesson runs long, move repeated trials into an exercise or split off a concept that has its own learning outcome.

title: For developers
text: Engraving lesson examples Let the music determine the width of a lesson example. Measure spacing in staff spaces , where one space is the distance between the centers of adjacent staff lines. The values below are starting points for Alto. Measure horizontal gaps between the visible edges of the symbols, except where the table specifies notehead centers. Where Starting spacing Clef to key signature Leave 1 staff space before the first sharp or flat and ¼ space between successive signature marks. Key signature to first note Leave 1½ spaces before the notehead or its local accidental. With an empty signature, measure directly from the clef. Local accidental to notehead Leave ¼ space so the sign reads with its note. Stagger accidentals in a chord as needed to clear other signs, notes, and ledger lines. Notes in a phrase Start equal quarter notes 3½ spaces apart, measured from center to center. Give longer values more room and shorter values less. Allow clearance for flags, dots, and accidentals. Keep simultaneous pitches at the same rhythmic position. End of a short staff End the lines about 2 spaces past the last symbol, including when the example shows only a key signature. Anchor short examples at the left. When the pane widens, let the extra room fall beyond the staff. When a longer phrase needs another line, wrap at a musical boundary and repeat the clef and key signature. For paired examples, align the left edges and clefs, keep the staff size consistent, and align corresponding beats when comparing phrases. Size the white box to the wider of the music and its caption, with a small margin around both. Once the example fits on one line, keep the box at that width as the pane grows. Let long captions wrap below the staff in a narrow pane. Allow enough height for the clef, accidentals, ledger lines, and every line of the caption. Group related staves and their playback button in one bordered panel. Arrange the staves in reading order across the panel, with a vertical divider between neighbors on the same row.
