Use continuous white notation paper all the way to the panel border, including between staves and behind the playback button beneath the music. Use the theme’s light button colors on that paper. At a lesson content width of 760 pixels or more, align the top of the panel with the top of the explanation. Below that width, place the panel after the opening paragraph and before the remaining text and question. Keep paired staves together whenever both fit and wrap them when necessary. Put each guided question in the Knowledge check callout. Keep its prompt, choices, hints, explanation, and retry control together. Let answer buttons wrap in reading order when space is tight. Use StaffPlayback for a playable staff example. Its callback identifies each onset by position, so repeated notes light in reading order and a chord lights together. When two diagrams show the same sounding note, highlight both. Clear the playback highlight at the end and when changing examples. Lesson diagrams use StaffWidget(lesson_layout=True) in alto/ui/lesson.py and the lesson’s scale explorer. The renderer measures the selected notation font and keeps each chord together when wrapping. In the scale explorer, a step label followed by an arrow leads to the first pitch on the next line. To check a layout change, view an F natural in G major, a three-flat bass-clef signature on its own, and a short run of quarter notes in both narrow and wide panes. The natural should read with the F, the flats should read as one group, and widening the pane should preserve the distance between the quarter notes. Also try a single note with a caption wider than its staff. Narrow the pane until the caption wraps, then widen it again. The last word should stay visible throughout, and the white box should stop growing once the caption fits on one line.

title: For developers
section: Reviewing the lesson sequence for gaps
text: Reviewing the lesson sequence for gaps Review the affected stretch whenever a lesson is added, moved, or substantially revised. Every few lesson changes, walk the full sequence in the order given by alto.lessons.LESSONS . Start with an absolute beginner and carry forward what each lesson actually teaches. An optional exercise or glossary lookup can reinforce a skill, but a learner can reach the next tile without doing either. Work through the next lesson’s examples and questions. For each, finish the sentence “To do this, I already need to be able to …” Include reading the diagram, hearing a difference, and interpreting the answer choices. For each prerequisite, record the earlier lesson and step that teaches it, or the worked example in the current lesson before its first use. Distinguish seeing a definition, following a demonstration, and using the idea on a fresh example. Match the evidence to what the question actually asks the learner to do. Try one fresh example with the same demands. For instance, after a learner reads a note just above a known line, ask them to read one just below it. When possible, watch a first-time learner try it before giving a hint. Record where their reasoning stops. A walkthrough by the author and an observed learner result are different evidence. Flag a blocking gap when an essential action requires knowledge the sequence has yet to teach. Flag a practice gap when the explanation exists but the jump to independent use needs a smaller example. Record one row per finding. Keep a row open until someone retries the original task using the revised sequence. First lesson and step that needs the skill What the learner must do Where it was taught Finding and smallest repair Recheck Scale Identification · The major scale pattern Locate middle C on a treble staff to follow the C-major example Intervals · C and E♭ on the staff traces E4 on the bottom line through D4 to C4 on its ledger line. The staff shows C4 and E♭4. The worked example now connects the bottom line to middle C before scales. Open. Ask a first-time learner to locate C4 on a fresh treble staff and explain how they found it. Prefer a short bridge at first use when it serves one lesson. Move a prerequisite earlier when several lessons rely on it. Add a separate lesson when the missing skill needs its own guided sequence to keep a first pass within about 20 minutes.

title: For developers
text: Example lesson plan for scales A lesson on Scales could ask, “How can the same major-scale pattern start on two different notes?” Have the learner play C major, locate the half steps, then start on G and decide whether F or F♯ preserves the pattern. Close by playing the G scale they predicted. An illustrative first pass allows four minutes for C major, six for the guided G major example, and three for the comparison and recap. Related exercise What the learner practices Scale Identification Given a written scale, identify its tonic or mode from the notes and their spacing. Scale Construction Given a tonic and a scale type, place the notes on the staff with the correct spelling.

title: For developers
text: Adding an exercise For an exercise with answer choices, subclass ChoiceExercise in alto/exercises/library.py and implement make_question . Supply the full set of eligible answers. Alto adds the Buttons submenu and applies Limited or All . A construction exercise whose buttons edit or submit an answer uses Exercise.generate . @ register class MyExercise ( ChoiceExercise ): name = "My exercise" category = "Intervals" description = "One line shown on the home screen." par_seconds = 5.0 # a good first-answer time; see Spaced Repetition def make_question ( self , rng ): ... return Question ( "What is this?" , choices = choices , answer = answer , staff = [[ note ]], clef = "treble" , ) Question describes everything the screen needs: a prompt, the answer buttons, the notes to draw, a key signature, a keyboard key to highlight, and so on. If your exercise reads user settings, override practice_signature() for a ChoiceExercise or settings_signature() for other exercises and return signature(...) of those settings. Stored questions are only replayed while the signature is unchanged. Give the exercise an icon in alto/ui/home.py so it appears properly on the home screen. Pick its category from the existing ones, or make a new one. @register places the exercise next to the others of its category, so the home screen and the exercise list show each category once, whatever order the classes are written in. Everything else comes with it: the question is recorded in the database, scored for speed, drawn in the chosen notation font and included in the statistics.

title: For developers
text: Adding an exercise option

title: For developers
text: Requesting exercise options Use the option names below when asking an agent to design or implement exercise settings. An option is a row in the exercise’s settings menu. A choice is a value inside that row, such as Descending under Motion . Answer buttons are the controls the learner presses during practice. The Buttons option configures them. What to ask What to expect “Propose options for Interval Identification.” A short table of options that fit the exercise. For each, give its menu label, what changes for the learner, the template exercise, the choices and default, and any behavior that would need new work. “Add standard Clefs to Interval Identification.” A working Clefs row modeled on Note Identification, with the shared picker and selected-clef preview. The exercise generates questions using the checked clefs. “Use Range from Keyboard Note Identification. Default to C4–C5.” The named exercise supplies the keyboard range editor, preview, and interactions. The requested range sets the initial endpoints. Standard means to reuse the option in the table below. From [exercise] selects a specific variant. An explicit override takes precedence. For example, “default to treble and bass” sets the boxes checked on first use. “Offer only treble and bass” limits which boxes appear. If the request leaves the default open, preserve the target exercise’s current behavior where possible. Reusing a picker gives the target exercise its own saved selection unless the request calls for a shared preference or the exercises already share it.

title: For developers
text: Exercise option vocabulary The template exercise gives you a place to try the option in Alto. Its panel is in alto/ui/settings_panel.py , and the named helpers are in alto/ui/settings_menu.py . Start with the option’s effect on the question or answer to choose among variants. Option to request What the learner gets Template to reuse Clefs (also “Clef”) A row showing the selected clef symbols. Its submenu has grouped, illustrated checkboxes. At least one stays checked. Offer the grand staff when the exercise supports questions on both staves. Note Identification uses ClefPictures with clef_choice_page . Scale Construction shows the single-staff variant of the same picker. Range Low and high pitches. Staff exercises can keep a range per clef. Keyboard exercises select a span on a piano and show a miniature keyboard in the row. Note Identification uses RangeEditor with RangePictures . Keyboard Note Identification uses KeyboardSpan and endpoint arrows. Staff Key Check which signatures can be drawn at the start of the staff, including the blank signature. The row previews the selection. Scale Identification uses KeyChecklist and KeyDiagram . Scale Key Choose the musical keys used in questions. Underlined Major and Minor tabs each offer 15 signatures. Either tab may be empty if the other has a selection. The row counts selections by mode. Scale Identification uses ScaleKeyPicker . When both key options apply, place Staff Key above Scale Key . Key signatures A single checklist of signature counts. Some exercises also let the learner turn signatures on or off. Note Identification uses KeyChecklist . For the version with a switch inside the submenu, follow Keyboard Note Identification and KeySignaturePage . Scales Check the scale types or modes that can appear, such as major, Dorian, and natural minor. Scale Construction uses ChoiceChecklist and shows the selected count in the row. Motion Choose Ascending or Descending with radio buttons. Scale Identification and Scale Construction share this page in KeySignatureSettingsPanel . Display Mode Choose how the notes appear on the staff. Checked presentations can be mixed. Interval Identification displays Ascending and Descending as indented checkboxes directly below Melodic when it is selected. At least one direction stays checked. Quality Choose Interval Only , Interval and Quality (default), or Quality Only . Interval Identification uses a submenu with three radio buttons. Inversions (written intervals) Show the selected interval and ask for its inversion in the chosen answer format. Interval Identification uses an inline switch, off by default. Question Type Choose what the learner is asked to do. Use radios for one format, or checkboxes when the question can combine parts. Notation Identification has Click on Staff and Answer Button radios. Scale Identification has independent Key and Mode boxes. Note Construction shows its keys and degrees when Scale and Degree is selected. Buttons One submenu for answer layouts. Limited caps the number offered, with Button count directly below it. All shows the full answer set. Scale Identification and Interval Identification share the Limited and All submenu. Keyboard Interval Identification adds Compact , where the learner picks a quality and an interval number in either order. Next Question Choose Immediately , Wait , or After Animation (default). Each exercise remembers its own pace. The shared settings panel adds this row to every exercise. Route completed answers through ExerciseView._finish_answer . Octave An inline switch that makes the octave part of the required answer. Note Construction uses ToggleRow . Keyboard Note Identification labels its variant Octave number . Note names , Note values , Accidentals Choose a naming system, check the durations that can appear, or switch on questions with written accidentals. These are separate options. Note Identification has the naming preview and Accidentals switch. Its illustrated note-value checklist is also used by Interval Identification under Note Value . For a choice of written signs, the Accidentals submenu in Interval Identification uses a checklist. Terms , Degrees , Arpeggio types , Inversions Check the items eligible for practice. Terms also restricts the distractors. Degrees is a section within Scale and Degree . All use ChoiceChecklist . Notation Identification groups terms, Note Construction lists degrees, and Arpeggio Identification has separate pages for types and inversions. Intervals Choose interval sizes individually or by endpoints. The available sizes depend on the keyboard range. Keyboard Interval Identification combines ChoiceChecklist and IntervalRangeSlider . Interval Identification uses the slider for interval numbers and the checklist for written spellings, so A4 and d5 can be selected separately. For exercise-specific options, use the existing exercise as the reference. Examples include Black keys in Keyboard Note Identification, Steps in Scale Construction, and Questions and Colors in Circle of Fifths.

title: For developers
text: Implementing the request Start by opening the template’s settings row and tracing its panel, saved settings, and question or answer behavior. Reuse the shared picker, preview, and selection rules where they fit. If two exercises need the same behavior and it currently lives inside one panel, share that implementation while preserving the original exercise’s behavior. When a new option needs a distinct interaction, describe the difference from its closest template. Add a vocabulary entry when introducing a reusable option or variant so it can be requested by name next time. Give the option a row on the exercise settings menu. Use the shared MenuRow in alto/ui/settings_menu.py with the option name, a short summary of the current selection, and the chevron. For a standalone on/off setting, such as Octave , an inline Switch in a row without a chevron is appropriate. Two named modes, such as Click on Staff and Answer Button , belong together in a submenu. Open the option with the panel’s SlideStack . Build its page with subpage so the title matches the row and Back returns to the settings menu. Use radio buttons when exactly one choice applies and checkboxes when several can apply. Group controls below the header at their natural height and leave extra space below the last row. For scrollable option lists, use scrolling for the body and fill=True on subpage so the viewport can grow while the choices stay together. Verify row spacing at short and tall window sizes and check that the last option remains reachable when scrolling. Load the saved value when building the panel, using a default for first use. When a choice changes, save it, update the row summary, and apply it to the exercise. Opening the submenu or pressing Back should keep the current question. Include settings that affect question selection in the exercise’s review signature. Test the path from the exercise gear through the row and back. Verify the first-use default, the effect on questions and answers, the updated summary, and the restored choice when reopening the app. For example, select only bass under Clefs , generate questions, and check that the row preview and each staff show bass. If the implementation touched a shared picker, run the original exercise’s settings tests too.

title: For developers
text: Adding an instrument Put its recordings in alto/assets/samples/<key>/ , one mono WAV per note, named by MIDI note number (for example 60.wav for middle C). Every semitone is best. Where a note has no recording, Alto shifts the nearest one. Add an Instrument to INSTRUMENTS in alto/audio.py . Mark it sustained=True if it is bowed or blown, so each note ends as the next begins. If it is another way of playing an instrument already listed, give both the same family and each its own variant (the viola’s “Arco” and “Pizzicato”), and they appear as one entry with a choice. Add an entry for the same key to INFO in alto/instrument_info.py : what it is, the source, who played it, and the terms. This is what the summary in the Sound settings shows. Credit the recordings in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and the folder’s SOURCE.txt . Only add recordings whose license allows redistribution.

title: For developers
text: Adding a notation font Alto draws notes with fonts that follow the SMuFL standard. Put the font file and its license in alto/assets/fonts/ . Add its stem anchors and engraving defaults to engraving.json , read from the font’s SMuFL metadata file. Register the file name in _FILES in alto/ui/engraving.py . Add a NotationStyle to STYLES in alto/ui/notation.py . Record the font in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Only add fonts whose license allows redistribution, such as the SIL Open Font License.

title: For developers
text: Adding a keyboard style Add a KeyboardStyle to STYLES in alto/ui/keyboard_styles.py : the colors of the naturals and sharps, and any extras such as a case, felt, bone caps or stop knobs. The settings page, the keyboard and the range picker all read from that list, so nothing else needs to be changed. Add a row to the table in docs/settings.md . The colors named after materials in the builder are MATERIALS in the same file.

title: For developers
text: Versions of the docs The docs exist in one copy for each release and one for the development version, and a dropdown in the top bar switches between them. A page of an old release says so in a banner, and links to the same page in the latest one. /alto/dev/ the development version, rebuilt when a change to docs/ is merged into main /alto/v0.1.0/ one folder for each release, built once when its tag is pushed and not changed after that /alto/latest/ the newest release again, built with its own address so that its links and its sitemap say /latest/ /alto/ goes to latest (to dev until there is a release); also versions.json, version-switcher.js, 404.html, robots.txt The Docs workflow ( .github/workflows/docs.yml ) builds them with Jekyll and keeps the result on the branch gh-pages , which GitHub Pages serves. scripts/docs_site.py writes what sits around the versions: versions.json , the home page that goes to the latest, and the sitemap. The files that belong to the whole site and not to one version are in docs/site-root/ . One of them, version-switcher.js , fills the dropdown from versions.json at run time, so a release made years ago still offers the newest versions, and a fix to the dropdown reaches all of them. The dev entry shows the short Git hash recorded when those docs were built. Search engines are told to prefer the latest version: every page has a canonical address under /latest/ , dev is noindex , and only latest is in the sitemap. A page that existed at the root before the docs had versions is sent to /latest/ by 404.html . To add a docs-only fix to an old release, there is nothing to do but publish a new release: a version is built once from its tag. To build a release that was tagged before it had a dropdown, run the Docs workflow by hand with ref set to its tag. It puts the current layout over that tag’s docs, and the words stay as they were. Switching a copy of the repository to this , once: after the first run has created the gh-pages branch, set Settings, Pages, Source to “Deploy from a branch”, gh-pages , / (root) . Until then GitHub builds a single copy from main:/docs as before. Do this soon after merging, because the one copy no longer has robots.txt , llms.txt or the Search Console file, which now live in docs/site-root/ .

title: For developers
text: Pages in the sidebar The sidebar and the “On this page” list are built from the pages themselves. A page is listed by what its front matter says: Key Meaning nav_order Where it goes, lowest first. A page without one is not in the sidebar. nav_group The heading it goes under (Using Alto, For developers, About). The headings open and close, and the pages of one heading must be next to each other in nav_order . Home has none. children , parent A page with children: name opens the pages with parent: name . Guide chapters use order for their reading sequence. The API reference lists packages alphabetically and sorts modules by title within each package. A heading that is also the title of a page (For developers) is that page’s link, and the page is not listed again under it. Whatever holds the page you are on is open. Which headings you closed is remembered in the browser. On a wide screen a page with two or more ## or ### headings gets an “On this page” list beside it, made in the browser from those headings, and on a narrower one a box above the text. Nothing needs to be written for it. A page that should not have one, such as the home page, says toc: false in its front matter. docs/api/index.md is written by scripts/api_docs.py , so change its front matter there. The previous and next links at the bottom of each page follow the sidebar’s reading order.

title: For developers
text: Pull request previews On a PR’s Conversation tab, click View rendered documentation in the GitHub Actions bot comment. The docs/preview check links to the same site. After each push, the bot updates its comment with the commit it verified. If the build or deployment fails, the link opens the run log. Docs check builds the proposed merge with read-only permissions. Publish docs preview runs from the default branch, finds the open PR and its current head through GitHub, and publishes the rendered files to the preview fork. The preview for PR 97, for example, is served at https://genedan.github.io/alto/pr-97/dev/ . Previously published previews remain accessible after the PR closes. The file .github/docs-preview-repository names the preview repository ( genedan/alto ). Set that repository’s Pages source to the root of its docs-previews branch with a .nojekyll file. Add a write deploy key to the preview repository and store the private key as DOCS_PREVIEW_DEPLOY_KEY in the upstream docs-preview-publisher environment. Restrict that environment to the main branch. Use a preview hostname separate from the production site, since the rendered content comes from PRs.

title: For developers
text: Building the docs The plugin tutorials are not stored in Alto. They live in altosaurus/viola-plugin-tutorial and altosaurus/harpsichord-plugin-tutorial , which mirror the paths of docs/ . The Docs and Docs check workflows run scripts/tutorial_docs.py before Jekyll. It copies in each tutorial page and only the files that page refers to: the artwork it links, and both themes of each screenshot. The download is a release asset of the tutorial repository, which its Release workflow builds when a tag is pushed, so the site links to it and does not host it. Nothing else in a tutorial repository is published. Run it once before a local build to see the pages. It clones both from GitHub, or takes one from a checkout of your own with --from : python scripts/tutorial_docs.py all python scripts/tutorial_docs.py harpsichord --from ../harpsichord-plugin-tutorial The files it writes are listed in .gitignore . A merge into Alto’s main rebuilds the docs, and a change to a tutorial reaches the site at the next build, so run the Docs workflow by hand after you push a tutorial. The pictures in each tutorial are made by that repository’s scripts/screenshots.py . The plugin tests keep only the manifest of each example pack in tests/packs/ (and the viola’s animation), and make its recordings, photographs and icons when they run ( tests/pack_fixtures.py ), because the plugin’s author provides the real ones. They also read the tutorial pages when they have been brought in. You need Ruby and Bundler. In docs/ , bundle install once, then build one version the way the workflow does: cd docs printf 'baseurl: /alto/dev\ndocs_version: dev\n' > /tmp/version.yml bundle exec jekyll build --destination /tmp/site/dev --config _config.yml,/tmp/version.yml bundle exec ruby ../scripts/docs_search.rb /tmp/site/dev git rev-parse --short HEAD > /tmp/site/dev/commit.txt python ../scripts/docs_site.py finish /tmp/site --root-files site-root --site-url https://altosaurus.github.io/alto then serve /tmp/site under a folder called alto (for example mkdir /tmp/www && ln -s /tmp/site /tmp/www/alto && python -m http.server -d /tmp/www ) and open http://127.0.0.1:8000/alto/ . tests/test_docs_site.py checks the script and the files without needing Ruby.

title: For developers
section: Keeping the docs and screenshots current
text: Keeping the docs and screenshots current The current app screenshots in docs/assets/img/ come in light and dark pairs. Regenerate them with scripts/screenshots.py : .venv/bin/python scripts/screenshots.py # every picture, both themes .venv/bin/python scripts/screenshots.py --only home stats # just these .venv/bin/python scripts/screenshots.py --out /tmp/shots # somewhere else, to look before replacing It runs against a made-up profile and a temporary settings folder, so it never touches your own history or settings. It needs a display or QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen . Fonts render slightly differently on each machine, so regenerate on the machine you normally use and look at the pictures before committing them. To add a picture, include it in a docs page with shot.html , and add its name to SHOTS in the script. tests/test_docs.py checks that both match and that both themes exist. The Developer guide uses component-shot.html for clickable screenshots. Give the include the capture’s width and height. In docs/_data/launch_components.json , each region records its label, class, destination, and rectangle (left, top, width, height as percentages of the image). The screenshot and its numbered key share those destinations. After a recapture, check that each region still covers its component in both themes. The pre-push hook runs scripts/check-docs.sh , which warns when the interface ( alto/ui ) has changed since the pictures were last updated. It only warns; set ALTO_DOCS_STRICT=1 to make it fail.

title: For developers
text: The API reference The pages under API reference ( docs/api/ ) are written from the docstrings by scripts/api_docs.py . Each module has a page with its public classes, methods and functions: the signature, then the NumPy-style docstring as Markdown. Names that begin with an underscore are left out. The script reads the source as text, so it needs neither Qt nor a display. python scripts/api_docs.py # rewrite docs/api python scripts/api_docs.py --check # list the pages that are out of date, and change nothing GitHub Pages cannot run the script, so the generated pages are committed. When you change a docstring or a public signature, run it and commit the pages with the change. tests/test_api_docs.py fails when they are out of date, so a forgotten run is caught by the tests, the pre-push hook and the pull request.

title: For developers
text: Changelog and releases CHANGELOG.md lists what changed for the people who use Alto, newest first, in the Keep a Changelog layout. A change a user would notice (a new exercise, a changed menu, a fixed bug) adds a line under Unreleased in the same pull request. Internal tidying does not need one.

title: For developers
text: Pre-release checklist Choose the version. Alto uses semantic versioning : a new feature raises the middle number, a fix raises the last. In CHANGELOG.md , rename Unreleased to the version with today’s date ( ## [0.1.0] - 2026-12-01 ), add a new empty Unreleased above it, and update the two links at the bottom. Then run python scripts/release_notes.py , which rewrites the Release notes page of the docs ( docs/release-notes.md ) from the changelog; --check says whether it is up to date, and a test fails when it is not, so a changelog line always arrives with its page. Set the same version in pyproject.toml . tests/test_changelog.py fails if the changelog has no notes for it. Check that every user-facing feature in the release has a guide entry explaining where to find it and how to use it. Compare the changes since the previous release tag with the changelog to catch any omissions. For each new or changed feature, follow the documented steps in the release candidate and add or correct instructions in the release PR. With the release candidate installed in .venv , run .venv/bin/python scripts/screenshots.py to refresh every screenshot in docs/assets/img/ in both themes. Review the light and dark images against their captions and alt text. Exclude the UI style guide and its versioned screenshots in docs/assets/ui-reference/ from this check. Update that baseline only for an explicitly requested visual change. For screenshots using component-shot.html , check that the image dimensions match the captures and each clickable region covers its component. Run sh scripts/run-tests.sh tests/test_docs.py tests/test_docs_site.py tests/test_guide_docs.py and include the updated images and any caption or region corrections in the release PR. Run the Release workflow manually on the versioned candidate. Complete the license compliance check on its Linux and Windows downloads and record the results in the release PR. Resolve any findings before tagging. Merge that as a pull request, then tag the merge commit and push the tag: git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0 . Pushing the tag starts the Release workflow (see below), which publishes the downloads. Publish a release as a normal release, not a pre-release: the update check asks GitHub for the latest release, which leaves pre-releases out, and compares version numbers ( 0.10.0 is newer than 0.9.0 ), so a tag must be plain numbers such as v0.1.0 . python scripts/changelog_section.py 0.1.0 prints the notes of one version, which is what a GitHub release shows. alto --version prints the version of the copy you run.

title: For developers
text: License compliance Bundled software and assets. Unpack the Linux tarball and install the Windows candidate. On each platform, inventory the interpreter, frozen Python packages, embedded native code, Qt plugins and system libraries. Compare the contents with the exclusions in packaging/alto.spec . Check redistribution terms for each component and for the fonts, recordings, score excerpts, icons and vendored documentation assets. Confirm that Alto’s MIT license and the applicable third-party licenses and credits accompany the copies users receive, including the versioned documentation. Installed notices. Compare the inventory with THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md and the installed licenses/README.txt . Check the notice texts against the exact upstream versions, including incorporated code such as CPython’s HACL*. Verify each SHA-256 in licenses/notices.json and resolve every license-file reference in licenses/Qt/upstream-notices.zip . Corresponding source. Match the Qt and Qt for Python source downloads to the versions and hashes in each installation. Verify that the Qt libraries and PySide6 and Shiboken bindings can be replaced and that Alto’s self-test still passes. Check the bundled Linux libraries against their package copyrights and verify the required Ubuntu source packages and file hashes in the companion archive. Verify the certifi source download and compare its CA bundle with the installed copy. Windows upgrade terms. Upgrade from the previous release with no recorded acceptance of the current Microsoft terms. Exercise both choices through Alto’s updater. Declining must preserve the old installation, and accepting must complete the upgrade and record acceptance. Release evidence. Record the workflow run, commit, artifact SHA-256s and results. The publishing tag triggers a fresh build. Verify that the signed SHA256SUMS covers the exact desktop downloads and source companions, and repeat the applicable checks on any files whose hashes differ from the reviewed copies.

title: For developers
text: Building the Linux download sh scripts/build-linux.sh # dist/alto-<version>-linux-<architecture>.tar.gz, and its .sha256 file PYTHON = /path/to/python3.13 sh scripts/build-linux.sh The script makes a clean virtual environment under .package-build/ , installs Alto and PyInstaller (the package extra in pyproject.toml ) in it, freezes Alto with packaging/alto.spec , and packs the result with packaging/linux/install.sh , a README, the license and the third-party notices. Nothing is installed on your computer. Before it packs anything it checks that the frozen program says Alto <version> and that it opens its window (under Qt’s offscreen platform, with its own data folder, so a real profile is never touched). The download is the program folder, which carries its own Python and Qt, so users need no Python. install.sh install copies it to ~/.local/opt/alto , links ~/.local/bin/alto and adds the menu entry; uninstall removes those and keeps the user’s data, and uninstall --purge deletes that too. tests/test_linux_install.py runs the real script in a scratch home. Two things to know when building a release: Build on an old Linux. The frozen program needs at least the C library of the system it was built on, so the release workflow builds on Ubuntu 22.04, and a build made on a newer system will not start on older ones. System libraries come from the build machine. PyInstaller copies the libraries Qt needs from the system it runs on (including GTK, glib and libstdc++ ), apart from a short list it leaves out (graphics drivers, libxcb and libwayland ). That includes the libraries of Qt’s X11 plugin ( libxcb-cursor , libxkbcommon-x11 and a few more), so the build machine must have them installed: the workflow does, and the build script fails if the X11 plugin of the finished folder cannot find any of them. If a build misbehaves on another distribution, check which libraries it loads, and exclude the offender in packaging/alto.spec . To try a build without touching your own install, extract it and run ./alto/alto , or run install.sh with ALTO_PREFIX , XDG_DATA_HOME and XDG_CONFIG_HOME pointing at scratch folders.

title: For developers
section: Building the Windows installer, and the release workflow
text: Building the Windows installer, and the release workflow scripts\build-windows.ps1 builds dist\alto-<version>-windows-x64-setup.exe . It needs Windows, Python 3.13 and Inno Setup 6 . Like the Linux script it freezes Alto with packaging/alto.spec and checks that the program starts; then it compiles packaging/windows/alto.iss and tries the installer for real: a silent install, a run, a silent uninstall that must keep the data, and an uninstall with /PURGE=1 that must remove it. That test uses the real %APPDATA%\Alto , so run it only on a computer where that folder may be touched, such as a CI runner. The installer is for one user (no administrator prompt); its AppId in alto.iss must never change, because a newer installer finds the copy it updates by it. The uninstaller asks whether to also remove the practice history ( %APPDATA%\Alto ) and the settings ( HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\alto ); a silent uninstall keeps them unless it is given /PURGE=1 . The installer is not signed, so Windows shows an “unknown publisher” warning. Microsoft’s Visual C++ runtime comes from Windows, not from the installer. packaging/alto.spec leaves out the copies that Python, Qt and Shiboken bring, fails the build if one remains, and records which runtime files the program needs and the newest version among them. The installer checks that Windows has them, at least that new, and otherwise downloads Microsoft’s Visual C++ Redistributable, checks Microsoft’s signature on it and runs it, both in an ordinary install and in the silent install of an update. The build test runs that step once with /RUNTIMETEST=1 , so it needs the internet. Alto does not use NumPy, which is only a test dependency.

title: For developers
text: Signing releases, once A packaged copy of Alto updates itself, and it installs only what is signed with a key that came with it. The key pair is made once: Run python scripts/make_signing_key.py . It prints a private key and a public key and writes nothing. Store the private key as the GitHub secret ALTO_SIGNING_KEY (the repository’s Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions), and keep an offline copy of it, for example in a password manager. Whoever has it can sign an update that every copy of Alto will install, and if it is lost no copy can be updated by a release signed with a new key: people would install the next version by hand. Put the public key in UPDATE_PUBLIC_KEYS in alto/updates.py and commit it. Until it is there a packaged copy does not replace itself; it is only told that a newer release exists, and the Release workflow refuses to publish. The Release workflow signs SHA256SUMS with the secret ( scripts/sign_release.py ) and uploads SHA256SUMS.sig with it. Before it builds anything it signs a probe file, and the script checks the signature against the public key in the code, so a secret that is not that key’s stops the release at once and not after the builds. UPDATE_PUBLIC_KEYS is a tuple so that a release can carry a second key before the first is retired. alto --self-test checks, with no network, that a packaged build has what an update needs (the certificate authorities, which the bundled Python cannot count on the system for, and the signature check). Both build scripts run it. The Windows script also runs a newer installer over a running Alto with the arguments Alto uses, and checks that the old one closed, the new one was installed and Alto opened again. What cannot be tested before a release exists is a copy checking a real release, which first happens when a release newer than the installed one is published; try the update on a real Linux and a real Windows machine then. Three GitHub workflows do the building: Build packages ( build-packages.yml ) builds and tests both packages: the Linux download on Ubuntu 22.04 and the Windows installer on a Windows runner, both with Python 3.13. The other two call it. Package runs it on a pull request that changes packaging/ , the build scripts, pyproject.toml or the assets, so a break shows before a release. It publishes nothing. Release runs when a tag such as v0.1.0 is pushed. It first checks that the tag is v plus the version in pyproject.toml and that CHANGELOG.md has notes for it; then builds both packages; then creates the GitHub release with both files, a SHA256SUMS file and the changelog notes. Started by hand from the Actions tab, it only builds, to rehearse a release. The release is a normal one and never a pre-release, because Alto’s update check asks GitHub for the latest release.

title: For developers
text: Reporting problems Open an issue on GitHub . Say which operating system and Python version you use, and which exercise you were in.

title: For developers
text: Adding a notation excerpt Choose a passage whose music and source edition are in the public domain. For a modern transcription, verify the transcriber’s public-domain dedication as well. Record the precise source file URL, its SHA-256 digest, the historical edition, the part, and the measure numbers in excerpt.json . Add the edition to THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Store the extracted score.musicxml and its engraved score.svg beside the manifest under alto/assets/excerpts/<work>-m<first-measure>-v<version>/ . Preserve the prevailing clefs, key, and meter. Give each independently selectable component a group ID such as mark-0 , and put its Alto notation term at the corresponding index in the manifest’s targets list. Mark every visible instance of a term that can be asked. Keep neighboring symbols as musical context. Tintable shapes inherit their group’s fill or use currentColor for strokes. Run QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen .venv/bin/python scripts/excerpt_hit_map.py <excerpt-directory> to generate hits.png from the engraved ink. Inspect both answer modes at narrow and wide sizes. Published IDs identify saved questions. Give corrected music or a changed marker order a new version and keep the original directory so older answers can still be opened.

title: Exercises
text: Exercises Each exercise has a ? button with a short explanation. Open the sliders button to change an exercise’s settings. Hover over an answer button to see its keyboard shortcut. In Note, Interval, and Scale Construction, use the arrow keys to move the note and Return to place it. For keyboard practice in Notation Identification, choose Answer Button under Question Type . Shortcuts Answer-choice exercises include Buttons in their settings. Choose All for the full answer bank or Limited to set a maximum. For questions with separate answer groups, such as a note name and an octave, the limit applies to each group. The exercise remembers its own selection. Each exercise remembers its own Next Question setting. Immediately flashes the correct button green and advances. The answer audio can finish while you read the next question. The music stays unanimated. Wait plays the animation and keeps the correct answer button green. Press Next when you’re ready. After Animation (default) advances automatically when the feedback finishes. With SM-2 or FSRS, a missed card returns later. If you grade correct answers yourself, choosing Hard , Good , or Easy schedules the card and advances to the next question. Spaced repetition

title: Exercises
text: MIDI keyboard input On Linux, connect a USB MIDI keyboard or open the Virtual MIDI Piano Keyboard (VMPK). In VMPK, choose Edit → MIDI Connections and set MIDI OUT Driver to ALSA . In Alto, open MIDI in the exercise toolbar and select the keyboard’s output. VMPK may appear as MIDI Out out . You can play in the VMPK window while Alto receives the notes. Note Identification. Play the note on the staff. Any octave counts when Octave is off. Interval Construction. Play the missing endpoint in the requested octave. For a perfect fifth above C4, play G4. Scale Construction. Play the scale in the requested direction. Undo removes the last note. The final note submits the scale unless the question asks for whole and half steps. In that case, mark the steps on screen and choose Answer . Alto uses the exercise’s written spelling for matching pitches. On Ubuntu, install alsa-utils if the MIDI menu prompts for it. Reopen the menu after connecting a device. Choose MIDI → Off to disconnect, or leave the exercise.

title: Exercises
text: Note Identification A note is drawn on a staff. Press the button with its name. In the exercise settings you can choose: Clefs: the grand staff, or any of the seven single-staff clefs, listed in three groups: treble, bass, alto and tenor; then soprano, mezzo-soprano and baritone (written as an F clef, or as a C clef if you choose that in Settings ). Each clef is shown with its name beside it. The same list is used by every exercise with these single-staff clefs. The staff interval exercises also offer the grand staff. Range: the lowest and highest note that can appear, per clef. Key signatures: which keys appear. When a key is on, the note’s name has to agree with the signature. Note values: whole notes up to thirty-second notes, and the double whole note. Note names: letters (C D E), solfège (Do Re Mi), or the Scale degrees group, with Caret (1̂ 2̂ 3̂) and Function (Tonic, Supertonic, Mediant, and so on). Every option has a text label beside its preview. Choose Major or Natural minor as the reference scale. The question names the key. With an empty key signature, the choices use C major or A natural minor. Caret labels use accidental prefixes, while function labels use words such as Raised Supertonic and Lowered Mediant . Accidentals: whether notes with their own sharp, flat or natural sign appear. Octave: turn this on to answer with both the note name and its octave. Middle C is C4. The settings open in a pane on the right of the exercise. Each row names an option, and clicking it opens a page for that option. Changes apply to the next question right away.

title: Exercises
text: Notation Identification Choose a Question Type in the exercise settings. Answer Button is the default. A short phrase appears with one marking highlighted in blue. By default, choose its name from up to four answers or press its number key. In Click on Staff , the prompt names a component. Move the pointer over the music to highlight a component, then click to answer. In a repertoire excerpt, any occurrence of the named component counts. In a generated phrase, the prompt can specify a particular notehead, stem, or staff line. Open Terms in the exercise settings to select a whole group or check individual terms. Only checked terms can be highlighted or offered as answers. Select none clears every checkbox. Check a term to start a new selection, or turn the switch off to restore your previous selection. Choices favor the target’s category, then draw from other checked terms if space remains. When visually similar alternatives exist, most questions favor them. For example, a turn often appears alongside inverted, slashed, and vertical turns. Eight piano excerpts from Schubert’s Erlkönig and Schumann’s Schöne Fremde and Die Lotosblume are installed with Alto. The composer, title, and measure numbers appear beneath the music. Try selecting Tie and Slur together to practice telling the two curves apart in context. Terms outside the collection use generated phrases. The original editions are in the public domain, and the digital scores come from the OpenScore Lieder corpus . Topics include note values and rests, clefs, accidentals and microtonal signs, meter, barlines, repeats, articulations, dynamics, ornaments, octave signs, and instrumental techniques. For example, you can isolate ties and slurs, compare quarter-tone accidentals, or practice bowing and pedal marks. For advanced markings, Alto uses the selected music font when it contains the symbol and the bundled Bravura font otherwise. Glyph codes follow the Standard Music Font Layout index .

title: Exercises
text: Rythmic Equations Use Answer Type to choose what fills the blank. Symbol (the default) asks for a note or rest. Number shows numbered buttons. A number can be a missing factor, as in “half note ÷ □ = quarter note,” or a duration. For a duration, the question gives the counting unit: with Count in eighth notes , a quarter note plus a quarter note equals 4 . Check both types to practice a mix. For symbol answers, choose the note symbol that makes both sides of the equation last the same amount of time. For example, a quarter note plus another quarter note equals a half note. The blank can appear on either side of the equals sign. Under Operators , set Left operators and Right operators to choose how many arithmetic signs appear on each side of the equals sign (0–3 per side). The default is one on the left and zero on the right. Use the checkboxes under each count to select the signs allowed on that side. For example, set both counts to one, select only Addition (+) on the left and only Multiplication (×) on the right, and you can get quarter note + quarter note = □ × 2 . Turn on Parentheses to practice order of operations. Set at least two operators on one side so there is something to group. For example, in (quarter note + quarter note) ÷ 2 = □ , add the two quarter notes first, then divide by two. With the switch off (the default), you can work from left to right on each side. Multiplication and division use whole-number factors from 2 through 8 when the selected symbols allow them. Use Symbols to select notes, rests, and dotted notes from double whole through thirty-second values. A selected note and rest of the same duration both count as correct. Turn on Ties or Beams to mix in questions where a pair of notes counts as one duration. Beams group eighth, sixteenth, or thirty-second notes.

title: Exercises
text: Keyboard Note Identification One key on a piano keyboard is highlighted. Press the button with its name. Use this exercise’s Note names setting to choose Letters , Solfège , Caret , or Function independently of Note Identification. Scale degrees follow the shown major key, or C major when key signatures are off. When octaves are required, degree and octave are separated: 1̂ / 4 . Black keys: include them. A black key has two names, such as C♯ and D♭, and either one is accepted. Octave number: also choose the octave from a second row. Octaves count up from C, so middle C is C4. Range: which part of the keyboard is asked. Key signatures: show a key signature above the keyboard. The name then has to follow that signature. F♯ and G♭ are no longer interchangeable.

title: Exercises
text: Note Construction The reverse of note identification. A note name is shown, and you click the staff where that note belongs. It uses the Note names setting from Note Identification. With scale degrees selected, the question names the key, degree and octave. Under Question Type , choose Notes Only for note names or Scale and Degree to use selected keys. Switch between Major and Minor to choose signatures for each. To practice just one group, leave the other tab’s keys unchecked. Minor uses the natural minor scale. Under Degrees , check the scale degrees to practice. For example, choose D major and degree 3 to practice placing F♯. Octave is on by default. Turn it off to place the note in any octave. Middle C is C4. On a grand staff, click the upper staff for notes from middle C up and the lower staff for the notes below. Staff Key selects the signatures drawn on the staff independently of the keys in the prompts. Choose the unmarked signature for a staff with no sharps or flats. If the signatures differ, use the accidental buttons as needed. Use the accidental buttons or right-click the staff to choose a sharp, flat, natural, or no sign. A wrong click shows the note you placed so you can adjust and try again. Only the exact spelling counts, so G♯ is not A♭. Without the mouse: the Higher and Lower buttons (or the ↑ and ↓ keys) move the note a line or space, and Octave ↑ and Octave ↓ ( Page Up and Page Down ) an octave. Typing a letter from A to G jumps to the nearest note with that name. Place note ( Return ) places it. A line under the staff says which note is chosen, in words a screen reader can read.

title: Exercises
text: Clef Basics Clef Basics has two kinds of question, chosen with Question Type in the exercise settings: Clef Construction , which is described first, and Clef Identification , described at the end. In Clef Construction a blank staff is shown with the question under it, such as “Place the mezzo-soprano clef.” Every clef is one of three symbols, the G clef , the C clef or the F clef , put on a particular line of the staff: Clef Symbol and line Treble The G clef on the second line French violin The G clef on the bottom line Bass The F clef on the fourth line Subbass The F clef on the top line Alto The C clef on the middle line Tenor The C clef on the fourth line Mezzo-soprano The C clef on the second line Soprano The C clef on the bottom line Baritone The F clef on the middle line, or the C clef on the top line: both are accepted Choose the symbol with the three buttons under the music, by turning the mouse wheel, or by right-clicking. Click where it goes. The symbol follows the pointer, in a lighter color, and is placed where you click. To mix things up it can be tried on any line or space of the staff, and on up to three ledger lines and spaces above and below it, but only the places in the table are right. Without the mouse: ← and → choose the symbol, ↑ and ↓ move it up and down a line or space, and Return presses Answer . The right symbol in the wrong place is wrong, and so is another symbol in the right place. A wrong try turns red and clears so you can try again; only your first try counts toward your score. This exercise makes no sound.

title: Exercises
text: Clef Identification A clef is drawn on a staff, with “Which clef is this?” under it. Press the button with its name. There is a button for each clef that is asked for, and at least two buttons even if only one clef is asked for. A baritone clef is drawn the way you chose in Settings . Like the other exercises with buttons, the buttons have keys, shown when you hover over them.

title: Exercises
text: Reference and lesson The book button (experimental), beside the help button, opens a reference in a pane on the right: the three symbols and a picture of each clef with where its symbol goes. A button at the top opens the Clef Basics lesson .

title: Exercises
text: Settings In the exercise settings you can choose: Question Type: Clef Construction or Clef Identification. Clefs: the clefs that are asked for: the seven clefs of the other exercises, then, at the bottom, the French violin and subbass clefs, which only this exercise has.

title: Exercises
text: Interval Identification Name the interval between the two written notes. By default the notes appear together on a treble or bass staff, and the exercise asks for both quality and number. An interval has a quality and a number. The number counts the letter names it spans, including both notes. The quality is P (perfect), M (major), m (minor), A (augmented) or d (diminished). So C to E is M3, and C to E♭ is m3. Clefs chooses which staves can appear, including the grand staff. Range sets the lowest and highest written notes for each checked clef. Both notes must fit. Staff Key selects the signatures drawn on the staff. Choose zero for a blank signature. Display Mode defaults to Harmonic , which shows and plays both notes together. Melodic shows and plays them one at a time. Under Melodic, check Ascending (lower note first, the default), Descending (higher note first), or both to practice them in random order. You can also check both Harmonic and Melodic to mix presentations. Quality sets what you identify. For C up to E♭, choose 3 in Interval Only , m3 in Interval and Quality (default), or m in Quality Only . Inversions asks you to name the inversion of the interval on the staff. For C4 up to E4, imagine moving C4 up an octave. E4 up to C5 is a minor sixth. Choose 6 , m6 , or m according to your Quality setting. Reduce compound intervals first. A major tenth inverts like a major third, and a perfect octave inverts to a perfect unison. Intervals selects the spellings you want to practice, including compound intervals through a fifteenth. Each row shows one interval number. From left to right, the columns are augmented, major or perfect, minor, and diminished. The checklist and slider offer intervals that fit at least one selected clef’s range. For example, a staff range from C4 to E4 offers seconds and thirds. Drag the handles to select a span of interval numbers, then check individual spellings. Select all temporarily includes every available spelling. Widening a range restores any previously checked intervals that now fit. Accidentals controls the signs allowed beside either note. ♮ allows an unmarked note following the staff key. For example, in G major an unmarked F sounds as F♯. The default selection is ♮ , ♭ , and ♯ . Check 𝄫 for double flats or 𝄪 for double sharps. Note Value chooses which written durations can appear. Both notes use the same value. Buttons defaults to Limited , with six answers. Choose a Button count from 2 to 10. The count includes the correct answer. Choose All to show every eligible answer for the current staff range and selected intervals. Each distinct number or quality appears once when practicing that part alone.

title: Exercises
text: Interval Construction Place a second note on the staff to form the requested interval. For a minor third above C, count C, D, E, then choose a flat and place E♭. Clicking the staff submits the note. You can also move the caret with the arrow keys and press Enter. You can also play the endpoint on a MIDI keyboard . Clefs , Range , and Staff Key determine where the notes can appear. Display Mode stacks harmonic intervals and places melodic notes in sequence, ascending or descending. Under Quality , choose Interval and Quality for an exact spelling, Interval Only for a number, or Quality Only for a quality. When several enabled intervals fit the prompt, any of their endpoints is correct. Intervals , Accidentals , and Note Value control which spellings, written signs, and durations appear.

title: Exercises
text: Keyboard Interval Identification Two piano keys are highlighted together. Identify the interval from the lower key to the higher key. Choose from a configurable number of interval buttons (six by default), show every selected interval, or answer with a quality letter and a number. The full answer bank stays in interval order and scrolls when needed. Count the half steps between the highlighted keys, including black keys. P means perfect, M means major, and m means minor. Six half steps form a tritone, shown as A4 / d5 : the keyboard cannot distinguish an augmented fourth from a diminished fifth without written note spellings. The other distances use their standard interval names. A correct answer plays both notes together. Open the exercise settings to choose: Range: drag on the keyboard, adjust the lowest and highest keys with the arrows, or choose Entire keyboard . Both highlighted notes stay within this range. Reset to default restores C3–C5. Intervals: select the interval distances to practice. Only selected intervals appear as questions and answer choices. The list shows every distance that fits the range, including compound intervals beyond an octave: for example, C3–C5 offers intervals through P15 (two octaves). Options use notation only and are grouped into Simple intervals (up to an octave) and Compound intervals (beyond an octave). Drag the two slider handles below Select all to select an interval range, such as m3–P8. Use the arrow buttons beside From and To to adjust either endpoint by one half step, or click an endpoint’s notation to choose an interval from its scrollable dropdown. These controls change the selected intervals, not the keyboard range. Select all temporarily selects every interval that fits; switching it off restores your previous selection. With no intervals selected, the exercise pauses until you select one. Narrowing the range removes intervals that no longer fit; if a nonempty selection no longer fits, minor seconds are selected so the exercise can continue. Open Buttons to choose one answer mode: Limited: use Button count , directly below this option, to choose the maximum number of answers (six by default). Type a count or use its arrows. The count includes the correct answer; fewer buttons appear when fewer intervals are selected. All: show every selected interval in a fixed, scrollable answer bank. Compact: click a quality letter and an interval number, in either order. Quality and Interval label the two groups above their buttons. Both A4 and d5 are accepted for a tritone, including corresponding compound spellings. The mode, limited button count, range, and interval selections are saved. These settings are saved independently of Keyboard Note Identification.

title: Exercises
text: Key Signature Identification A key signature is drawn on a staff and you press the tonic of the scale it belongs to. The kind of scale is written under the staff with a blank for the tonic: “_ Major”, “_ minor” or, for a mode, “_ Dorian”. This exercise makes no sound: a right answer plays no tone. The speaker button is a mute for the whole app, so it works here as everywhere else, but has nothing to silence in this exercise. A mode uses the key signature of a major key and starts from another note of it, so D Dorian has the signature of C major (no sharps or flats), started from D. By default Alto asks major and natural minor keys, on the treble and bass staves. In the exercise settings you can choose: Clefs: any of the seven clefs (treble, bass, alto, tenor, soprano, mezzo-soprano and baritone), for the signature that is drawn. Scales: major (Ionian), Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, minor (Aeolian) and Locrian. Key signatures: which of the fifteen signatures, from seven flats to seven sharps, can appear.

title: Exercises
text: Key Signature Construction The reverse of the exercise above. A blank staff is shown with the name of a key under it, such as “D Major”, “A♯ minor” or “E Dorian”. Build that key’s signature with the fork under the staff, then press Answer (or Return ). The fork is shaped like a tuning fork lying on its side. Its stem, on the left, ends in a natural sign: no sharps or flats, C major. The stem opens into two tines: the top one has the sharps, 1 to 7, and the bottom one the flats, 1 to 7. A circle marks what you have chosen, and the staff shows that many sharps or flats as you move it. To choose: Click a number, or the natural sign. A number lights up a little as the mouse passes over it. Drag the circle along the fork. It follows the mouse, around the bend and out along either tine, and slides to the nearest number when you let go. Turn the mouse wheel to move the circle along the fork, one number for each notch: up toward more sharps, down toward more flats, passing through the natural sign on the way from one side to the other. The wheel works over the staff and the Answer button too. Press the arrow keys ( ↑ or → for a sharp, ↓ or ← for a flat) wherever the keyboard is on the exercise screen, and Home to go back to the natural sign. Then press Return . A wrong signature turns the circle red and puts it back on the natural sign so you can try again; only your first try counts toward your score. Like Key Signature Identification, this exercise makes no sound. In the exercise settings you can choose: Clefs: any of the seven clefs, for the staff the signature is built on. Scales: major (Ionian), Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, minor (Aeolian) and Locrian. Key signatures: which of the fifteen signatures, from seven flats to seven sharps, can be asked. The settings are kept apart from those of Key Signature Identification.

title: Exercises
text: Order of Keys Read the key below the blank staff. Choose ♯ or ♭ , then click the line or space for each sign in order. Each click fills the next slot after the clef. For D major in treble clef, place F♯ on the top line, then C♯ in the third space. Use Undo (Backspace) to remove the last sign and Answer (Return) to submit. Submit the empty staff for a key with no sharps or flats, such as C major, A minor, or D Dorian. With the keyboard, choose a sharp with + or a flat with − , move up or down with the arrow keys, and press P to place each sign. Open the exercise settings to choose Clefs , Scales , and Key Signatures . By default, questions use treble and bass clefs, major and natural minor scales, and all 15 signatures. You can select any of the seven single-staff clefs and any of the seven diatonic modes. For example, selecting alto clef, Dorian, and two flats gives you C Dorian on an alto staff. Starting Accidentals lets you choose how many sharps or flats are already on the staff. The default, 0 , starts with a blank signature. For example, with 2 ♯ selected, a question in A major shows two of its three sharps in their usual positions. Place the missing signs from left to right. You can enter up to seven signs in total, including those already shown. If the key needs six and you submit seven, the answer is marked wrong. Undo removes only signs you placed. When all the signs are already present, press Answer . Counts must fit one of your selected key signatures. If changing keys rules out every selected count, the setting returns to 0 .

title: Exercises
text: Scale Identification Read the eight notes on the staff. The first and last notes give the tonic. The pattern of whole and half steps gives the mode. For example, a scale from D to D with no sharps or flats is D Dorian. Under Question Type , check Key to answer D, Mode to answer Dorian, or both to identify the full scale. Open Clefs and Scales to choose the staves and modes to practice. Motion sets the direction of the written scale. Scale Key selects the signatures the scales may use, with separate Major and Minor tabs. Staff Key controls the signature drawn beside the clef. Read any accidentals beside the notes when the two signatures differ. Under Buttons , Limited offers complete answers up to the selected button count. With All and both question types enabled, choose a tonic and a mode from separate groups in either order.

title: Exercises
text: Scale Construction A blank staff is shown with the name of a scale under it, such as “D Major”, “E♭ minor” or “A Dorian”. Click the staff to place the scale’s notes from left to right in the requested direction, ending an octave from the first note: eight notes in all. In Motion , choose Ascending or Descending. The next note follows the pointer, snapped to a line or space, and each click puts it in the next place, so the notes do not move as you add more. With Octave off, choose any starting octave that leaves room for all eight notes. You never have to click the staff. Higher , Lower , Octave ↑ and Octave ↓ under it move the next note, the sign buttons choose its sign, and Place note puts it in the next place; the same things are on the keys (see Shortcuts ), and Return places the note and, when everything is placed, answers. By default the staff has no key signature, so a note that needs a sharp or a flat needs its own sign (see the staff’s key signature below for a staff that has one). To choose the sign for the next note: Right click the staff to step through no sign, ♯ and ♭, and around again. Turn the mouse wheel over the staff to step through them the same way: up goes no sign, ♯, ♭, and down goes the other way around. Press one of the sign buttons under the staff. Then click to place the note. A sign is used up by the note it goes on. Only the exact spelling counts, so G♯ is not A♭. Undo (or Backspace) takes back the last thing you placed. Answer (or Enter) hands in the scale once everything is placed. A wrong scale is cleared so that you can try again, and only your first try counts toward your score. With After Animation or Wait , a correct scale plays back. Each note turns green as it sounds, with the same timing when muted. In the exercise settings you can choose: Clefs: any of the seven clefs, for the staff the scale is placed on. Scales: major (Ionian), Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, minor (Aeolian) and Locrian. Staff Key: which key signatures may be drawn on the staff, from seven flats to seven sharps. It is separate from the scale’s own signature (below). By default only the blank staff, with no sharps or flats, is chosen. Scale Key: choose signatures separately on the Major and Minor tabs. Natural minor uses the Minor tab. Major and the other modes use the Major tab’s signatures. Octave: a switch, off by default. When it is on, the scale has to start in the octave named (below). Steps: a switch, off by default. When it is on, you also mark the whole and half steps between the notes (below). The settings are kept apart from those of the other exercises.

title: Exercises
text: Starting in the right octave By default the first and last notes must be an octave apart, and the scale is named without a starting octave, such as “G Major”. With Octave on, the name says which octave the first note is in, such as “G2 Major” or “B♭4 minor”, using the same numbers as note names everywhere in Alto (middle C is C4). The scale then has to be placed there: the right notes an octave higher or lower are wrong. The octave is part of the question, so scales are asked from well below to well above the staff. Alto only asks a scale that can be placed in full: all eight notes lie on the staff or on its ledger lines, within the furthest ledger line the staff can be clicked on. A bass clef G2 Major, which starts on the bottom line, can be asked; a scale that would run off the top of the ledger lines cannot.

title: Exercises
text: The staff’s key signature The key signature on the staff and the key signature of the scale are two separate settings, so a scale can be asked on a staff whose signature is not its own. Each question picks one of each. For example, with two flats on the staff (the signature of B♭ major) and a C major scale to place: A note you place with no sign takes the sign the staff’s signature gives its letter, as it would when you read music. With two flats, B and E are flat. So C major needs a natural (♮) on its E and its B, which you choose with the sign buttons, a right click or the wheel. Right click and the wheel step through no sign, ♯, ♭ and ♮ when the staff has a signature. Going the other way, a scale that has a flat the staff does not give needs that flat written as a sign. The notes the staff’s signature already covers are written with no sign, as in any score; only the notes that differ from it get one. Only the exact spelling counts, as ever.

title: Exercises
text: Marking the steps With Steps on, once the eight notes are placed two lines rise from each pair of neighboring notes to a point above them, starting with the first pair, with the step written over the point. The step that a click would mark is shown there in blue, as W (a whole step, two semitones) or H (a half step, one semitone). It starts as W. To choose: Turn the mouse wheel over the staff to switch between W and H (the wheel is for the signs until all the notes are placed). Right click the staff to switch between W and H. Press the W or H button under the staff. Then left click the staff to mark the step and move on to the next pair. Each new pair starts as W again, since most steps are whole. Undo takes back the steps, last first, before it takes back any notes. The scale is right when the notes and every step are right: a major scale is W W H W W W H, and a natural minor scale is W H W W H W W. The lines and letters turn green with the notes as the right scale plays.

title: Exercises
text: Circle of Fifths A circle of fifths, drawn as two rings of twelve wedges. The outer ring holds the major keys, with C at the top and each step clockwise a fifth higher: G, D, A, E, B, then F♯ at the bottom, and around through the flats back to F. The inner ring holds their relative minors, so A minor sits under C major, E minor under G major, and so on. The wedges are colored by key signature: cyan for the flat keys on the left, through royal blue at C, to indigo for the sharp keys on the right (the colors can be changed). The disc in the middle, which is the color of the window, shows the staff. Every question lights one cell and leaves its answer blank. There are three kinds, and the exercise settings (the sliders button) switch each on or off: Relative major. A minor key is shown, such as “F♯ minor”, with the wedge of the outer ring beside it blank. Press the name of its relative major, which has the same key signature: A, in this case. Relative minor. A major key is shown and the inner wedge beside it is blank. Press the name of its relative minor. Roman numerals. A key is in the middle with its staff and signature, and the six chords of the key that fit on the circle are lit. One of them is outlined. Press its Roman numeral. All of them are on buttons at the bottom, laid out like the Keyboard Note Identification screen: the letters in the middle row, the sharps above them and the flats below. For the minor keys the buttons read Am, F♯m and so on. You can also type: a letter, Shift and a letter for a sharp, or Ctrl and a letter for a flat. The numerals are on 1 to 6 .

title: Exercises
text: Colors The Colors row of the exercise settings (the sliders button) chooses how the circle is colored. Pick one of fourteen presets, or press Create your own… to make one. Cyan to indigo is the default. Cyan runs through the flat keys, royal blue marks C and indigo the sharp keys, so a key’s color tells you how far it is from C. Midnight, Deepening, Two blues, Checker and Glacier are other blues to go with this site. Glacier, like Paper, has pale wedges with dark names, for a light window. Sharps and flats, Major and minor, Spectrum, After Scriabin, Ink, Ember, Color-blind safe and Paper are the other presets. Color-blind safe uses six hues from the Okabe and Ito palette. A scheme of your own is made in one of five ways: One color , Two rings (one color for the major keys and one for the minor), By key signature (a color for the flat keys, for C and for the sharp keys, blended between), Distance from C (a color for C and one for F♯, mirrored on both sides) and Around the circle (one color, turned a twelfth of the wheel for each step). The colors you choose are what a cell looks like when it is lit; the quiet cells are made from them. You can choose dark wedges with light names or light wedges with dark names, name the scheme, edit it later and delete it. Your schemes are saved with your other settings, up to 24 of them. The colors apply to every picture of the circle: the exercise, the lessons and the reference. Changing them keeps the question you are on.

title: Exercises
text: Keys with two names Three of the wedges have two names on the circle: B and C♭, F♯ and G♭, and D♭ and C♯, with their minors G♯m and A♭m, D♯m and E♭m, and B♭m and A♯m. For these you press both names, in either order. A right first name is marked and its button is switched off, the middle of the circle says “and its other name”, and nothing is scored until the second is pressed. A wrong button at any point counts as a miss, and you can carry on until both are found.

title: Exercises
text: Roman numerals on the circle A key has seven chords, and the circle has room for six of them: its own wedge and the wedge on each side, on both rings. The outer ring holds the major chords, so it gets the capitals: I (the key itself), IV (one step counterclockwise) and V (one step clockwise). The inner ring holds the minor chords, so it gets the small letters: vi (under the key), ii (under IV) and iii (under V). In C major that is I = C, ii = Dm, iii = Em, IV = F, V = G and vi = Am. If you have seen pictures of this with two sets of numerals, one outer and one inner, they are one set shared between the two rings. The seventh chord, vii° (B diminished in C major), is diminished and does not sit on the circle, so it is never asked. A chord is spelled as its key spells it: in F♯ major the V is C♯, although that wedge is labeled D♭ with C♯ as its other name.

title: Exercises
text: Right and wrong answers A right answer brightens the cell and writes its name in it, and puts the key’s staff and signature in the middle: “A major, 3 sharps”. For a numeral question all six numerals appear. The book button (experimental), beside the help button, opens a reference in a pane on the right: a short description and an interactive circle with every key named. Click a key on either ring, or move with the arrow keys (Left and Right go around, Up and Down switch rings, Escape or a click in the middle starts again). The circle lights that key’s six chords, shows its key signature in the middle, and the text underneath explains it: its sharps or flats, which key it follows, its relative minor or major, and its chords. It shares the right-hand side with the settings, so opening one closes the other. It is a study aid, so it also gives away the answers. A button at the top of the pane opens the circle of fifths lesson . A wrong answer flashes the cell in the same red as the wrong button, striped so that it still shows on the red wedge at the top. The button is switched off and you can try again. Only your first try counts toward your score. This exercise makes no sound.

title: Exercises
text: Chord Quality A chord is drawn in root position on a treble or bass staff. Press its type: major, minor, diminished, augmented, major 7th, dominant 7th, minor 7th, half-diminished 7th and diminished 7th. Check the size of the intervals stacked above the lowest note to tell the types apart.

title: Exercises
text: Arpeggio Identification A chord is drawn one note at a time, rising from its lowest note to the same note an octave higher. Press its type, then press its inversion. The answer counts once you have chosen both, in either order, and a wrong pair is cleared so you can try again. The inversion is which chord tone is lowest: Inversion Lowest note Root position the root 1st inversion the third 2nd inversion the fifth 3rd inversion the seventh (seventh chords only) By default Alto asks major, minor, dominant 7th and diminished 7th arpeggios on the treble and bass staves, in every inversion. In the exercise settings you can choose: Clefs: any of the seven clefs, from treble to baritone. Arpeggio types: any of major, minor, diminished and augmented triads, and dominant 7th, major 7th, minor 7th, half-diminished 7th and diminished 7th chords. The type buttons below the staff follow your choice. Inversions: root position and the first three inversions. A triad has no 3rd inversion, so that choice only applies to seventh chords. Key signatures: draw a key signature from the keys you pick. The arpeggio then only gets a sign where it differs from the signature, so a natural sign appears where the chord needs one.

title: Exercises
text: Instrument pack exercises Installed packs add exercises to the Instruments category. The example viola pack includes Viola Note Identification and Parts of the Viola . The example harpsichord pack adds Harpsichord Interval Identification and Parts of the Harpsichord . Download an example and follow its tutorial to create exercises with your own artwork and recordings. Viola plugin tutorial · Harpsichord plugin tutorial
