title: Getting started
text: Linux download Download Alto for Linux for an x86-64 desktop. The archive includes Python and Qt. Extract the archive, open a terminal in the extracted folder, and run sh install.sh install . Open Alto from your application menu. The installer puts Alto in ~/.local/opt/alto and creates the command ~/.local/bin/alto for your account. For other processor architectures, see Running from a source checkout .

title: Getting started
text: Windows installer Windows code-signing certificate. We’re working on getting a certificate to sign Alto’s Windows installer. Until then, Windows may show Unknown publisher or block the installer before setup starts. Help with Windows installation warnings Download the 64-bit Windows installer for Windows 10 or 11. Open the downloaded .exe and follow the setup prompts. Open Alto from the Start menu. The installer includes Python and Qt and installs Alto for your account.

title: Getting started
text: Mac source installation On Mac, you can try Alto from source. macOS is currently untested. With Git and Python 3.11 or newer installed, open Terminal and run: git clone https://github.com/altosaurus/alto.git cd alto python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -e . .venv/bin/python -m alto To open Alto again, run .venv/bin/python -m alto from the same alto folder.

title: Getting started
text: Check your download Download SHA256SUMS from the same release as your download. It lists the SHA-256 checksum of each file. In the folder containing the archive and SHA256SUMS , run: sha256sum --check --ignore-missing SHA256SUMS Look for OK after the archive name. Open PowerShell in the folder containing the installer. Use the exact name of the file you downloaded: Get-FileHash ".\alto-0.0.2-windows-x64-setup.exe" -Algorithm SHA256 Open SHA256SUMS in Notepad and find the line naming that same .exe . Every character in its checksum should match the Hash printed by PowerShell (uppercase and lowercase are equivalent). If they differ, discard the installer and download it again from the official Alto release.

title: Getting started
text: Windows installer troubleshooting

title: Getting started
section: Edge says the download is uncommon
text: Edge says the download is uncommon An uncommon-download warning means Microsoft Edge has little download history for that file. Check that you started from the altosaurus/alto GitHub release. If you choose to keep the file, check its checksum before opening it. If the browser or antivirus identifies a specific threat, stop and leave the file blocked. Microsoft’s SmartScreen guidance

title: Getting started
text: “Windows protected your PC” or “Unknown publisher” If SmartScreen calls Alto an unrecognized app, select More info to see the filename and publisher. Unknown publisher is expected for the current unsigned installer. On your own PC, if the filename and checksum match the official release and you trust the download, choose Run anyway to start setup. Choose Don’t run if you’re unsure. How SmartScreen checks app reputation

title: Getting started
section: Windows blocks the installer with no “Run anyway” option
text: Windows blocks the installer with no “Run anyway” option On a work or school PC, your organization may control which apps can run. Give your IT team the Alto release link and the exact message so they can review it. If Windows 11 names Smart App Control , it has no per-app exception. Keep the protection enabled and check back for a signed release. Microsoft’s Smart App Control FAQ

title: Getting started
section: Setup stops at “Microsoft Visual C++ Runtime”
text: Setup stops at “Microsoft Visual C++ Runtime” Alto needs Microsoft’s x64 Visual C++ Redistributable . If setup asks for administrator permission for that component, check that the prompt identifies Microsoft Corporation as the publisher. If its download fails or you’re installing offline, get the x64 package from Microsoft, install it, restart if prompted, then run Alto’s installer again. Microsoft’s runtime download If you’re still stuck, include the Alto installer filename, your Windows version, and the exact message when you report an installation issue .

title: Getting started
text: Install as a program (Linux) To install from GitHub with uv , run sh scripts/alto-install.sh install from the repository. Open Alto from the application menu. Use sh scripts/alto-install.sh update to update the program and refresh its menu entry and icon. The in-app updater can update this installation too. Choose Follow the main branch in Settings → Updates to get changes before release. Packaged installations follow releases.

title: Getting started
text: Running from a source checkout For development, install Git and Python 3.11 or newer. Alto installs PySide6 and the other dependencies into the virtual environment. Run the following commands, then use git pull from the checkout to get source updates. git clone https://github.com/altosaurus/alto.git cd alto python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -e . .venv/bin/python -m alto git clone https://github.com/altosaurus/alto.git cd alto py -3 -m venv . venv . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e . . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m alto

title: Getting started
text: Updating Alto Open ☰ → Tools and choose Check for updates… to check manually. Alto also checks for releases when the main grid is active, up to once every 24 hours. Settings → Updates shows your version and lets you turn automatic checks off. For a packaged installation, choose Yes to download an offered release, No for a reminder after 24 hours, or Don’t remind me again to skip it. Alto verifies the signature on SHA256SUMS with its built-in public key and checks the package against the signed list before installation. Press OK when prompted to restart. You can also unpack a newer archive and run sh install.sh install again. A failed installation keeps your previous copy. If you run Alto straight from the unpacked folder, download the new archive yourself. You can also run a newer Windows installer to update your copy. Close Alto and run these commands in Terminal from your alto folder to update the source and its dependencies: git pull .venv/bin/python -m pip install -e . .venv/bin/python -m alto

title: Getting started
text: Uninstalling Alto For the Linux download, run sh install.sh uninstall from the extracted folder. For the uv installation, run sh scripts/alto-install.sh uninstall from the repository. Both commands remove the program and its menu entry and keep your practice history and settings. Add --purge to delete them too. Open Settings → Apps , select Alto , and choose Uninstall . The uninstaller asks whether to also remove your practice history and settings. Quit Alto. If you no longer need the source checkout, move the cloned alto folder, including its .venv , to the Trash. Your practice history is stored separately in ~/Library/Application Support/Alto/alto.db . To keep a copy of your practice history and settings, choose Export backup… in Alto before uninstalling. Your data

title: Getting started
text: First launch The first time you open Alto it asks you to create a profile. Type a name and press Create profile . There is no password, and the name is only a label that keeps your history separate from anyone else who uses the same computer. Next time Alto opens straight into the profile you used last. To switch to someone else, or add another profile, open the menu (☰) and choose Profile . Alto includes the default Finale Maestro notation font. To use the optional Noto Music style, install the Noto Music font on your system and choose it in Settings .

title: Getting started
text: Your first session Click an exercise on the home screen. Follow the prompt. Click an answer button or use the shortcut in its tooltip. For a construction question, place the requested note or sign. A correct answer turns green. With the default scheduler, try a missed question again. With SM-2 or FSRS, a miss moves the card to the learning queue for a later retry. The counter at the top shows how many you have right and your current streak. The Exercises / Lessons control at the top left selects what to browse. Alto starts with tiles. Navigation Pane opens the matching list on the left; before you start an activity, the main panel says “Select an exercise to begin.” or “Select a lesson to begin.” Use the separate Tiles grid button to return to tiles without losing your place. The icon-only Exercises / Lessons pair sits at the top left, followed by an open/close navigation-pane button, a divider, and a separate grid button for returning to tiles. Hover over an icon to see its name. The search field below filters the selected section by name, description or category, and follows the sidebar’s width. On the tile grid or during an exercise, click the funnel icon at the right end of the search row to open the filter sidebar. Click it again to collapse the sidebar and keep your filters. The sidebar opens on the right with every category expanded. Check or clear a category to include or hide its activities, or check individual exercises or lessons. The tiles and navigation list show the same matches. A dash means some activities in a category are checked. All categories selects or clears the whole list. Turn on Shuffle exercises , just left of the funnel, to practice the exercises in your filtered list. After each right or wrong answer, Alto prefers an exercise from another category. If the other available exercises are in the current category, it picks one of those. For example, selecting only Note Identification and Keyboard Note Identification makes them alternate when both have questions available. Your Next Question setting controls when the switch happens. With Wait , click Next after reviewing your answer. You can change the filters while answering a question. Shuffle uses the updated list for the next question and returns to the tiles if the list is empty. Click the highlighted shuffle icon again to turn it off. Only the checked exercises appear in the grid. The New, Learn, and Due totals at the left count cards from these two exercises. During an exercise or lesson, Exercises / Lessons switches the list while keeping your activity on screen. Selecting an item starts or resumes it. The top-left pane button hides and shows the list without leaving your activity. Statistics and Browse database are at the top right. The sliders button opens the exercise’s own settings, and ? explains it. The navigation pane lists the same two exercises as the filtered grid. The blue shuffle button stays available while you practice.

title: Getting started
text: Glossary Open Glossary in the top toolbar to look up a term. Search for minor , for example, and select harmonic minor scale . You can hear the scale, try another example, or open a related exercise from the same page. In A harmonic minor, listen for the three half steps from F to G♯ and the half step from G♯ to A.

title: Getting started
text: Running the tests From a source checkout, install the development dependencies and run the test suite. .venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ".[dev]" .venv/bin/python -m pytest . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -e ".[dev]" . \.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pytest

title: Animation
text: Animation Alto moves a few things on purpose: the exercise list slides shut, the settings pane slides open and its pages slide in and out, switches slide, and an answer button fades to green or red. None of it is decoration. Motion tells the eye what changed and where it went . This chapter explains Qt’s animation tools, how each of Alto’s animations is built, the patterns that keep them from going wrong, and the design rules that decide how long and in what manner to move something.

title: Animation
text: What an animation is An animation changes a value over time. Everything else follows from that sentence. Pick a value that describes the look: a number from 0 to 1, a position, a width, a color. Pick a start and an end and a duration . At each tick Qt computes where the value is on its way (a number between the start and the end, shaped by an easing curve ) and hands it to you. You apply it: move something, resize it, set a color, call update() and repaint with it. A screen refreshes about 60 times a second, so a 200 ms animation is roughly twelve frames. Qt drives the ticks from its event loop, which means they stop if you block the loop. That is why the first rule of Qt and PySide6 (never block) is also the first rule of animation.

title: Animation
text: The tools Qt provides Class What it does QVariantAnimation Animates any value (a float, a color, a point) and calls a function with each value: valueChanged . The general tool. QPropertyAnimation Animates a named property of an object ( b"pos" , b"maximumWidth" , b"volume" ) directly, so you do not write the callback. QParallelAnimationGroup Runs several animations at once. QSequentialAnimationGroup Runs them one after another. QEasingCurve Shapes the progress: OutCubic , InOutQuad , Linear , OutBack and about forty more. QTimer Not an animation, but the tool for “do this once, later”. Two of these cover nearly everything. Use QPropertyAnimation when the thing you are animating is already a Qt property, and QVariantAnimation when it is not (or you need to draw from the value).

title: Animation
text: Easing A linear animation moves at constant speed, which looks mechanical, because real things accelerate and slow. An easing curve changes the speed over the animation. The names say where the speed changes: In starts slowly, Out ends slowly, InOut does both. Alto uses OutCubic almost everywhere: it starts fast and settles gently, which feels responsive, because the first thing the user sees is immediate movement. The curves go back to the easing equations of Robert Penner, which Qt’s set is based on. Rules of thumb that most design systems agree on: use ease- out for things entering or responding to the user (they arrive and settle); ease- in for things leaving (they accelerate away); ease- in-out for things that move from one place to another on screen; and linear only for color fades, rotations and progress bars, where no physical object is implied.

title: Animation
section: Alto’s animations, one at a time
text: Alto’s animations, one at a time

title: Animation
text: The settings page slide: SlideStack SlideStack in settings_menu.py is a QStackedWidget whose pages slide instead of switching. It is a good model of how to build a transition by hand: def slide_to ( self , index ): if self . sliding or index == self . currentIndex (): return # ignore requests mid-transition old , new = self . currentWidget (), self . widget ( index ) w , sign = self . width (), 1 if index > self . currentIndex () else - 1 new . setGeometry ( 0 , 0 , w , self . height ()) new . move ( sign * w , 0 ) # park the new page just outside, on the side it enters from new . show () new . raise_ () group = QParallelAnimationGroup ( self ) for widget , start , end in (( old , 0 , - sign * w ), ( new , sign * w , 0 )): anim = QPropertyAnimation ( widget , b "pos" , group ) # animate the widget's own position property anim . setDuration ( 220 ) anim . setEasingCurve ( QEasingCurve . Type . OutCubic ) anim . setStartValue ( QPoint ( start , 0 )) anim . setEndValue ( QPoint ( end , 0 )) group . addAnimation ( anim ) group . finished . connect ( done ) # setCurrentIndex(index) and put both pages at (0, 0) motion . play ( group ) # group.start(), held still in tests until they settle it Points to copy: the new page is positioned off-screen before it is shown (otherwise it flashes in place for one frame); the two pages move in parallel; a request that arrives mid-slide is ignored rather than queued (so a double click does not slide twice); and the final state is set in finished , not assumed, so the widgets always end in a clean position.

title: Animation
section: Opening and closing a pane: animate a limit
text: Opening and closing a pane: animate a limit The exercise’s settings pane opens by animating maximumWidth of the pane from 0 to PANE_WIDTH ( QPropertyAnimation(self.pane, b"maximumWidth", self) , 220 ms, OutCubic ). The layout does the rest: as the pane’s allowed width grows, the layout gives it the room and shrinks its neighbor. This is a common Qt trick: animate a constraint, not a position , and let the layout move everything. The pane is hidden when it finishes at zero ( _pane_settled ) so it takes no space and cannot be tabbed into.

title: Animation
text: The sidebar: animate the splitter The sidebar collapse in MainWindow._set_sidebar uses a QVariantAnimation from the current width to the target and, on each tick, calls splitter.setSizes . The animation is a number; the callback decides what the number means. Two details: It temporarily lowers the list’s minimum width so the width can pass through values below the usual minimum, and restores it in done . It stops the previous animation first ( self._sidebar_anim.stop() ) and starts from wherever the sidebar currently is, so clicking the toggle in the middle of a slide reverses smoothly instead of jumping.

title: Animation
section: The switch knob: animate a number, paint from it
text: The switch knob: animate a number, paint from it Switch (also in settings_menu.py ) holds a float _pos between 0 and 1. A QVariantAnimation of 140 ms moves _pos , and each tick calls update() . paintEvent draws the track color as blend(off, b=on, t=self._pos) and the knob at margin + r + _pos * travel . One number drives both the color and the position, so they cannot disagree. The class setChecked skips the animation ( “no animation when set programmatically” ) so that loading a setting at start-up does not make every switch slide.

title: Animation
section: The right/wrong flash: animate a color
text: The right/wrong flash: animate a color ExerciseView._flash fades an answer button from black to the correct-answer green in 180 ms. Calling it without a target uses CORRECT_ANSWER_COLOR from alto/ui/colors.py . The wrong-answer handler passes red explicitly. The flash uses QVariantAnimation with a start of 0.0 and an end of 1.0 and in its callback computes blend(start, b=end, t=t) and sets the button’s style sheet from the result. The animations are kept in a list ( self._anims ) that is cleared when the next question appears, so nothing animates a button that no longer exists. Pass the answered notes to ExerciseView._finish_answer , grouped by onset. In After Animation and Wait , the playback callback colors each sounding staff column or piano key green and clears the highlight at the end. After Animation then starts the advance timer. Wait keeps the answer on screen until the learner presses Next . Immediately gives the answer button a brief green flash and plays the same audio without highlighting the music or delaying the next question.

title: Animation
text: The fade of a sound Not visual, but the same idea: Sounds._release fades a QSoundEffect ’s volume property to 0 in 70 ms with a QPropertyAnimation , then stops it. See Computer audio .

title: Animation
text: Patterns that keep animations correct Keep a reference. A QVariantAnimation created in a function with no parent and no stored reference can be garbage collected while running, and simply stops. Give it a parent ( QVariantAnimation(self) ) or store it ( self._anim = ... ). Stop the old one first. If an animation of the same property may already be running, call .stop() before starting a new one, and start from the current value, not from a remembered end. Otherwise two animations fight. Set the end state in finished . Do not rely on the last tick landing exactly on the end value. Guard against re-entry. Ignore a request while a transition is running ( SlideStack ), or cancel and restart (the sidebar). Decide deliberately which; the one you did not decide on is the one with the bug. Cancel late callbacks with a token. A QTimer.singleShot cannot be canceled once scheduled. If the callback might fire after the state has moved on (a new question has appeared), have it compare a counter it captured against the current one and do nothing if they differ. ExerciseView._pair_token and Sounds._sequence_run do this. Do not animate loading. Setting a value from saved settings should jump, not animate (see Switch.setChecked ). Animate cheap things. Each tick repaints. Moving a widget or changing a width is cheap; repainting a large, complex widget sixty times a second is not. If a widget is expensive to draw, draw it once into a QPixmap and animate the pixmap.

title: Animation
text: Testing animations A test checks one thing. A test of whether an answer is right should not depend on how long the feedback takes to fade, and a test of a fade should not depend on what was answered. Alto’s tests come in three kinds: Kind Tests Motion Logic Questions, answers, scheduling: exercise.generate , question.check , the learner None: no widgets Screen What the interface shows and does: a click answers, a wrong answer clears the staff to try again Held until the test settles it Motion The animation or the timing itself: a flash fades, notes light up as they sound Real durations, marked @pytest.mark.motion Animations and feedback delays go through alto/ui/motion.py : motion.play(animation) starts an animation, in place of animation.start() . motion.later(delay, owner=..., step=...) runs a step after a delay, in place of QTimer.singleShot . motion.start_timer(timer, delay=...) starts a single-shot timer. motion.set_shortcut(button, key=...) gives a button a key. Pressing the key shows the button pressed for a moment and then clicks it, as Qt does, but in tests the key clicks the button at once. In the app these take their real time. In tests, tests/conftest.py turns on instant motion for every test not marked motion . Then nothing moves on by itself: an animation holds at its start, and a delayed step or timer waits, however long the test takes, until the test calls motion.settle() . That runs everything waiting, in order, at once. So a screen test looks like this: view . answer_button . click () assert ( view . missed and view . scale_input . locked ) # the wrong-answer feedback is showing motion . settle () # the feedback ends assert not view . scale_input . locked # cleared to try again There is no wait to guess at, so the test is as fast on a slow machine as on a fast one, and it cannot fail because a machine was busy. Use QTest.qWait only in a motion test. New animations and delays should go through alto/ui/motion.py so their tests can settle them. SlideStack.sliding reports whether a slide is underway; to test that a request during a slide is ignored, call it twice in a row and assert one slide happened.

title: Animation
text: Deciding how it should move A few principles, from animation and interface design. Duration. Interface animations feel good between about 150 and 300 ms. Under 100 ms the eye barely registers movement; over 500 ms it feels slow, and a user doing something repeatedly is made to wait. Larger moves can take longer than small ones. Alto’s are 70 to 350 ms. Purpose. Each animation should answer a question: where did that come from, what changed, did my action work? An animation that only decorates is noise the second time you see it. Direction means something. A page that slides in from the right says “forward”; sliding back from the left says “back”. Alto’s settings pages use this, and so should anything new. Continuity. Moving the object from where it was to where it is, instead of cutting, preserves the user’s sense of what it is. Follow-through and easing. Real objects do not stop dead. Easing out gives a soft landing. Respect the user’s settings. Many people turn on a “reduce motion” option in their operating system. Alto does not read it yet, which is a good first improvement: if it is set, use durations of 0. Stay consistent. Same durations and curves for the same kinds of motion, so the program feels like one thing. The 12 principles of animation from the Disney studios (squash and stretch, anticipation, staging, slow in and slow out, and so on) were written for cartoon characters, and the subset that applies to interfaces is the last three paragraphs above.

title: Animation
text: Words to search for Tweening (calculating the frames between two states). Easing, ease-in, ease-out, Bézier easing, cubic-bezier. Spring animation (physically based, overshoots; not in Qt’s standard set). Frame rate, vsync, jank. Dirty rectangle (repaint only what changed). Compositing. Reduced motion (an accessibility setting). Skeleton screens and loading states .

title: Animation
text: Further reading The Qt documentation: “The Animation Framework”, and the class pages for QVariantAnimation , QPropertyAnimation , QAbstractAnimation , QParallelAnimationGroup and QEasingCurve (which has a picture of every curve), at doc.qt.io. Robert Penner, Programming Macromedia Flash MX (McGraw-Hill/Osborne, 2002), chapter 7: the easing equations that nearly every animation library, Qt included, implements. Val Head, Designing Interface Animation: Improving the User Experience Through Animation (Rosenfeld Media, 2016): the book on motion in interfaces, with guidance on duration, easing and purpose. Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation (Abbeville Press, 1981): the twelve principles. Richard Williams, The Animator’s Survival Kit (Faber and Faber, 2001): timing and spacing in depth. Page Laubheimer, “Executing UX Animations: Duration and Motion Characteristics”, Nielsen Norman Group, nngroup.com (2014): research-backed guidance on how long interface animations should last. World Wide Web Consortium, Web Content Accessibility Guidelines 2.1 , success criterion 2.3.3 “Animation from Interactions”, w3.org/TR/WCAG21: on motion and people who are sensitive to it.

title: Computer audio
text: Computer audio Alto plays notes: when you answer correctly, when you press “hear it” on an instrument, when an arpeggio is sounded. That needs very little code, but a few ideas about how computers represent and play sound, and a few about how instruments sound, are what make the code readable and what let you change it safely. This chapter starts with those ideas, then walks through alto/audio.py .

title: Computer audio
text: Sound as numbers Sound is air pressure varying over time. A microphone turns it into a voltage, and an analogue-to-digital converter measures that voltage many times a second. The list of measurements is a digital audio signal . Playing it back reverses the process. Three numbers describe a recording: Sample rate : how many measurements per second. Alto uses 44,100 Hz (the Compact Disc rate; SAMPLE_RATE in audio.py ). Bit depth : how precisely each measurement is stored. WAV files in Alto are 16-bit : each sample is an integer from -32,768 to 32,767. Each bit adds about 6 dB of dynamic range (the gap between the quietest and loudest sound), so 16 bits give about 96 dB. Channels : one (mono) or two (stereo). Alto’s recordings and everything it makes are mono. The encoding of plain samples like this is called PCM , pulse-code modulation . A WAV file is a PCM stream with a small header (the RIFF container) saying the rate, depth and channels. Python’s standard wave module reads and writes them, which is all audio.py needs: with wave . open ( str ( path )) as w : pcm = array . array ( "h" ) # signed 16-bit integers pcm . frombytes ( w . readframes ( w . getnframes ())) samples = [ value / 32768 for value in pcm ] array.array("h") holds signed 16-bit integers. A WAV file stores them little-endian, least significant byte first, and wave hands them over in the computer’s own byte order, swapping them itself on a big-endian computer, which is the order array reads. Dividing by 32,768 turns the integers into floating-point numbers between -1 and 1, which are easier to compute with. Writing does the reverse: multiply by 32,767 and store as 16-bit integers, which wave writes little-endian.

title: Computer audio
text: The sampling theorem and aliasing The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem says that a signal can be captured perfectly if it is sampled at more than twice its highest frequency. At 44,100 Hz, nothing above 22,050 Hz can be represented, which is just above what people hear. A frequency that is too high is not lost but folded back down to a wrong, lower one. That is aliasing , and it is why recording equipment filters before sampling. It matters in Alto only when you change a sample’s speed (see below) or generate a sound with many high partials, which is why synth_piano stops adding partials above 12,000 Hz.

title: Computer audio
text: Loudness Clipping : a sample cannot go beyond -1 or 1. A calculation that goes past it is flattened (“clipped”), which sounds harsh. Anything you generate should be scaled down ( normalized ) so its peak is below 1. synth_piano scales its result so the loudest sample is 0.8. Decibels are a logarithmic scale for amplitude: 20 * log10(ratio) . Halving the amplitude is -6 dB. Because hearing is roughly logarithmic too, a linear volume of 0.5 does not sound “half as loud”; it sounds only a little quieter. Qt’s QSoundEffect.setVolume is linear. If you want a volume control that feels even, map it through a curve (Qt provides QtAudio.convertVolume for that). Summing sounds adds amplitudes , so a chord of four notes is louder, and can clip. Alto’s play_notes plays each note of a chord at 1.4 / sqrt(count) of full volume: that keeps the loudness of a chord about the same however many notes it has, because uncorrelated signals add in power (the square of amplitude), not in amplitude.

title: Computer audio
section: Pitch, frequency and the numbers behind notes
text: Pitch, frequency and the numbers behind notes A musical pitch is a frequency in hertz (cycles per second). Western music divides the octave into 12 equal ratios, equal temperament , so each semitone multiplies the frequency by 2^(1/12). MIDI (the Musical Instrument Digital Interface standard) numbers the notes: middle C is 60, A above it is 69, and each semitone adds one. The reference pitch A4 is 440 Hz (set by an international standard, ISO 16). The formula in synth_piano is the whole story: f0 = 440.0 * 2 ** (( midi - 69 ) / 12 ) # midi 60 gives 261.63 Hz Note.midi in alto/theory/pitch.py computes the MIDI number from a spelled note. Note that C♯4 and D♭4 have the same MIDI number and the same frequency (in equal temperament), which is why audio works with MIDI numbers while the rest of Alto works with spelled notes. A real note is not a pure tone. It is a fundamental at f0 plus overtones , or partials , at higher frequencies. In a string or a pipe the partials are close to whole-number multiples (the harmonic series : 2×, 3×, 4× …), and the mix of their strengths is what we hear as timbre , the difference between a flute and a viola playing the same note.

title: Computer audio
text: How Alto plays a note Everything is in the class Sounds and a single shared instance, sounds , in alto/audio.py .

title: Computer audio
text: Instruments and recordings An Instrument (a frozen dataclass) has a key , a label , a folder under alto/assets/ and a few flags: gain (its level relative to the piano), sustained and, for instruments with several ways of playing (the viola’s arco and pizzicato), a family and a variant . Recordings are one mono WAV file per note , named by MIDI number: alto/assets/samples/flute/72.wav is the flute’s C5. Most come from the University of Iowa Electronic Music Studios’ Musical Instrument Samples, recorded in a studio, in most cases at every semitone. An instrument that plays one recording for each pitch is a sampler , and the technique is multisampling . Professional samplers add more: several recordings per note at different loudnesses ( velocity layers ), alternating takes to avoid a machine-gun repetition ( round robin ), and repeating a section of a long note to sustain it ( looping ). Alto needs none of these, since each note is played once at one level.

title: Computer audio
text: Creating the sound play_midi(midi) -> _effect(inst, midi) get or make a QSoundEffect for (instrument, note) -> _note_file(inst, midi) find the WAV; make one if the note has no recording -> setVolume(...), play() _note_file returns the recording’s path if that note has one. If it does not, it picks the nearest recorded note and makes a new WAV by shifting its pitch (below), saved in alto_sounds in the system temporary folder and reused after that. The file’s name includes the size and modification time of the recording it came from, so a plugin update that replaces a recording gets a new file. The piano is special: beyond two semitones from a recording it is synthesized instead (below). Making a note takes a few tens of milliseconds, so alto.ui.warmup makes the current instrument’s missing notes ahead of time ( Sounds.unrecorded and Sounds.prepare ), one per idle moment after the window opens. _effect wraps the file in a QSoundEffect the first time and keeps it, so a note is loaded once. QSoundEffect is Qt Multimedia’s class for short, uncompressed sounds that must start with low delay: it loads the whole file into memory, so play() is quick. Qt has two others: QMediaPlayer streams longer, compressed audio and starts slower, and QAudioSink is a lower-level output that you feed raw samples yourself. Short WAV notes are what QSoundEffect is for. play_midi sets the volume (the requested volume times the instrument’s gain, capped at 1) and plays. It is wrapped in try/except and prints rather than raises: audio must never break an exercise , and machines with no sound card exist. sounds.enabled is the master switch the sound button controls; force=True plays anyway, for the instrument preview. A preview (the phrase played when you choose an instrument, and the sequences in some exercises) is one WAV with every note in it, so the notes stay evenly spaced whatever the computer is doing. _preview_file mixes it without leaving 16-bit integers: it reads the part of each note that is heard, fades out its tail, and adds the notes together with map(operator.add, ...) , so Python’s own C code does nearly all the work, at the rate the recordings share, so nothing is resampled. That is about as quick as NumPy would be. The clip is kept under a name made of everything it depends on, so a phrase is mixed once.

title: Computer audio
text: Pitch shifting by resampling def shift_pitch ( samples , * , semitones ): ratio = 2 ** ( semitones / 12 ) count = math . ceil (( len ( samples ) - 1 ) / ratio ) return _interpolate ( samples , step = ratio , count = count ) # the value at 0, ratio, 2 * ratio, ... _interpolate takes each position x , the sample a just before it and the one after, and returns a + (after - a) * (x - i) , where i is the whole part of x : a straight line between the two neighbors. To raise a recording by two semitones, read it 12% faster: take the samples at positions 0, 1.122, 2.245, … and interpolate between neighbors. This is resampling , and it is the simplest pitch shifter. It has two well-known side effects: the sound gets shorter (a note shifted up two semitones lasts 1/1.122 of the time, which the arithmetic above confirms: 70,560 samples become 62,861), and the timbre changes, because everything speeds up together (the “chipmunk effect”). For one or two semitones on a flute or a viola neither is noticeable, which is why Alto shifts only to fill the odd missing note. If you ever need large shifts, there are better algorithms, each a topic of its own: Phase vocoder : works in the frequency domain, so it can change pitch without changing duration, at some cost in clarity. PSOLA ( pitch-synchronous overlap-add ): cuts the sound into one-period grains and overlaps them at new spacing; good for speech and single voices. Better interpolation : drawing straight lines is linear interpolation , which smooths the high frequencies slightly. Sinc or polynomial interpolation is more accurate (a polyphase resampler such as scipy.signal.resample_poly ).

title: Computer audio
text: Making a piano with arithmetic synth_piano(midi) makes a piano note without any recording. It is additive synthesis : build the sound by adding sine waves, one per partial. The code has several pieces of real physics, each one line: f0 = 440.0 * 2 ** (( midi - 69 ) / 12 ) for n in range ( 1 , 17 ): # the first 16 partials f = ( n * f0 * math . sqrt ( 1 + inharm * n * n ) ) # stiff strings: partials sit slightly sharp amp = 1.0 / n ** 1.15 # higher partials are quieter if n % 7 == 0 : amp *= 0.3 # the hammer strikes ~1/7 along the string, which suppresses these decay = ( 2.2 + 1.1 * n + ( midi - 60 ) * 0.03 ) # higher partials, and higher notes, die faster phase = rng . uniform ( 0 , 2 * math . pi ) # one hammer strikes both strings, so they start together for detune in ( - 0.0008 , 0.0008 , ): # two strings per note, slightly apart: the shimmer # amp * 0.5 * sin(2π f (1 + detune) t + phase) * exp(-decay t), made one sample at a time step = 2 * math . pi * f * ( 1 + detune ) / SAMPLE_RATE turn = complex ( math . cos ( step ), math . sin ( step )) * math . exp ( - decay / SAMPLE_RATE ) z = amp * 0.5 * complex ( math . cos ( phase ), math . sin ( phase )) for k in range ( count ): out [ k ] += z . imag z *= turn Inharmonicity. A stiff string’s partials are not exact multiples of the fundamental; they are slightly sharper , by a factor of sqrt(1 + B n^2) for a constant B of the string. This is why a piano’s octaves are tuned wide, and why a pure harmonic sound would not sound like a piano. Decay is an exponential, exp(-decay * t) ; higher partials fade quicker, so the sound mellows as it rings. Strike point. Where the hammer hits a string, the partials that have a node there are not excited. Envelope. After the partials come an attack of a couple of milliseconds ( 1 - exp(-t / 0.002) ), a dip into the sustain, a short burst of filtered noise for the hammer’s thump (white noise smoothed by a moving average, a crude low-pass filter), and a 50 ms fade-out so the file does not end with a click. Alto computes this in plain Python, without NumPy: multiplying a complex number by the same small rotation, which also shrinks it a little, traces a decaying sine one sample at a time, so no sine or exponential is computed per sample. A note takes a fraction of a second, and the result is saved, so each note is made once. You can check the result in a few lines. A Fourier transform shows the spectrum, and the loudest peak of a synthesized middle C is at 261.9 Hz (the frequency resolution of a 1.6 second clip is about 0.6 Hz, so this is the fundamental, 261.63 Hz). This uses NumPy, which the tests install ( pip install -e ".[dev]" ) and Alto itself does not need: import numpy as np from alto.audio import synth_piano , SAMPLE_RATE x = synth_piano ( 60 ) spectrum = np . abs ( np . fft . rfft ( x * np . hanning ( len ( x ))) ) # a window function reduces leakage freqs = np . fft . rfftfreq ( len ( x ), 1 / SAMPLE_RATE ) print ( freqs [ spectrum . argmax ()]) To listen, write it with to_wav_bytes and open the file: from alto.audio import to_wav_bytes open ( "/tmp/c4.wav" , "wb" ). write ( to_wav_bytes ( synth_piano ( 60 )))

title: Computer audio
text: Sustained and plucked sounds A marimba bar, once struck, rings and fades whatever you do. A flute or a bowed string ends when the player stops. Instrument.sustained captures that: when a sustained instrument plays a note, any note still sounding is released by _release : a 70 ms fade of the effect’s volume property with a QPropertyAnimation , then stop() . Without that, melodies on a flute would pile up. stop_all cancels all fades and silences everything. A piano is in between. Its recordings ring for a long time, but on a real piano a damper stops each string when the key is let go. A recording played in full sounds as if the damper pedal were held down: the notes of a scale pile up into a blur. Instrument.damped marks an instrument that is played without the pedal, and it gets the same release as a sustained one, so each note ends as the next begins, the way fingers move from key to key. The last note of a melody is left to fade by itself. An abrupt stop is audible as a click, and a fade avoids it. The same idea ( an envelope ) shapes every synthesized note. The classical envelope is ADSR : attack (how fast the sound begins), decay , sustain level, release (how it ends).

title: Computer audio
text: Timing a sequence To play a melody or an arpeggio, _play_sequence schedules each step with QTimer.singleShot and has three safeguards. Wait for loading. QSoundEffect loads in the background, and a note started before it is ready is silent. The sequence polls status() every 10 ms for up to a second before starting. Anchor the schedule to the start. Step i schedules step i + 1 a full gap after step i starts , not after it finishes. If starting one note takes a while, the others are not pushed later and the rhythm stays even. The test test_a_note_that_is_slow_to_start_does_not_upset_the_rhythm checks this. A newer sequence cancels an older one. Each sequence has a run number, and a step that finds a newer number does nothing. This pattern, a token , appears in the animations too: callbacks scheduled for later cannot be canceled easily, so they check whether they are still wanted.

title: Computer audio
section: Latency and the limits of this design
text: Latency and the limits of this design Latency is the delay between asking for a sound and hearing it. QSoundEffect is good enough here: a few tens of milliseconds. Real-time musical instruments need under about 10 ms, and for that you would use an audio library with a callback, such as PortAudio , and fill small buffers on a high-priority thread. If your program fills a buffer too late you get an underrun (a glitch). None of that applies to Alto, and it is the reason the playback code is short.

title: Computer audio
text: Adding an instrument The steps are in For developers : the WAV files named by MIDI number in alto/assets/samples/<key>/ , an Instrument in INSTRUMENTS , an entry in instrument_info.INFO , and the credit in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Check that the license permits redistribution. A few practical points: Trim silence at the start , or the note feels late. Normalize levels so that notes of one instrument are similar, then set gain to balance instruments against each other. Mono, 16-bit files at any common rate (44.1 or 48 kHz) work; QSoundEffect resamples at playback. Mark sustained=True for bowed and blown instruments, and damped=True for an instrument with dampers, such as the piano; leave both off for struck and plucked ones that ring on. Gaps are fine: a missing note is made from its nearest neighbor.

title: Computer audio
text: Testing audio without speakers Tests never play sound. tests/conftest.py turns sounds.enabled off for every test, and tests/test_audio.py replaces QSoundEffect with a FakeEffect that records play , stop and setVolume calls in a list, so assertions are about what would have been played , in what order and how loudly. This is the general approach to testing anything with a side effect on the world: replace the world with a recorder.

title: Computer audio
text: Words to search for PCM, WAV, RIFF. Nyquist frequency, aliasing, anti-aliasing filter. Quantisation, dither. Dynamic range, decibel, loudness, psychoacoustics, equal-loudness contours. Overtone, partial, harmonic series, timbre, inharmonicity. Additive, subtractive, FM, wavetable and physical-modeling synthesis. Karplus-Strong algorithm (a famous few-line plucked-string model). Convolution and impulse response (how reverb is done). Fourier transform, FFT, spectrogram, window function. Resampling, interpolation, sinc interpolation, polyphase filter. Time-stretching, phase vocoder, PSOLA. Sampler, multisampling, velocity layer, round robin, loop point. SoundFont and SFZ (sample instrument formats). Latency, buffer, underrun, callback. MIDI (the standard also defines messages, channels and file formats).

title: Computer audio
text: Further reading Julius O. Smith III, Mathematics of the Discrete Fourier Transform , Introduction to Digital Filters , Physical Audio Signal Processing and Spectral Audio Signal Processing (W3K Publishing, 2007; free at ccrma.stanford.edu/~jos, the author’s Stanford page, which is the primary source). The best free route from the sampling theorem to physical modeling of instruments. Ken C. Pohlmann, Principles of Digital Audio , 6th ed. (McGraw-Hill, 2010): sampling, quantisation, converters, file formats. Alan V. Oppenheim and Ronald W. Schafer, Discrete-Time Signal Processing , 3rd ed. (Pearson, 2010): the standard textbook on the mathematics behind everything above. Claude E. Shannon, “Communication in the Presence of Noise”, Proceedings of the IRE 37(1), 1949: the sampling theorem. Miller Puckette, The Theory and Technique of Electronic Music (World Scientific, 2007): a gentle book on building sound from oscillators and envelopes, and a good second read after this chapter. Curtis Roads, The Computer Music Tutorial (MIT Press, 1996): the broad survey of the field. Udo Zölzer (ed.), DAFX: Digital Audio Effects , 2nd ed. (Wiley, 2011): resampling, pitch shifting and time stretching, with the phase vocoder in detail. Mark Dolson, “The Phase Vocoder: A Tutorial”, Computer Music Journal 10(4), 1986; and Jean Laroche and Mark Dolson, “Improved Phase Vocoder Time-Scale Modification of Audio”, IEEE Transactions on Speech and Audio Processing 7(3), 1999. Kevin Karplus and Alex Strong, “Digital Synthesis of Plucked-String and Drum Timbres”, Computer Music Journal 7(2), 1983. Harvey Fletcher, “Normal Vibration Frequencies of a Stiff Piano String”, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 36(1), 1964: the inharmonicity formula used in synth_piano . Neville H. Fletcher and Thomas D. Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments , 2nd ed. (Springer, 1998): why instruments sound as they do. MIDI 1.0 Detailed Specification , MIDI Manufacturers Association, midi.org. The University of Iowa Electronic Music Studios, Musical Instrument Samples , theremin.music.uiowa.edu/MIS.html: the source of the recordings Alto ships. The Qt documentation for QSoundEffect , QMediaPlayer , QAudioSink and “Qt Multimedia”, doc.qt.io.

title: Data and persistence
text: Data and persistence Alto keeps two kinds of stored information in two places, and keeps the code that touches them apart. This chapter explains what is stored where and why, how the SQLite database is used, and, most important for the long run, how to change the database structure without losing anyone’s practice history.

title: Data and persistence
text: Two stores Kind Where Written by Contains History one SQLite file, alto.db , in the user’s data folder alto/learning/database.py profiles, every answer, what is known about each question Preferences QSettings("alto", "alto") , in the user’s configuration folder alto/ui/store.py and the save_* functions in alto/ui/exercise_settings.py and the theme, notation, keyboard and instrument modules theme, notation font, keyboard style, instrument, each exercise’s settings, sidebar width, the profile used last The split is by nature : history is a large and growing table of facts you can query, so it belongs in a database. Preferences are a few dozen small values, so they belong in the platform’s settings mechanism. Your data tells users where both are. The settings objects in alto/settings.py are plain data and never save themselves; saving is a UI concern, so alto/learning , alto/exercises and alto/theory never touch the disk except through Database .

title: Data and persistence
text: SQLite in one page SQLite is a database that is a library, not a server: a database is one file, and your program reads and writes it directly. Python includes it as the standard sqlite3 module. It is the right tool for a single-user desktop program. Concepts the code relies on: Tables, rows, columns, and a primary key that identifies a row. PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON (set on every connection, because SQLite’s default is off ) makes a foreign key enforced: attempts.profile_id REFERENCES profiles(id) ON DELETE CASCADE means deleting a profile deletes its attempts and items. SQL with parameters : execute("SELECT ... WHERE profile_id = ?", (profile_id,)) . The ? is filled by the library, never by string formatting your values in. That is what prevents SQL injection , and it is a rule with one narrow exception: in database.py a few queries build a WHERE clause from fixed strings in the code , never from user text, and still pass every value as a parameter. Transactions. with self.conn: groups statements so they all happen or none do, and commits at the end. Alto writes the attempt, item summary and any review schedule update in one transaction in Learner.record . Indexes. CREATE INDEX attempts_by_item ON attempts(profile_id, exercise, item_key) makes “find all attempts for this question” fast. Without it SQLite reads every row. An index can also be the slower way: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows which one SQLite picked. The database page’s newest answers are found faster by walking the table from its end and stopping at the limit, so that query writes +a.profile_id , which keeps SQLite from using an index for that column. sqlite3.Row ( conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row ) lets you read a column by name: row["strain"] . In-memory databases. Database() with no path uses ":memory:" : a fresh database that vanishes when closed. Every test and every doctest uses one, and the simulation in Spaced repetition does too.

title: Data and persistence
text: The schema CREATE TABLE profiles ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE COLLATE NOCASE , created_at REAL NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE attempts ( -- one row per answer, wrong ones included id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , profile_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES profiles ( id ) ON DELETE CASCADE , exercise TEXT NOT NULL , item_key TEXT NOT NULL , attempt_no INTEGER NOT NULL , -- 1 for the first answer to this showing of the question answer TEXT NOT NULL , correct INTEGER NOT NULL , duration_ms INTEGER NOT NULL , answered_at REAL NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE items ( -- one row per question per profile: the current state profile_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES profiles ( id ) ON DELETE CASCADE , exercise TEXT NOT NULL , item_key TEXT NOT NULL , strain REAL NOT NULL , seen INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 , first_try_right INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 , wrong_attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 , total_first_ms INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 , last_seen REAL NOT NULL , signature TEXT NOT NULL , payload TEXT NOT NULL , PRIMARY KEY ( profile_id , exercise , item_key ) ); The current definitions are _SCHEMA and _CALENDAR_SCHEMA in alto/learning/database.py . Two design decisions are worth understanding. attempts is the log; items is a summary. The log is append-only : facts that happened, never edited. The summary is derived : it could be rebuilt by replaying the log through update_strain . This is a miniature of a well-known pattern ( event sourcing ): keep the facts, derive the state. It is what lets you change the scheduler’s formula later and recompute strains without losing anything, and it is why the statistics (accuracy, speed, activity over time) are computed from attempts , which has the full history, rather than from items , which only has the current state. Times are numbers. answered_at and last_seen are seconds since 1970 ( REAL ), and durations are integer milliseconds. This sorts and subtracts without date parsing. Convert to local dates only when displaying (the statistics code groups into local days, weeks and months; see _floor in stats.py ). The question is stored in the row. items.payload is the Question as JSON ( Question.to_dict ). That is how an old question can be asked again without regenerating it, and also why changing Question is a data-format change: old payloads must still load. Learner.pick handles an unreadable payload by skipping it, which is a safety net, not a plan. Add fields with defaults.

title: Data and persistence
text: Changing the schema: migrations A shipped database has users’ history in it, so the structure cannot just change. A migration is a script that takes a database from one version to the next. SQLite has a built-in integer for this, the user_version pragma , which belongs to the application and which SQLite does not otherwise use. Alto applies missing migrations in order within one transaction. When a 0.0.1 database is opened in 0.0.2, its profiles, answers, and question history are preserved. SM-2 and FSRS start with a fresh review queue. Eligible earlier answers can still contribute to response-time grading. Schema version 7 records each profile’s grading thresholds and whether an answer’s timing is usable.

title: Data and persistence
section: What each Database method is for
text: What each Database method is for You can find all of them in the API reference . In groups: Profiles: profiles() , profile(id) , add_profile(name) (names are unique ignoring case), delete_profile(id) (cascades). Writing history: add_attempt(...) appends to the log; save_item(...) upserts the summary ( INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE : insert, or update if the key exists). Reading state for the scheduler: get_item(...) for one question; replay_candidates(...) for the questions that may be asked again (the 25 highest-strain plus 10 random ones, for the same exercise and settings signature). Statistics and the browser: attempts(...) , attempts_in(...) , strained_items(...) , count_attempts(...) and the *_rows methods that feed the read-only tables in the database page. ORDER BY RANDOM() LIMIT 10 is not efficient for huge tables (it sorts everything), but at this size it is instant. If a profile ever has millions of items, replace it with a cheaper sampling method.

title: Data and persistence
text: Saved preferences The preferences are read and written through four small functions, because QSettings returns whatever it finds, which on some platforms is a string where you stored a number: store() returns the single QSettings . int_value(settings, key=, default=) reads an integer and falls back to the default. text_value(settings, key=, default=) reads a string likewise. booleans are stored as the text "true" or "false" , because that is the form that survives every platform. Adding a saved preference means: pick a key ( "ui/something" , a “group/name” path), read it with a default at start-up, write it when it changes. Tests redirect the settings to a throwaway folder, so use store() and nothing else.

title: Data and persistence
text: Backup and restore A backup must be complete enough that importing it into a clean install leaves the program as if nothing had changed, so it holds both stores : the whole database and every saved preference. The code is in three places. alto/learning/backup.py (no Qt) writes and reads the file. A backup is a zip with alto.db (the database), settings.json (the preferences) and manifest.json (a format number, the Alto version, the schema version, the counts and a SHA-256 of each of the other two parts). read_backup checks everything before returning anything: that the file is a zip with the three parts, that the format is not newer than this version knows, that both checksums match, and that the database is an intact Alto database ( check_snapshot ). Any failure is a BackupError with a sentence fit to show the user. Database.snapshot() and Database.restore() in alto/learning/database.py . A snapshot is sqlite3.Connection.serialize() : the whole database as bytes, consistent even while the program runs. Restoring loads the bytes into a throwaway in-memory database, checks it, and then copies it into the live connection with SQLite’s online backup API ( copy.backup(self.conn) ). The live connection is never closed or swapped, so every object that holds it keeps working, and the ids of profiles and items are exactly what they were, which is why the saved “last profile” id still points at the right person. (Do not use Connection.deserialize on the live connection: it would detach it from its file.) export_settings() and import_settings() in alto/ui/store.py . Export reads every key in QSettings ; import clears the settings and sets the backup’s, so a key the backup lacks does not survive. Both keep the marker migratedFromMtheory : without it store() would bring old “mtheory” preferences back in on the next call. alto/ui/backup_flow.py asks the questions: the file dialogs, a description of the backup before it is applied, and a safety copy of the current data saved beside alto.db before anything is replaced. MainWindow._restored then picks up the profile, applies the theme and opens a fresh window, which loads every setting as it starts. What this means when you change the program: A new table or column is in backups automatically (the whole database is copied). Give it a migration as described above, and an older backup is brought up to date by _migrate as it is restored. A new saved preference is in backups automatically, whatever its key. Keep values to text, numbers, true and false, lists and bytes, which is what the backup format can hold. Anything stored somewhere else , such as a file in the data folder, a new QSettings organization, or state kept only in memory that the user would expect to survive, is not in a backup. Add it to write_backup and import_backup , and extend tests/test_backup_flow.py , whose end-to-end test is the statement of the promise. A change to the backup format itself (the files in the zip, or the manifest) must raise FORMAT in backup.py and keep reading the old one. A file with a format number above the running version’s is refused, which is the safe behavior for a backup made by a later Alto. Schema compatibility only goes one way. A backup from an older schema is migrated; one from a newer schema is refused, because the older program cannot know what the newer one added. The tests ( tests/test_backup.py , tests/test_backup_flow.py ) cover the exact round trip of every row, the refusal of each kind of damaged or foreign file, a restore replacing rather than merging, the safety copy being a working undo, and an end-to-end import into a clean install through the real window.

title: Data and persistence
text: Privacy Profiles and practice history stay in the local database. On supported installations, Alto checks GitHub for a published release up to once a day while the main grid is active. The request does not include profile names or practice records. Turn off automatic checks in Settings → Updates , or check manually with Tools → Check for updates… . Updating Alto

title: Data and persistence
text: Words to search for ACID (what a transaction guarantees). Write-ahead logging (SQLite’s journal_mode = WAL , a faster and more concurrent journal; Alto uses the default). Schema migration, schema versioning. Event sourcing, append-only log. Normalization (why items and attempts are separate tables). Upsert. Index, covering index, query plan ( EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN ). ORM (object-relational mapper; Alto does not use one, deliberately). Serialization (JSON for the question payload).

title: Data and persistence
text: Further reading The SQLite documentation, sqlite.org/docs.html: especially “Datatypes in SQLite”, “Foreign Key Support”, “ALTER TABLE” (with the steps for changes it cannot do directly), “PRAGMA user_version”, “UPSERT” and “Appropriate Uses For SQLite”. Python Software Foundation, the sqlite3 module documentation, docs.python.org: transactions, row_factory , parameters. Martin Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications (O’Reilly, 2017): chapters 1 to 3 explain schemas, storage and indexes; the chapter on stream processing covers the log-and-derived-state idea. C. J. Date, An Introduction to Database Systems , 8th ed. (Pearson, 2003): the relational model from its source.

title: Building an exercise
text: Building an exercise This chapter follows one new exercise from idea to published documentation, then covers the harder cases: exercises with settings, with a staff, a keyboard, a second row of buttons, or a note to place. The short version of the steps is in For developers ; here are the reasons.

title: Building an exercise
text: What an exercise is An Exercise is a small class with four attributes and one method that matter. Everything else comes from the framework.     name , category , description What the home screen and the sidebar show. The category groups exercises. par_seconds How long a good first answer takes. The scheduler judges speed against it. generate(rng) Returns one Question . This is the whole of the exercise. settings_signature() Only for exercises with settings (see below). card_prompt(question) Optional. The instruction on an Anki card, where no buttons or staff explain the task. The default uses the question’s prompt. interval_voices Optional. True when two notes on the staff are an interval, so they are drawn as two voices. A Question says everything about one question. Its fields are the whole vocabulary of what the screen can show: Field Meaning prompt The text above the question (may be empty). choices The answer buttons, in order. answer The right answer; it must be one of choices . staff Notes to draw: a list of chords, each a list of Note s. Empty for no staff. clef , key , value The clef, the key signature (sharps positive, flats negative) and the note value to draw. keyboard , key_staff , keyboard_range Highlight a piano key instead of drawing a staff; optionally with a small key signature above; and the range of keys to draw. octaves , second_label , joiner A two-part answer: a choice, then one of a second row of buttons (“C” then “4” gives “C4”). construct , accidentals A “place this note” question: the answer is a position on a clickable staff, not a button. grid Where to put each button, as (row, column) , instead of one row. explanation Text shown after the answer says why it is right. Use ChoiceExercise.make_question for questions answered by choosing buttons. Supply the full eligible bank. Alto adds the Buttons option, applies the limit, and retains required answers in each group. Use practice_signature() for additional question settings.

title: Building an exercise
text: A complete example We will add “Sharps and flats”: it names a major key and asks how many sharps or flats it has. This code runs as written. import random from alto.exercises.base import ( ChoiceExercise , Question , register , ) from alto.theory.scales import ( MAJOR_KEYS , format_key_signature , ) @ register class SharpsAndFlats ( ChoiceExercise ): name = "Sharps and flats" category = "Notation" description = "How many sharps or flats does a major key have?" par_seconds = 4.0 def make_question ( self , rng : random . Random ) -> Question : count = rng . randint ( - 7 , 7 ) # -7 flats ... +7 sharps return Question ( f "How many sharps or flats are in { MAJOR_KEYS [ count ] } major?" , choices = [ format_key_signature ( n ) for n in range ( - 7 , 8 )], answer = format_key_signature ( count ), explanation = f " { MAJOR_KEYS [ count ] } major has { format_key_signature ( count ) } ." , ) To try it without the program, in a Python session: >>> q = SharpsAndFlats().generate(random.Random(1)) >>> q.prompt, q.answer ('How many sharps or flats are in D♭ major?', '5 flats') and to see it in a window: from PySide6.QtWidgets import QApplication from alto.ui.exercise_view import ExerciseView app = QApplication ([]) view = ExerciseView ( SharpsAndFlats (), rng = random . Random ( 1 )) view . show () app . exec () Things to notice: rng is an argument, not a global. The exercise never calls random.randint . That is what makes the example above repeatable and the exercise testable with a seed. @register puts the class in REGISTRY next to the other exercises of its category , so the home screen and the sidebar list it with them, whatever order the file is written in. Pick an existing category or invent a new one. Choices must be unique and the answer must be one of them. A test, test_every_exercise_generates_valid_questions , draws 300 questions from every registered exercise and checks both. A new exercise is covered the moment it is registered. Distractors. The wrong answers matter as much as the right one. pick_distractors(correct, pool=..., n=..., rng=...) in base.py returns the right answer shuffled in with n others drawn from a pool; use it, or write your own, with plausible wrong answers (for intervals: the neighboring qualities, not random words). A question where only one answer is conceivable teaches nothing. Where the logic lives. Anything about music itself (spelling, intervals, scales) belongs in alto/theory/ , with tests, and is used by the exercise. If your generate contains theory, move it.

title: Building an exercise
text: Calibrating par_seconds par_seconds estimates how long a fluent first answer takes. ASRS uses it to adjust a question’s strain. To estimate par for a new exercise, answer fifty questions at a fluent pace and check the median first-answer time in Statistics. Alto uses 3 seconds for Note Identification, 8 seconds for Interval Construction, and 25 seconds for Scale Construction. The full table appears under Response time .

title: Building an exercise
text: Adding settings to an exercise If users should be able to change what is asked, there are four more places to touch. The NoteNames exercise is the model. A settings object in alto/settings.py : a dataclass with the fields and the rules about them, and a module-level instance ( note_names = NoteNameSettings() ). Keep it free of Qt and of saving. The exercise reads it when it generates a question: settings.note_names.active_clefs() . Because the instance is shared, a change takes effect on the next question. A signature. For a ChoiceExercise , return signature(...) from practice_signature() . The framework includes the button layout when matching stored questions. Other exercises return their signature from settings_signature() . A panel and persistence. In alto/ui/settings_panel.py , a panel class and an entry in PANELS . The panel subclasses ExerciseSettingsPanel from alto/ui/settings_menu.py (or ClefsPanel if it has a Clefs page), builds its pages from that module’s rows and pages, and overrides _persist to save; _save_and_emit then saves and emits changed . In alto/ui/exercise_settings.py , load_* and save_* functions that read and write QSettings through store() with the readers in alto/ui/store.py , and a call to your load_* in load_exercise_settings so settings are restored at start. The screen connects changed to next_question , so edits apply at once. The panel is the largest piece of code in the program, and that is mostly widgets: copy a panel with a similar shape (for a menu of pages, ArpeggioSettingsPanel ) and change it.

title: Building an exercise
section: Showing a staff, a keyboard or a clickable staff
text: Showing a staff, a keyboard or a clickable staff Fill in the fields and the screen does the rest. A note on a staff: staff=[[note]] , clef="treble" . Several notes at once (a chord) go in one inner list; several columns in sequence (an arpeggio) are several inner lists. A key signature: key=3 for three sharps. The staff draws it after the clef. A piano key: keyboard=note , and keyboard_range=(low_midi, high_midi) to show only a span. key_staff=True adds a small key-signature staff above the keyboard. Place a note: construct=note and choices=[] . The user clicks the staff, StaffInput.note_at turns the click into a Note , and Question.check_placed compares it, spelling and octave included (G♯4 is not A♭4). Set accidentals=True to show the sharp, flat and natural buttons. A two-part answer: choices=["C", "D", ...] , octaves=["3", "4", "5"] , joiner="" , so the right answer is the choice joined to the octave. The screen shows two rows and submits when both are chosen. If your question needs something the fields cannot say, the right move is to add a field to Question (with a default, so old stored questions still load), teach ExerciseView to draw it, and add it to to_dict / from_dict . Decide whether it belongs in item_key() : if two questions that differ in the new field are different questions, it does.

title: Building an exercise
text: The icon The home screen shows an icon per exercise. alto/ui/home.py has EXERCISE_ICONS , a dictionary from the exercise’s class name to an SVG snippet in alto/ui/icons.py (a 24-by-24 drawing whose fill is the word COLOR ). An exercise with no entry gets a default, which tests/test_main_window.py checks. Make a simple monochrome icon in an SVG editor such as Inkscape, copy the path data into a new constant, and add the dictionary entry.

title: Building an exercise
text: Documenting it A section in docs/exercises.md that says what is shown, what to press, and what the settings do. Write it for a user. A screenshot if you want one: add a name to SHOTS in scripts/screenshots.py , write the few lines that open your exercise and call save(window, name="your-name") , include it in the page the way the other pages do (copy a line that uses the shot.html include), and run python scripts/screenshots.py --only your-name . tests/test_docs.py checks that every picture a page shows exists in both themes. The instructions shown behind the “?” button: override instructions() to return a little HTML. The API reference: run python scripts/api_docs.py . A line in ARCHITECTURE.md only if the exercise changes the picture of how the program fits together.

title: Building an exercise
text: Testing it Write the tests that the existing exercises have: A generation test: seed an rng , draw some questions, and assert on what you can predict (the answer is in the choices; a question for G major shows one sharp). A settings test: change a setting in the test (tests start from the defaults and restore them afterwards) and check the questions follow it. A screen test: build an ExerciseView(YourExercise(), rng=random.Random(1)) , click an answer, and check the score. The tests/test_exercise_view.py helpers view_of and asked do the work; set sounds.enabled = False in any test that submits an answer, or it will try to play. A docstring with an example for every function, which tests/test_docstrings.py demands and pytest then runs.

title: Building an exercise
text: Further reading Fluent Python (see Python beyond the basics ) on abstract base classes and decorators for the framework side. Music theory references for exercise content: Stefan Kostka and Dorothy Payne, Tonal Harmony , 7th ed. (McGraw-Hill, 2013), and Edward Aldwell, Carl Schachter and Allen Cadwallader, Harmony and Voice Leading , 4th ed. (Schirmer, 2011). They agree on terms, and when they disagree, that is a sign the exercise needs a setting. Thomas M. Haladyna, Developing and Validating Multiple-Choice Test Items , 3rd ed. (Lawrence Erlbaum, 2004): the standard book on writing good questions and, above all, good distractors.

title: Resources
text: Resources This guide is written so that one person, with basic Python and no help beyond the internet and a library card, can pick up Alto and keep developing it. It explains how the program works, and also the ideas underneath it that a Python programmer may never have met: how computers make sound, how music notation is drawn, how a flash-card program decides what to ask you next, how to make a Qt program look and move the way you want. It does not replace the shorter pages. For developers is the quick reference for commands and tooling, ARCHITECTURE.md is a one-page map of the code, and the API reference lists every public class and function. This guide is the explanation that ties them together.

title: Resources
text: How to use this guide Read Getting oriented first, whatever else you do. Then read what you need: If you want to … Read Get the program running, find your way around, and follow the project’s rules Getting oriented Understand the Python features the code leans on (dataclasses, type hints, keyword-only arguments, closures) Python beyond the basics Understand Qt: the event loop, signals, painting, ownership, and the traps in each Qt and PySide6 Change how the program looks (colors, themes, stylesheets, icons, custom widgets) Styling beyond QtWidgets Change how music is drawn (clefs, noteheads, key signatures, fonts) Rendering music notation Change or add sounds (instruments, pitch shifting, timing) Computer audio Change what gets asked and when Spaced repetition and adaptive practice Add or change movement on screen Animation Add an exercise, from idea to published docs Building an exercise Change what is stored, or add a column Data and persistence Run the checks, understand CI, and release Testing, quality and release Work out why something strange is happening Pitfalls and debugging Look up a term, or find a book to read Glossary and further reading

title: Resources
section: The mental model in one page
text: The mental model in one page Alto is four layers. Only the top one knows that Qt exists. alto/ui windows, drawing, animation, saved settings (Qt) | alto/audio.py sample playback, pitch shifting, synthesis (Qt Multimedia) | alto/learning profiles, SQLite, the scheduler, statistics (no Qt) | alto/exercises Exercise and Question, the eight exercises (no Qt) | alto/settings the user's choices as plain objects (no Qt) | alto/theory spelled notes, intervals, scales, chords (no Qt) Three ideas carry the whole design. If you remember nothing else, remember these. A Question is plain data. An exercise’s only job is to turn a random number generator and the current settings into a Question : a prompt, some buttons, what to draw, which answer is right. The screen, the scheduler and the database know nothing about any particular exercise. They only handle Question s. That is why adding an exercise needs no new interface code. Each question has a strain. The database keeps one number for every question a person has met: how much practice it still needs. Wrong answers and slow answers raise it, quick right answers lower it. The chance of a question being asked is an exponential function of that number. There are no due dates and no schedules. Everything is drawn, not assembled. Staffs, keyboards, charts, switches, even the pictures in the settings panes are painted with QPainter from numbers. That is why they follow the theme, scale cleanly and animate, and also why a drawing bug is a geometry bug, not a layout bug.

title: Resources
section: If you can no longer use an LLM
text: If you can no longer use an LLM The code base was written with an assistant’s help, and was shaped so that you do not need one to maintain it. These habits are what make that true, and the guide assumes you keep them. Every function explains itself. Each module, class and function has a NumPy-style docstring with every parameter, the return value and a runnable example. Read the docstring before the code. pytest runs the examples, so they are never out of date. Types are complete. Every signature is annotated and Pyright checks them. When you are unsure what a value is, the signature tells you. The tests are the safety net. More than a thousand tests and doctests run in a minute. Make a change, run pytest , and fix what turns red. The tests drive widgets with Qt’s offscreen platform, so no screen is needed. The rules are mechanical. Ruff, Pyright, the pre-commit hooks and the tests check the style for you. You do not have to remember the rules, only to run the checks. Getting oriented lists them. Hard parts have a chapter. Audio, notation, spaced repetition, styling and animation each have a chapter that starts from first principles and ends with a reading list. A workflow that works without an assistant: Find the code. Search the API reference or run grep -rn "name" alto/ . Read the docstring and its example. Open a Python shell and run the example with small changes until the behavior is clear. Write a failing test for the change first, in tests/ . It tells you when you are done. Make the change. Run pytest -x -q often, since most mistakes show up in seconds. Run the full checks listed in Getting oriented before you commit. If you change a docstring or a public signature, run python scripts/api_docs.py . If you change anything the user can see, regenerate the screenshots with python scripts/screenshots.py .
