SMuFL. Glyph. Engraving. Sample. Sample rate. PCM. MIDI note number. Equal temperament. Resampling. Strain. Spacing effect. Retrieval practice. Softmax. Easing. Property animation. Offscreen platform. Doctest. Fixture. Monkeypatch.

title: Resources
section: A word on the reading lists
text: A word on the reading lists Each chapter ends with further reading. They favor books, peer-reviewed papers, standards and official documentation over blog posts. Where a source is on the author’s own site (as the Stanford audio books are), it is there because it is the primary source. Web addresses change, so the lists give authors, titles, publishers and years, which are enough to find a book or paper even when a link has gone. Treat the addresses as hints.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Rendering music notation Drawing music notation is a craft with a long history and a surprising amount of geometry. This chapter explains how Alto puts a clef, a key signature and a note on a staff, from the musical rules to the pixels, and where in the code each step happens. It assumes you can read music a little, and explains the engraving side from scratch.

title: Rendering music notation
text: The vocabulary Printing music is called engraving , from the days when plates were cut by hand. Software that does it is a music engraver or notation program (Finale, Sibelius, Dorico, MuseScore, LilyPond). The notation most of us read is Common Western Music Notation , abbreviated CWMN . The pieces Alto draws: The staff (plural staves ): five horizontal lines and the four spaces between them. A clef at the start says which pitch each line means. A treble clef curls around the second line from the bottom and says “this is G above middle C”. A bass clef puts F below middle C on the second line from the top. A C clef says “middle C is here” and can sit on any line (alto, tenor, soprano, mezzo-soprano, and the baritone variants). The key signature is the group of sharps or flats after the clef. A note has a notehead (filled, open or double whole), usually a stem , and for short notes flags . Accidentals (sharp, flat, natural) go in front of the head. Ledger lines are short extra lines for notes above or below the staff. The grand staff joins a treble and a bass staff with a brace .

title: Rendering music notation
section: The unit of measure: the staff space
text: The unit of measure: the staff space Everything in engraving is measured in staff spaces : the distance between two adjacent staff lines. A notehead is about one space tall. A stem is about three and a half spaces long. A bass or alto clef is three to four spaces high, and a treble clef is almost nine, because it rises well above and below the staff. Measure in spaces, and the same drawing code works at any size by choosing what one space is in pixels. In Alto this number is called gap (or GAP on StaffWidget ): “the distance between staff lines in pixels”. A StaffWidget for the exercise uses 16, and the small key-signature staff uses 8. Every drawing function takes gap and multiplies.

title: Rendering music notation
section: From a note to a position
text: From a note to a position A staff is a ladder: each line and each space is one step , so a note moves up one step when you go from a line to the space above it. Alto numbers every note with a diatonic index , octave * 7 + letter (letters C=0 to B=6), so C0 is 0, D0 is 1, and middle C (C4) is 28. Note.diatonic gives it, and it ignores sharps and flats, because an accidental changes the sound but not the position on the staff. (C♯ and C are on the same line.) Interval size in steps is just a subtraction. A clef fixes which index sits on the bottom line, BOTTOM_LINE in alto/ui/staff.py : Clef Bottom line Index treble E4 30 bass G2 18 alto F3 24 tenor D3 22 soprano C4 28 mezzo-soprano A3 26 baritone (F clef) B2 20 Given the bottom line’s y on screen, the height of any note is steps = ( note . diatonic - BOTTOM_LINE [ clef ] ) # 0 on the bottom line, 1 in the first space, 2 on the second line ... y = ( bottom - steps * gap / 2 ) # screen y grows downward, and each step is half a gap and that is the heart of it. The reverse, from a click to a note, is StaffInput.note_at(y) : round((bottom - y) / (gap / 2)) gives the step, and Note.from_diatonic gives the note, clamped to five ledger lines. Ledger lines are needed when steps is below 0 or above 8 (the staff covers steps 0 to 8). They are drawn at every even step outside the staff, as far as the note.

title: Rendering music notation
section: Which way does the stem go?
text: Which way does the stem go? The rule every musician learns: notes on or above the middle line get stems pointing down; notes below it get stems up. The middle line is step 4, so stem_down = steps >= 4 . Stems join the head on the right when up and the left when down. Chords and beamed notes have more complex rules (the side of the stem with the most distant note wins), which Alto does not need, because its questions are single notes or simple chords.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Key signatures A key signature is a row of sharps or flats in a fixed order (sharps F C G D A E B, flats B E A D G C F). The order is the same in every clef, but the positions are not: engravers choose positions so the accidentals zigzag and stay inside the staff (each one a fourth up or a fifth down from the last, with a few exceptions). key_signature_positions(clef, sign=) searches for a placement that keeps all seven on or near the staff, and that reproduces the traditional signatures for treble, bass, alto and tenor and works out the others. tests/test_clefs.py checks that no signature needs a ledger line.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Fonts for music: SMuFL A text font has letters. A music font has noteheads, clefs, accidentals and flags as characters. The modern standard is SMuFL , the Standard Music Font Layout , maintained by the W3C Music Notation Community Group. It does three things: It assigns every musical symbol a name (such as noteheadBlack , gClef , accidentalSharp , flag8thUp ) and a code point in Unicode’s Private Use Area (U+E000 to U+F8FF), so any SMuFL font puts the sharp at the same code. It says how big things are: the font is drawn so that four staff spaces equal one em . The em is the font’s nominal size, so a glyph at font size S has staff space S / 4 . It publishes metadata in a JSON file next to each font: engraving defaults (how thick a staff line, a stem and a ledger line should be) and anchors (exact points on a glyph, such as where a stem should attach to a notehead). Bravura (the reference font), Leland (MuseScore’s), Petaluma, Finale Maestro, Leipzig and others follow it, so Alto can offer ten looks with the same code. alto/assets/fonts/engraving.json holds, per font, the numbers Alto needs, copied from each font’s metadata: line, stem and ledger thickness and the stem anchors.

title: Rendering music notation
text: From glyph to pixels alto/ui/engraving.py draws SMuFL fonts, and its method is worth understanding, because it is not “draw text”. A glyph’s outline is read out of the font as a QPainterPath : path.addText(0, 0, font, chr(codepoint)) . The outline is taken once at 100 pixels to the em (so one staff space is 25 units) and cached with @cache . The code works out where the glyph’s origin belongs and moves and scales the outline there: _place builds a QTransform that translates to the position and scales by gap / 25 . The outline is filled with the current color. Why not simply call drawText ? Because text drawing positions glyphs by the font’s advance widths and snaps to the pixel grid (“hinting”), which makes noteheads wobble by a pixel and defeats the anchors. Filling the outline gives exact positions in fractions of a pixel, and the same code scales to any size. A note is built from parts, the way an engraver would: # alto/ui/engraving.py: draw_note, simplified left , _ , right , _ = _ink ( font , name = "noteheadBlack" ) # the head's ink box, in staff spaces ox = x - ( left + right ) / 2 * gap # center the drawn head on x _fill ( p , path = _place ( _outline ( font , name = "noteheadBlack" ), x = ox , y = y , gap = gap ), color = color , ) ax , ay = _anchor ( font , name = "noteheadBlack" , anchor = "stemUpSE" ) # where an up-stem attaches thick = _metrics ( font )[ "stem" ] * gap # stem width from the font p . drawRect ( QRectF ( left_of_stem , stem_top , thick , stem_bottom - stem_top ) ) # the stem is just a rectangle Notice that the stem is a rectangle the code draws , not a glyph. SMuFL leaves stems to the program, because their length varies. The flag is a glyph, placed by lining up its stem anchor with the end of the rectangle. STEM_LENGTH gives the lengths: three and a half spaces, longer for notes with more flags. The clef is a glyph placed so that its reference line (the G, F or C it names) sits on the right staff line: draw_clef has a table of (glyph name, line) , for example treble is the gClef on line 1 (the second line from the bottom). Heights in font units go upward ; on screen y goes downward. That sign flip is the source of many bugs when you first work on this code. Keep both in your head: up in the font is minus in y .

title: Rendering music notation
text: The built-in drawing One style, “Noto Music”, is not SMuFL. alto/ui/notes.py builds notes from Google’s Noto Music font, which is read from the system and not bundled. Because that font has only stem-up notes, a stem-down note is made by rotating the glyph half a turn (which puts the stem on the left and keeps the head’s tilt) and mirroring the flags. It exists for users who like that look; the SMuFL path in engraving.py is the main one.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Putting it together: StaffWidget.paintEvent alto/ui/staff.py is the widget. Its paintEvent does these steps, in order, and each is a few lines you can find: Choose the font from the current notation style ( current_style , from notation.py ). Compute the staff lines’ bottoms with staff_bottoms() (one staff, or two for the grand staff with GRAND_BETWEEN spaces between). Draw the five lines at bottom - i * gap for i in 0 to 4, with the font’s line thickness. Draw the clef, and the brace and the barline for a grand staff. Draw the key signature ( _draw_key_signature ). For each note: its y from the formula above, ledger lines if needed, accidental signs, then the note itself. Draw the caption under the staff if there is one. The same functions are reused for the small pictures in the settings panes ( alto/ui/pictures.py ), so a clef drawn in a setting looks the same as in a question.

title: Rendering music notation
text: A script you can run This draws a treble clef and a stem-down quarter note on the fourth line (D5). It is the quickest way to try engraving code: import os os . environ [ "QT_QPA_PLATFORM" ] = "offscreen" from PySide6.QtGui import QColor , QImage , QPainter from PySide6.QtWidgets import QApplication from alto.ui import engraving app = QApplication ([]) gap , bottom = 20 , 150 image = QImage ( 300 , 200 , QImage . Format . Format_ARGB32 ) # kept in a variable: the painter paints on it image . fill ( QColor ( "white" )) p = QPainter ( image ) p . setRenderHint ( QPainter . RenderHint . Antialiasing ) for i in range ( 5 ): p . drawLine ( 20 , bottom - i * gap , 280 , bottom - i * gap ) engraving . draw_clef ( p , font = "bravura" , clef = "treble" , x = 30 , bottom = bottom , gap = gap , color = QColor ( "black" ), ) engraving . draw_note ( p , font = "bravura" , value = "quarter" , x = 140 , y = bottom - 6 * gap / 2 , gap = gap , color = QColor ( "black" ), stem_down = True , ) p . end () image . save ( "/tmp/notation-example.png" ) Change font="bravura" to "leland" or "petaluma" and compare. Change 6 to 4 and the note moves to the middle line.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Adding a notation font The steps are in For developers . In outline: put the .otf and its license in alto/assets/fonts/ , add its numbers to engraving.json from the font’s SMuFL metadata, register the file in _FILES , and add a NotationStyle . Fonts without full SMuFL metadata may need the fallback numbers in _anchor . The test suite draws every style and checks that something appears ( tests/test_rendering.py ). Look at the result by eye too: a wrong anchor still draws, just slightly off.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Where else notation appears StaffInput ( alto/ui/staff_input.py ) is a staff you click to place a note; note_at converts a mouse position to a note. KeyboardWidget ( alto/ui/keyboard.py ) draws a piano keyboard to real proportions and can highlight a key. Its geometry has the same flavour: white keys have equal width, and black keys are narrower and shorter and sit between them. QuestionPreview , which the database browser opens, redraws a stored question in the same widgets.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Words to search for Engraving rules. Optical sizing (staff lines thinner at small sizes). Collision avoidance and spacing (the hard parts Alto avoids: moving objects apart, and spacing notes by duration). Beaming. Cue notes. Proportional spacing. SMuFL ranges. MusicXML and MNX (formats for exchanging scores). Font hinting. Bézier curves (glyph outlines are made of them, as QPainterPath lines and curves). Ink box or bounding box of a glyph.

title: Rendering music notation
text: Further reading Elaine Gould, Behind Bars: The Definitive Guide to Music Notation (Faber Music, 2011). The modern authority on how notation should look. The chapters on noteheads, stems, accidentals and key signatures are what the code in this chapter encodes. Ted Ross, The Art of Music Engraving and Processing (Hansen Books, 1970). The classic engraver’s manual, with the plate engraver’s proportions and tricks. Gardner Read, Music Notation: A Manual of Modern Practice , 2nd ed. (Allyn and Bacon, 1969). Wide coverage of conventions. Standard Music Font Layout (SMuFL) specification, W3C Music Notation Community Group, w3c.github.io/smufl/latest. The glyph names, code points, metadata format and the rules about the four-spaces-per-em. Donald Byrd, Music Notation by Computer (PhD dissertation, Indiana University, 1984). An early and careful treatment of the problem of laying out notation by program; still the best account of why it is hard. The LilyPond documentation, lilypond.org/documentation: an open-source engraver, with an unusually thorough “Essay on automated music engraving” that explains its design decisions. Michael Scott Cuthbert and Christopher Ariza, “music21: A Toolkit for Computer-Aided Musicology and Symbolic Music Data”, Proceedings of the 11th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (2010): a model for representing notes, pitches and intervals in code. The W3C Music Notation Community Group’s MusicXML 4.0 specification, w3.org, if you ever import or export scores.

title: Getting oriented
text: Getting oriented This chapter gets you from a fresh clone to a working change: setting up, finding your way around the code, and the rules the project follows. Those rules are collected here on purpose. They are the same ones enforced by Ruff, Pyright and the tests, and writing them down means you can follow them without remembering them.

title: Getting oriented
text: Set up You need Python 3.11 or newer. Alto supports every Python version that has not reached end of life (see the matrix in .github/workflows/tests.yml ), so do not use syntax newer than 3.11. git clone https://github.com/altosaurus/alto.git cd alto python -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install -e ".[dev]" .venv/bin/pre-commit install .venv/bin/python -m alto # run the app .venv/bin/pytest # run every test and every docstring example On Windows the programs are in .venv\Scripts\ instead of .venv/bin/ . Three things in that list deserve a sentence each. -e (editable install). Python installs the project as a link to the folder you are working in, not a copy, so edits take effect without reinstalling. It also makes import alto work from anywhere, which the tests and scripts rely on. pip install -e reads pyproject.toml , which is where the dependencies, the entry point ( alto = "alto.__main__:main" ) and the tool settings live. [dev] is an optional dependency group in pyproject.toml : pytest, coverage, Ruff, Pyright and pre-commit. pre-commit install installs quick checks on commit, tests and type checking on push, and local branch cleanup after a merge or fast-forward pull on main . If the program starts but the notation looks odd, see Rendering music notation . The default style, Finale Maestro, and the other SMuFL styles use fonts bundled with the program. Only the “Noto Music” style needs a font from your system.

title: Getting oriented
text: Running without a screen All the tests, and the screenshot script, run on Qt’s offscreen platform , which draws into memory. Set QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen and nothing opens on screen. The test configuration sets it for you. It is how continuous integration runs the tests on a machine with no display, and it is how you can draw a widget to a PNG in a script.

title: Getting oriented
text: A tour of the repository alto/ the program __main__.py starts the app: python -m alto audio.py samples, pitch shifting, the piano synthesizer, playback instrument_info.py facts about each instrument's recordings settings.py the user's choices as plain objects (no saving) theory/ notes, intervals, scales, chords exercises/ Exercise and Question, and the eight exercises learning/ profiles, SQLite, the scheduler, the statistics ui/ everything that needs Qt assets/ fonts, instrument recordings, icons (ship with the package) tests/ the tests, one file per area docs/ this website (Jekyll, published to GitHub Pages) api/ generated API reference (do not edit by hand) guide/ this guide scripts/ screenshots.py, api_docs.py, typecheck.sh, check-docs.sh, run-tests.sh ARCHITECTURE.md a one-page map of how the pieces fit pyproject.toml dependencies, entry point, pytest, Ruff, Pyright and coverage settings .pre-commit-config.yaml the checks run on commit and on push .github/workflows/ continuous integration: tests, Pyright, coverage alto/ui/ is large because drawing is verbose. The biggest files are settings_panel.py (the sliding settings panes for every exercise, built from the rows and pages in settings_menu.py ), charts.py , pictures.py (the small illustrations in the settings), staff.py , keyboard.py and exercise_view.py . You will rarely need to read any of them from top to bottom. Read one class, and use its docstring.

title: Getting oriented
text: The files to read first If you read only five files, read these, in this order. alto/exercises/base.py : Question , Exercise and register . Everything revolves around them. alto/exercises/library.py : one real exercise, NoteNames , to see how a Question is made. alto/learning/scheduler.py : forty lines of arithmetic that decide what is asked next. alto/learning/learner.py : how a question is chosen and an answer recorded. alto/ui/exercise_view.py : next_question , submit and _record , the loop the user lives in.

title: Getting oriented
section: Learn the code by running it
text: Learn the code by running it Every docstring has an Examples section, and pytest runs it. That makes the docstrings a guided tour you can execute: .venv/bin/python >>> from alto.theory.pitch import Note, Interval >>> Note.parse ( "C4" ) .transpose ( Interval.parse ( "M3" )) The examples in alto/ui/ create real widgets, because the root conftest.py gives every example a QApplication called app . Copy one into a script, add widget.show() and app.exec() and you have a window. To draw a widget to a file: import os os . environ [ "QT_QPA_PLATFORM" ] = "offscreen" from PySide6.QtWidgets import QApplication from alto.ui.staff import StaffWidget app = QApplication ([]) staff = StaffWidget () staff . resize ( 400 , 200 ) staff . grab (). save ( "/tmp/staff.png" ) # grab() renders the widget into a pixmap This is the quickest feedback loop for drawing work: change a number, save the picture, look at it.

title: Getting oriented
text: The rules These are enforced by tools wherever a tool can do it. Where none can, they are marked.

title: Getting oriented
text: Layout Wrap Python code at 79 characters and docstrings and standalone comments at 72. Strings use double quotes. Anything with several elements that does not fit on a line (a list, dictionary, tuple, call or signature) goes one element per line with a trailing comma . A trailing comma you write yourself keeps even a short list exploded; that is how you ask for one-per-line. Function definitions with two or more parameters, and calls, collections and tuples with four or more elements, are written one per line. Short calls stay on one line. Run the formatter and then the linter, in this order: ruff format . then ruff check --fix . . The formatter splits long lines, and the linter adds the trailing commas it leaves out. In the other order they fight each other.

title: Getting oriented
text: Arguments Only the first parameter of a function may be positional. The rest are keyword-only (written after a bare * ), and every call names them: Note(3, letter=1) , not Note(3, 1) . Ruff enforces it ( PLR0917 ). Calls then read as sentences, and adding a parameter later cannot silently change what an existing call means. Tests that stand in for Qt functions, which Qt calls positionally, may need # noqa: PLR0917 with a reason. Test functions receive pytest fixtures as plain parameters, which is allowed.

title: Getting oriented
text: Imports Absolute only. from alto.ui.store import store , never from .store import store ( TID252 ). All at the top of the file. None inside a function ( PLC0415 ). The >>> lines of a docstring example are the one exception, because an example has to import what it uses. When two modules need each other, do not import one lazily: move the shared thing, or have one register a callback with the other. alto/ui/notation.py and alto/ui/staff.py do this with on_redraw . Sorted like isort , with alto as its own section after the third-party packages ( I ). Two or more names from one module: one per line, in parentheses, with a trailing comma. Ruff cannot enforce this; it only keeps an import that is already written this way: from alto.learning.database import ( Database , ItemRecord , Profile , ) In the two conftest.py files the imports that come after the environment setup carry # noqa: E402 , on the first line of the statement. The setup must run before anything from Alto is imported.

title: Getting oriented
text: Docstrings and types Every module, class, function, method, nested function and test has a NumPy-style docstring . The text starts on the line after the opening """ . Describe every parameter with its type, every return and yield, and, with Raises , every error the function raises. Add an Examples section that runs as a doctest. Tests are exempt from Examples . tests/test_docstrings.py checks all of this for every file, including private and nested functions that Ruff skips. Every signature is fully annotated, and Any is not used: write the real type. Pyright runs in basic mode as if on Python 3.11 ( sh scripts/typecheck.sh ). Use a raw docstring ( r""" ) if it contains a backslash.

title: Getting oriented
text: No warnings There must be no warnings from Ruff, Pyright or PyCharm. Where a tool is wrong, silence it narrowly and say why: # pyright: ignore[ruleName] , # noqa: CODE , or # noinspection InspectionName for PyCharm (in a doctest, a line >>> # noinspection InspectionName covers the next statement). For developers lists the PyCharm settings a fresh clone needs.

title: Getting oriented
text: Before you commit .venv/bin/ruff format . .venv/bin/ruff check --fix . sh scripts/typecheck.sh .venv/bin/pytest If you changed a docstring or a public signature: python scripts/api_docs.py . If you changed anything visible: python scripts/screenshots.py and look at the pictures before committing them (fonts render slightly differently on every machine, so regenerate on the machine you normally use).

title: Getting oriented
text: Git Work on a branch. Open a pull request into main ; CI runs the tests on every supported Python version, Pyright, and coverage. Commits are yours. Write the message as a short summary line, a blank line, and a paragraph on why . pre-commit may change files and stop the commit. Look at the change, git add the files, and commit again.

title: Getting oriented
text: What to read next If you are going to add an exercise, read Building an exercise . If you are about to touch the user interface, read Qt and PySide6 first. It will save you from the traps that are hard to see.

title: Getting oriented
text: Further reading Python Packaging User Guide , packaging.python.org (the Python Packaging Authority): pyproject.toml , editable installs and virtual environments, from the people who maintain the tools. Python Software Foundation, The Python Tutorial and The Python Standard Library , docs.python.org. Pro Git, Scott Chacon and Ben Straub (Apress, 2014; free at git-scm.com/book): the standard book on Git. Brian Okken, Python Testing with pytest , 2nd ed. (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2022). The Ruff documentation, docs.astral.sh/ruff, for what each rule code means. A rule code such as PLR0917 is looked up there. PEP 8, Style Guide for Python Code , and PEP 257, Docstring Conventions , at peps.python.org.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Pitfalls and debugging This is the chapter to open when something strange happens. Each entry below is a mistake that was actually made while building Alto, with the symptom you will see, the cause, and the fix. After them come the tools for finding a problem you do not recognize.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Qt objects and their lifetimes Symptom: a widget you created never appears, or a doctest that builds a widget in one line gives nothing. QLabel("hi").show() creates a widget with no parent and no Python variable. Python frees it immediately, and Qt deletes it. Fix: keep it in a variable ( label = QLabel("hi") ), or give it a parent. Symptom: the program crashes (a segmentation fault, with no Python traceback) when painting onto an image. QPainter(QImage(...)) paints on a temporary. Python frees the image while the painter still uses it. Fix: put the image in a variable and keep it alive until after p.end() . Symptom: RuntimeError: Internal C++ object (...) already deleted . You kept a Python reference to a widget whose C++ side has been deleted, because its parent was deleted or deleteLater() ran. Fix: do not use a widget after you closed it; clear your reference when you delete it; check shiboken6.isValid(obj) if you must. Symptom: an animation or timer you started simply stops. It was garbage collected. Fix: give it a parent ( QVariantAnimation(self) ), or store it ( self._anim = ... ). See Animation . Symptom: a doctest prints True where you did not expect output. QPainter.end() returns True , and an interactive session prints return values. Fix: write the True in the expected output or assign the result ( _ = p.end() ). Symptom: a widget’s size is wrong in a test, or a resize handler never runs. Qt does not send resize events to a widget that has not been shown. Fix: call widget.show() ; on the offscreen platform nothing appears.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
section: A test run that passes but exits with an error
text: A test run that passes but exits with an error Symptom: every test reports “passed”, and then the process dies with a signal: exit status 139 (segmentation fault), 135 (bus error) or -7 , and a message such as pure virtual method called or terminate called without an active exception . Because the exit status is non-zero, the pre-push hook fails. Cause: the doctests create hundreds of widgets they never close. When Python exits it destroys the last objects in whatever order, and Qt’s destruction of widgets after the QApplication has gone aborts. Fix: the root conftest.py has a pytest_sessionfinish hook that closes and deletes every widget and runs the garbage collector while Python and Qt are both still alive. If the symptom returns, a new kind of object is probably outliving the application; look at what the last test created. Run python -X faulthandler -m pytest to see where it dies. Always check the exit status, not just the summary line: pytest -q; echo $? .

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Sound in tests Symptom: a test makes noise, or fails on a machine with no audio. It submitted a right answer, which plays a sound. Fix: the test fixtures turn sounds.enabled off for every test. A doctest that submits an answer must set sounds.enabled = False and restore it afterwards.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Imports Symptom: NameError for a name that Pyright says is fine. The name is imported under if TYPE_CHECKING: but used at run time. Pyright sees the import and is satisfied; Python skips the block. Fix: import it normally, above the guard. Symptom: ImportError: cannot import name ... (most likely due to a circular import) . Two modules import each other. Fix: do not move the import into a function (Ruff forbids it). Break the cycle: move the shared piece to a third module, or have one module register a callback with the other, as notation.on_redraw does for the staff. Symptom: Ruff reports E402 in a conftest.py . The settings folders must be redirected before anything from Alto is imported, so those imports come after code. Mark each with # noqa: E402 , on the first line of the statement.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Tools that disagree Pyright is satisfied and PyCharm warns about str(settings.value(...)) , or the reverse. The two infer types differently. Alto has helpers ( text_value , int_value ) so that neither complains. Where one tool is simply wrong, silence it narrowly and say why: # pyright: ignore[rule] , # noqa: CODE , # noinspection Name . Pyright loses a type through @cache . A cached function’s signature can be hidden from the checker. Fix: give the wrapper an explicit annotation, or add a cast . ruff check and ruff format undo each other. Run them in order: ruff format . then ruff check --fix . . In the other order the trailing-comma rule ( COM812 ) and the formatter fight. Ruff says PLR0917 on a call or a definition. Only the first parameter may be positional. Add *, after the first parameter and name the arguments at the call. In a fake that Qt calls positionally, add # noqa: PLR0917 with the reason.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: PySide6 and Qt Symptom: a program that ran fine for a while aborts with no traceback after a lot of painting, on Python 3.11. PySide6 6.12.0 has a reference-counting bug on that Python. pyproject.toml excludes it. If you change the PySide6 requirement, test a long session. Symptom: a setting you saved as a number comes back as a string. QSettings gives back whatever it finds. Read with int_value or text_value ; store booleans as "true" and "false" . Symptom: str.format raises KeyError or IndexError when you edit the style sheet. app_style fills a template with .format , so every literal { and } of CSS is doubled in the template. A new rule needs doubled braces. Symptom: a lambda connected in a loop always uses the last value. Late binding. Fix: capture the value as a default argument: lambda _=False, k=key: self.show(k) . Symptom: the first note of a sequence is missing. QSoundEffect loads in the background, and a note played before it is ready is silent. Sounds._play_sequence waits (for up to a second) for loading. Anything new that plays a sound should do the same, or play something already loaded. Symptom: the screenshots differ after regenerating. Fonts render slightly differently on each machine and each version of the platform libraries. Regenerate on the machine you normally use, look at the pictures, and commit only intended changes.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: The docs site Symptom: a page on the website is blank, or shows Liquid errors, after adding a code sample. Jekyll runs the Liquid template language over every page, and two opening curly braces in a row, or an opening brace followed by a percent sign, in a code block is taken as template code. Fix: wrap the page or the block in raw and endraw tags, as the generated API pages do, or avoid the braces. Symptom: tests/test_api_docs.py fails. The generated API pages are out of date. Run python scripts/api_docs.py and commit the result.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
section: Finding a problem you do not recognize
text: Finding a problem you do not recognize

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Reproduce it small Almost every bug becomes obvious when reduced. Write a ten-line script that builds only the widget in question and draws it: import os os . environ [ "QT_QPA_PLATFORM" ] = "offscreen" from PySide6.QtWidgets import QApplication app = QApplication ([]) w = SomeWidget () w . resize ( 400 , 300 ) w . show () w . grab (). save ( "/tmp/w.png" ) # then look at the image If the bug appears, you have a test: put the script’s assertions in tests/ .

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Tools Need Tool A crash with no Python traceback python -X faulthandler , which prints the Python stack on a fatal signal. For C-level detail, run under gdb . Which tests fail, fast pytest -x -q (stop at the first failure), -k word (only matching tests), -s (show prints), --pdb (debugger on failure). What a widget looks like widget.grab().save("/tmp/x.png") , then open the file. What Qt is doing at start-up QT_DEBUG_PLUGINS=1 python -m alto (platform plugin problems); QT_LOGGING_RULES="*.debug=true" . Every widget alive QApplication.allWidgets() ; for one widget’s children, widget.findChildren(QPushButton) . Slow code python -m cProfile -s cumtime script.py ; for paint speed, QElapsedTimer around the drawing. Memory growth the standard library’s tracemalloc . A signal that never fires QSignalSpy(widget.someSignal) , then spy.count() . Why a test passed alone and fails with the others a shared singleton changed state. Check tests/conftest.py resets it. A caution about debuggers: pdb and an IDE’s breakpoints work in a Qt program, but stopping in the middle of a handler freezes the event loop and the windows. That is expected. Do not stop inside a paintEvent while the window is repainting; use prints, or save an image and stop afterwards.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Questions to ask Is it the data (the wrong Question ), the drawing (the right data drawn wrongly), the flow (the right thing drawn at the wrong time) or the environment (a font, a platform, a library version)? Print the Question first. What changed? git bisect finds the commit that broke it, using your test as the judge. Does it happen with default settings and a fresh profile? Start with XDG_CONFIG_HOME and XDG_DATA_HOME pointing at an empty folder (as the tests do) to rule out stale saved state.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Words to search for Segmentation fault, core dump, faulthandler. Garbage collection, reference counting, object lifetime, ownership. Late binding, closure. Circular import. Flaky test, test isolation, global state. Bisecting. Race condition. Event loop starvation.

title: Pitfalls and debugging
text: Further reading Andreas Zeller, Why Programs Fail: A Guide to Systematic Debugging , 2nd ed. (Morgan Kaufmann, 2009): the scientific method applied to bugs, including bisecting and reducing a failure. Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer , 20th anniversary ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2019): the chapter on debugging. Python Software Foundation, the faulthandler , pdb , cProfile and tracemalloc pages in The Python Standard Library , docs.python.org. The Qt documentation, “Object Trees and Ownership”, “Debugging Techniques” and “Environment Variables Recognized by Qt”, doc.qt.io. The Qt for Python documentation, “Shiboken” and the pages on object ownership, doc.qt.io/qtforpython-6. Scott Chacon and Ben Straub, Pro Git (Apress, 2014; free at git-scm.com/book), the section on git bisect .

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Python beyond the basics Alto uses ordinary Python, but it leans on a handful of features that a first course does not reach. This chapter names each one, shows where Alto uses it, and says what to read to learn it properly. If a line of code in Alto puzzles you, the cause is probably here.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Dataclasses A dataclass is a class whose job is to hold fields. You list the fields with their types and Python writes __init__ , __repr__ and __eq__ for you. from dataclasses import dataclass @ dataclass class Profile : id : int name : str Alto uses them for Question , Note , Instrument , NotationStyle , KeyboardStyle , the settings objects and the rows read from the database. Two options matter: frozen=True makes instances immutable, so they can be dictionary keys and cannot be changed by accident. Note and Profile are frozen. KW_ONLY is a marker field. Every field after it must be given by name. Question("prompt", choices=[...], answer="C") works because prompt comes first and choices and the rest come after _: KW_ONLY . This is how the “only the first parameter is positional” rule is applied to data. Read: the dataclasses module documentation; PEP 557 (the proposal that introduced them); Luciano Ramalho, Fluent Python , 2nd ed. (O’Reilly, 2022), the chapter on data class builders.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Type hints A type hint says what a value should be: def pick(self, exercise: Exercise, *, rng: random.Random) -> Question . Python ignores them at run time. Pyright reads them and reports contradictions before the program runs, and PyCharm uses them for completion. Alto annotates everything. Things you will meet: int | None means “an int or nothing”. It replaced Optional[int] in Python 3.10. A value of this type must be checked before use ( if x is not None: ), and Pyright will insist. list[str] , dict[str, int] , tuple[int, int] are the built-in generic types (Python 3.9 and later). from __future__ import annotations is at the top of nearly every file. It makes annotations plain text that is never evaluated at import, so you can mention a class before it is defined and import a name only for typing. if TYPE_CHECKING: guards imports that exist only for annotations. The block is skipped when the program runs and read when Pyright runs. If you use such a name at run time (for example to call it), you get a NameError , so the import belongs above the guard. It is an easy trap, because Pyright is satisfied either way. Callable[[int], str] is a function taking an int and returning a str. Callable[..., int] is “any arguments”. # pyright: ignore[reportAttributeAccessIssue] silences one specific message on one line. Always add the reason. Read: PEP 484 (type hints), PEP 604 (the X | Y syntax), the Python documentation’s typing module, and the Pyright documentation (microsoft.github.io/pyright), whose “type concepts” pages are a good short course in the ideas. Ramalho’s Fluent Python has two chapters on type hints.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Keyword-only arguments def record ( self , exercise , * , question , answer , correct ): ... Everything after the bare * must be given by name. Alto requires this for every parameter after the first, and Ruff checks it. When you write Note(4, letter=0) you can read the call without knowing the signature.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Abstract base classes and decorators Exercise is an abstract base class : it declares generate as @abstractmethod , so you cannot create an Exercise without writing generate . @register is a class decorator : a function that receives the class you just defined, records it (in REGISTRY ), and returns it. The @ line is shorthand for MyExercise = register(MyExercise) . @ register class NoteNames ( Exercise ): ... Decorators are everywhere in Python: @property (a method read like an attribute), @staticmethod , @cache , @pytest.fixture . A decorator is a function that takes a function or class and returns a replacement. Read: Ramalho’s Fluent Python , the chapters on decorators and closures, and on interfaces and abstract base classes.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Closures A closure is a function defined inside another function that remembers the outer function’s variables. Alto uses them constantly for Qt callbacks, because a callback has to remember something: def _flash ( self , button , * , target ): end , start = QColor ( target ), QColor ( "black" ) def step ( t : float ) -> None : # remembers `button`, `start` and `end` button . setStyleSheet ( self . _style ( blend ( start , b = end , t = t ))) anim . valueChanged . connect ( step ) When a lambda is created in a loop, beware late binding : lambda: self.show(i) looks i up when called, not when created, so every callback sees the last i . The fix, used throughout alto/ui/ , is a default argument that captures the value now: lambda _=False, k=key: self.show_table(k) .

title: Python beyond the basics
text: functools.cache @cache memoizes a function: the first call with given arguments computes the result and later calls return the stored one. alto/ui/engraving.py uses it so each glyph outline is built once. Two consequences: arguments must be hashable (immutable), and Pyright cannot always see through the decorator, so type information is sometimes lost at the call site.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Random numbers you can repeat random.Random(seed) is a generator with its own state. Alto passes an rng argument into every exercise’s generate , rather than calling the module-level random functions, because a test can then pass random.Random(1) and get the same questions every time. This is called dependency injection : the dependency (the random source) is passed in, not reached for. Learner.pick takes an rng for the same reason. If you write code that makes random choices, take an rng argument.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Dates and times The database stores timestamps as seconds since 1970 ( time.time() ), which sort and subtract easily. Durations are measured with time.monotonic() , a clock that never jumps backwards when the system time changes. Use monotonic for “how long did that take” and time for “when did that happen”.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Paths pathlib.Path represents file locations: Path(__file__).parent / "assets" / "fonts" . The / operator joins parts and works on every operating system. __file__ is the path of the current source file, which is how the program finds its fonts and recordings wherever it is installed.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Testing tools: doctest, fixtures, monkeypatch A doctest is an example inside a docstring. Lines starting >>> are run, and the line below must match the output. pytest runs them with --doctest-modules . Two flags are on: NORMALIZE_WHITESPACE (ignore differences in spacing) and ELLIPSIS ( ... matches any text). A fixture is a function pytest runs to prepare something a test needs. A test asks for it by naming a parameter: def test_x(app, tmp_path) . app is Alto’s fixture that provides the QApplication ; tmp_path is pytest’s own, a fresh empty folder. monkeypatch is a fixture that replaces something for one test and puts it back afterwards: monkeypatch.setattr(sounds, "play_notes", lambda *a, **k: None) . It is how tests keep the sound off and avoid real dialogs. The thing replaced is named by a string, which is why an IDE cannot always check it. A fake is a small class a test writes to stand in for something real (a QSoundEffect , a settings store). Because Qt calls fakes positionally, they sometimes need # noqa: PLR0917 . Read: Okken’s Python Testing with pytest ; the doctest and unittest.mock pages in the standard library documentation.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Packaging in one paragraph pyproject.toml is the single description of the project (PEP 621): its name, version, dependencies, the command alto , which files ship with the package (the fonts and recordings), and the settings of every tool. setuptools builds it. pip install -e . reads it. When you add a dependency, add it there.

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Words to search for If you want to go further: context managers ( with statements: used for database transactions and QPainter save/restore), generators and yield (used by fixtures), comprehensions , the descriptor protocol (how @property works), the data model and dunder methods ( __eq__ , __lt__ : Note defines ordering), structural subtyping and Protocol (PEP 544).

title: Python beyond the basics
text: Further reading Luciano Ramalho, Fluent Python , 2nd ed. (O’Reilly, 2022): the best single book for the “beyond basics” material above. Brett Slatkin, Effective Python , 2nd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2019): short, practical items on closures, decorators and typing. Python Software Foundation, The Python Language Reference , “Data model” chapter, and the dataclasses , typing , functools , pathlib and doctest library pages, at docs.python.org. PEP 8, PEP 257, PEP 484, PEP 557, PEP 604, PEP 621, at peps.python.org. The numpydoc docstring standard, numpydoc.readthedocs.io (the “format” page): the layout of Alto’s docstrings.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Qt and PySide6 Qt is a C++ toolkit for building desktop programs, and PySide6 is the official Python binding to it (it is “Qt for Python”, maintained by The Qt Company). Alto’s interface is entirely PySide6. This chapter covers the ideas you need to read and change alto/ui/ , and the traps that bite people who know Python but not Qt. Qt’s own documentation (doc.qt.io) is written for C++, but it is accurate for Python: every class and method has the same name, and the Qt for Python site (doc.qt.io/qtforpython-6) has the Python signatures. When this chapter says “see QPainter”, look it up there.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: The event loop A graphical program is not a script that runs top to bottom. It starts, builds its windows, and then calls app.exec() , which runs the event loop : a loop that waits for something to happen (a click, a key press, a timer firing, a window needing to be redrawn), then calls the code that handles it, then waits again. Everything in Alto happens inside handlers called by that loop. app = QApplication ( sys . argv ) # exactly one per program window = MainWindow ( learner ) window . show () return app . exec () # does not return until the last window closes The most important rule follows directly: never block the event loop. While your handler runs, the window cannot repaint or respond. A time.sleep(2) in a click handler freezes the whole program for two seconds. To do something later, use a timer ( QTimer.singleShot(ms, callback) ); to do something over time, use an animation (see Animation ). Alto does nearly all its work in the one thread. The exceptions are network work, such as checking for a new release or installing a plugin, which goes through run_in_background in alto/ui/background.py . It runs the slow part on another thread and calls you back on the window’s thread with the result or the error. The slow part must not touch widgets: touching a widget from another thread is not allowed. There is one QApplication , and QApplication.instance() returns it (or None if none exists). Tests create one through a fixture, because widgets cannot exist without it.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Widgets, layouts and size A widget ( QWidget ) is a rectangle on screen that can draw itself and receive input. Buttons, labels and lists are widgets, and so are Alto’s StaffWidget and KeyboardWidget . Widgets nest: a widget made with a parent lives inside it. You rarely set positions yourself. A layout ( QVBoxLayout , QHBoxLayout , QGridLayout ) arranges child widgets and resizes them as the window changes. Each widget tells its layout how big it would like to be ( sizeHint() ) and how it may stretch (its size policy ). If a custom widget has the wrong size, the answer is usually its sizeHint or setFixedSize . Custom positioning, as in SlideStack , sets geometry directly; that is the exception, and it is done with care.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Signals and slots A signal is an announcement that something happened; a slot is any callable that wants to hear about it. You connect them: button . clicked . connect ( self . next_question ) # call this method when clicked self . settings_panel . changed . connect ( self . next_question ) You can define your own signals on a class that inherits QObject (every widget does): class StaffInput ( StaffWidget ): placed = Signal ( object ) # the note that was clicked accidental_cycled = Signal () and self.placed.emit(note) sends it. This is how Alto keeps parts independent: the settings panel does not know about the exercise screen, it only emits changed , and the screen decides what to do. The tests use QSignalSpy to watch a signal. A trap with lambda slots: they capture variables late. See the closures section of Python beyond the basics .

title: Qt and PySide6
section: Who owns an object, and when it is deleted
text: Who owns an object, and when it is deleted This is the most common source of mysterious crashes. A Qt object is really a C++ object with a Python wrapper. Two different mechanisms decide its life. Parent ownership. A widget created with a parent (or placed in a layout that has one) is owned by it. When the parent is deleted, its children are deleted. The Python wrapper may stay around, but pointing at a dead object. Python references. A widget with no parent is owned by Python, and is destroyed when the last Python reference goes. Consequences you will hit: QLabel("hi").show() in one expression shows nothing for long: the label has no other reference, so it is deleted at once. Keep it in a variable. This bit the doctests more than once. An animation or timer with no reference may be collected mid-run. Alto passes self as its parent ( QVariantAnimation(self) ) and often also keeps a list of live animations ( self._anims ). widget.deleteLater() schedules deletion for when control returns to the event loop. Deleting a widget while one of its own handlers is running can crash. In tests, QApplication.sendPostedEvents(None, QEvent.Type.DeferredDelete) runs the pending deletions. Methods that return an object may return None ( layout() , widget() , QApplication.instance() ). Pyright makes you check.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Painting A widget draws itself in its paintEvent method, which Qt calls whenever the widget must be redrawn. You create a QPainter on the widget and issue drawing commands. def paintEvent ( self , _ : QPaintEvent ) -> None : p = QPainter ( self ) p . setRenderHint ( QPainter . RenderHint . Antialiasing ) # smooth edges p . setPen ( QPen ( color , 1.5 )) # outlines p . setBrush ( QBrush ( fill )) # fills p . drawLine ( QPointF ( 0 , 10 ), QPointF ( 100 , 10 )) p . drawPath ( path ) Rules that explain most drawing bugs: Never draw outside paintEvent . To change the picture, change state and call self.update() , which asks Qt to schedule a repaint. repaint() draws immediately and is rarely right. A painter must finish before its device goes away. p.end() finishes it (it returns True , which a doctest then prints). Painting on a temporary object ( QPainter(QImage(...)) ) crashes, because Python frees the image under the painter. Keep the image in a variable. Coordinates : the origin is the top left, y grows downward. The same drawing code can be moved or scaled with a QTransform . p.save() and p.restore() bracket changes to pen, brush and transform so one drawing step does not leak into the next. Pixels are not pixels. On a high-resolution screen Qt works in logical pixels and multiplies by the device pixel ratio (often 2 or 3) at the end, so a 10-pixel line is crisp at any density. To make an image look sharp, render it at twice the size and call setDevicePixelRatio(2) ; alto/ui/icons.py does this. Floats matter. Use QPointF and QRectF , not QPoint and QRect , when positions are fractional; integers round and make lines wobble. QPainterPath describes a shape (lines and curves) that you can fill, stroke, transform, measure and hit-test. It is how Alto draws musical symbols. See Rendering music notation . The whole system is documented under “Paint System” in the Qt documentation.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Models and views A list or table in Qt separates the model (the data) from the view (the widget that shows it). The model answers questions like “what is the text of row 3, column 1?” and the view asks. Alto’s database browser ( alto/ui/database_page.py ) defines RowsModel , a small QAbstractTableModel , and puts a QSortFilterProxyModel between the model and the table to give sorting and searching for free. The idea, called Model-View-Controller in the wider world, is worth knowing even if you never write another model.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Saved settings QSettings stores values by key in the operating system’s usual place (an INI file on Linux, the registry on Windows, a property list on macOS). Alto wraps it in alto/ui/store.py : store() returns the one QSettings("alto", "alto") , and int_value , text_value , bool_value , list_value , choices_value and keys_value read a value as the right type, because QSettings may hand back a string where you stored a number, or a list where you stored text with commas. Exercise settings are loaded and saved by the functions in exercise_settings.py . Nothing saves the plain settings objects in alto/settings.py . Tests point the settings at a throwaway folder (the XDG_CONFIG_HOME variable on Linux), so no test can change your real settings.

title: Qt and PySide6
section: Timers and the passage of time
text: Timers and the passage of time QTimer.singleShot(150, callback) calls callback after 150 ms. A QTimer(self) object with setSingleShot(True) can be started, stopped and restarted, which is how the exercise screen cancels the delay before the next question when the user moves on. Timers run in the event loop, so they are as accurate as the loop is free; do not expect better than a few milliseconds.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Testing widgets Use QTest (in PySide6.QtTest ) to act like a user: QTest.mouseClick(widget, Qt.MouseButton.LeftButton) , button.click() , QTest.keyClick(widget, Qt.Key.Key_1) . QTest.qWait(300) runs the event loop for 300 ms, which lets animations and timers progress, but Alto’s own animations and delays wait for motion.settle() in tests (see the Animation guide). A widget that has not been shown gets no resize or paint events, so show() it (the offscreen platform makes this safe) before testing anything about its size.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Enums, the full form PySide6 lets you write Qt.AlignLeft as well as Qt.AlignmentFlag.AlignLeft , but Pyright can only see the second. Alto writes the full form everywhere.

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Known problems with the library pyproject.toml excludes PySide6 6.12.0 on Python 3.11: that release drops a reference to None on every call that returns nothing, and enough painting aborts the interpreter. If you ever upgrade PySide6 and the program crashes after a while with no traceback, suspect the library, and run with python -X faulthandler .

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Words to search for QObject (the root of Qt’s object tree), the meta-object system (how signals work), Graphics View (a framework for many movable items; Alto draws by hand instead, which is simpler for a fixed diagram), QML and Qt Quick (the other way to build Qt programs, declarative and GPU-based; not used here), HiDPI , platform plugin ( xcb , wayland , cocoa , windows , offscreen ), accessibility (Qt supports screen readers; Alto does not yet do much).

title: Qt and PySide6
text: Further reading The Qt documentation, doc.qt.io/qt-6 and doc.qt.io/qtforpython-6: start with “Signals & Slots”, “The Event System”, “Layout Management”, “Paint System”, “High DPI” and “Model/View Programming”. Jasmin Blanchette and Mark Summerfield, C++ GUI Programming with Qt 4 , 2nd ed. (Prentice Hall, 2008). Written for an older Qt and for C++, but its explanation of layouts, painting and the event system is still the clearest book-length account. Mark Summerfield, Rapid GUI Programming with Python and Qt (Prentice Hall, 2007): the same ideas in Python, for PyQt4. Guillaume Lazar and Robin Penea, Mastering Qt 5 , 2nd ed. (Packt, 2018): architecture of a larger application. Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, Design Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 1994): the observer pattern is what signals and slots are, and MVC’s origins are described there.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Testing, quality and release This chapter is about how Alto stays correct as it changes: what the tests are, how the automated checks fit together, how the documentation is kept honest, and how to release a version. The commands are collected in Getting oriented and For developers ; here is the reasoning.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: The safety net, in layers Layer Catches Where When it runs Doctests a docstring example that no longer matches the code every >>> line under alto/ with pytest Unit and widget tests wrong behavior tests/ with pytest Docstring check missing or incomplete documentation tests/test_docstrings.py with pytest Docs checks a screenshot or API page out of date tests/test_docs.py , tests/test_api_docs.py , scripts/check-docs.sh with pytest , and on push Ruff style, unused code, import order, many bugs ruff format , ruff check on commit, in CI Pyright type errors scripts/typecheck.sh on push, in CI PyCharm inspections more type and style warnings the IDE while you edit CI checks selected by the files changed, on a clean machine .github/workflows/ on every pull request A change is done when every layer is green. None of them needs a person to remember anything.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: The tests pytest is configured in pyproject.toml : it looks in tests/ and alto/ , and runs docstring examples as tests ( --doctest-modules ), ignoring differences in whitespace and allowing ... as a wildcard in expected output. A run takes about a minute and covers every line of alto/ .

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Layout One file per area: test_theory.py , test_exercises.py , test_learning.py , test_database.py , test_exercise_view.py , test_main_window.py , test_settings_panels.py , test_rendering.py (every widget draws something) and so on. A test function is named as a sentence for what should be true ( test_a_wrong_note_is_shown_then_cleared_for_another_try ), so a failing name tells you what broke. Each test has a docstring that begins “Check that …”.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Fixtures Two conftest.py files set the stage. The root conftest.py serves the doctests: it points the settings and data folders at a temporary directory (so an example that saves a setting cannot touch yours), gives every doctest a QApplication as app , and, when the run ends, deletes leftover widgets so Python’s exit does not crash (see Pitfalls ). tests/conftest.py serves the tests: the same isolation, a session-wide app fixture, and an automatic fixture that, around every test, resets the exercise settings to their defaults, resets the keyboard and notation styles, clears the saved settings, turns sound off, closes every window and closes every database a test left open. That is why tests do not affect each other: each starts from the same state. practiced_learner builds a learner with months of made-up answers for tests that need history.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: What to test Pure logic (theory, scheduler, statistics): plain functions with plain asserts; use a seeded random.Random . Exercises: the generation tests in tests/test_exercises.py , which loop over the whole registry. Widgets: build it, show() it, act on it with QTest , assert on state and on signals. Widgets are drawn into memory on the offscreen platform, so you can also check a drawing: widget.grab().toImage() and look at pixels ( tests/test_rendering.py counts dark pixels to prove something was drawn). Things with side effects (audio, dialogs, saved settings): replace them with a recorder, using monkeypatch . Tests never play a sound or open a real dialog.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Writing a test well Write it so that it fails first. A test that has never failed has not been shown to test anything. One reason to fail. If it asserts five unrelated things, you cannot tell which broke. Seed every random source. A flaky test teaches people to ignore red. Do not test private details if a public behavior says the same thing. The exceptions are private helpers that are hard to reach through the public interface (the animations’ final states, for example). Test one thing. Check answers in logic tests, without widgets. In a screen test, call motion.settle() to end feedback and animations instead of waiting; keep QTest.qWait , which costs real time, for tests marked motion that are about the timing itself.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Coverage pytest --cov --cov-report=term-missing prints the lines the tests never ran. Alto aims for every line, so a pull request that adds code should add its tests. Coverage measures what was executed , not whether the assertions are good, so treat the number as a floor, not a goal. Codecov displays it on pull requests but, by design, does not block them ( codecov.yml ).

title: Testing, quality and release
text: The automated checks

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Ruff Ruff is a linter (it finds problems) and a formatter (it lays code out). It replaces several older tools (pycodestyle, pyflakes, isort, pyupgrade, flake8 plugins). The rules enabled in pyproject.toml are named in groups by their letter prefixes, and each has a comment saying why: E / W style, F unused names and similar, I import order, UP outdated syntax, B likely bugs, D docstrings, ANN annotations, TID252 no relative imports, PLC0415 no imports inside functions, PLR0917 only the first argument positional, and several more. To see what a rule means, look up its code in the Ruff documentation, or run ruff rule <CODE> .

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Pyright Pyright reads the type hints and reports contradictions. It is run through scripts/typecheck.sh so it uses the project’s virtual environment and can read PySide6’s type information. Basic mode, as if for Python 3.11. Tests have two optional-access checks relaxed (in pyproject.toml ), because tests deliberately assert on widgets that the application keeps optional.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: pre-commit .pre-commit-config.yaml installs hooks into Git. On commit : trailing whitespace, final newline, YAML and TOML validity, large files, ruff format , ruff check --fix . On push : the whole test suite, the docs freshness check (a warning only) and Pyright. If a hook changes a file the commit stops so you can look; commit again. After a merge or fast-forward pull on main , a third hook cleans up merged local branches .

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Continuous integration GitHub Actions selects checks by change type on pull requests. Pushes to main get the full checks. tests.yml runs the suite on main on every Python version that has not reached end of life (a matrix, currently 3.11 to 3.15). When a version stops being supported, drop it here and in pyproject.toml . pyright.yml runs Pyright. codecov.yml uploads the coverage report attached to the pytest run. It uses the repository secret CODECOV_TOKEN when available. The workflows install a few system libraries ( libegl1 , libxkbcommon0 and others) because Qt’s offscreen platform needs them even though nothing appears on screen. If CI fails on a missing library with a message about libGL or xcb , that list is where to look.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Keeping the documentation true Two things generate documentation, and tests insist they are current. Screenshots ( docs/assets/img/ ) come from scripts/screenshots.py , which runs the real program against a made-up profile and a temporary settings folder, in both themes. tests/test_docs.py checks every picture a page shows exists in both. The pre-push hook runs scripts/check-docs.sh , which only warns when alto/ui has changed since the pictures were made. Look at the pictures after regenerating: fonts render slightly differently on each machine, so regenerate on the one you normally use. The API reference ( docs/api/ ) is generated by scripts/api_docs.py from the docstrings, and tests/test_api_docs.py fails if it is stale. The docs site itself is Jekyll, served by GitHub Pages from the docs/ folder. To preview it locally you need Ruby and the github-pages gem, which is outside the Python toolchain; most changes can be checked by reading the Markdown and the layout in docs/_layouts/ .

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Releasing a version Alto is installed from source today. When you want to cut a release: Decide the version ( version in pyproject.toml ). Use semantic versioning : MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH . Bump PATCH for fixes, MINOR for new features, MAJOR for changes that break users. For a program with a database, a change that needs a schema migration is at least MINOR. Make sure the checks pass on a clean checkout , in CI, on all Python versions. Migrations. If the database changed, confirm the migration works on a copy of a real older database, and say in the notes to copy alto.db first. Refresh and review the screenshots in both themes using the pre-release checklist . Regenerate the API pages and check that Your data is current. Check license compliance on both packaged downloads. If you added fonts or recordings, verify their redistribution terms and update THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Follow the release license compliance check . Build the package: python -m pip install build then python -m build produces a source distribution and a wheel in dist/ . Open the wheel (it is a zip) and check that the fonts and recordings are inside; pyproject.toml lists them under package-data . Tag the commit ( git tag v0.2.0 , git push --tags ) and write release notes: what changed for users, in plain words. Publish if you want to: PyPI via twine upload dist/* , or attach the files to a GitHub release. A GUI program is also often distributed as a standalone application (see “Packaging” in the reading list); that is a separate project.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Words to search for Unit test, integration test, end-to-end test. Test double: fake, stub, mock, spy. Fixture. Flaky test. Property-based testing (the hypothesis library, which would suit the theory code). Mutation testing. Continuous integration. Semantic versioning. Linter, formatter, static analysis, type checker. Wheel and sdist. Reproducible build. Changelog.

title: Testing, quality and release
text: Further reading Brian Okken, Python Testing with pytest , 2nd ed. (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2022). Kent Beck, Test-Driven Development: By Example (Addison-Wesley, 2002): the method of writing the failing test first. Michael C. Feathers, Working Effectively with Legacy Code (Prentice Hall, 2004): how to put tests around code that has none. Gerard Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns (Addison-Wesley, 2007): the vocabulary of test doubles (fake, stub, mock, spy). Jez Humble and David Farley, Continuous Delivery (Addison-Wesley, 2010): why every change goes through the same automated checks. Tom Preston-Werner (and the community), Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 , semver.org: the specification. The pytest documentation, docs.pytest.org: fixtures, monkeypatch and parametrisation. Python Packaging Authority, Python Packaging User Guide , packaging.python.org: building and publishing wheels and pyproject.toml . The Ruff documentation, docs.astral.sh/ruff, and the Pyright documentation, microsoft.github.io/pyright. The Qt documentation, “Qt Test Overview”, doc.qt.io: the tools behind QTest and QSignalSpy .

title: Glossary and further reading
text: Glossary and further reading The first part of this page is a glossary of terms used in the guide and in the code, each with something to search for. The second is a reading list by subject, favoring books, peer-reviewed papers, standards and official documentation over blog posts. Web addresses change; the authors, titles and years are given so you can find a source even after a link has moved.

title: Glossary and further reading
text: A suggested order for learning If you are new to some of this, this order builds on itself. The program as a user. Run it, use every exercise, open every settings pane, look at the statistics and the database page. Python’s less common features : Python beyond the basics , with Fluent Python beside it. Qt’s model : Qt and PySide6 ; build a ten-line window that draws a rectangle and responds to a click. One small change in alto/ui : alter a color, a radius, a duration. See Styling and Animation . One new exercise : Building an exercise . It touches the data model, the tests and the docs, in a small way. A change to the scheduler , tested by simulation: Spaced repetition . Then whichever of notation and audio you need. They are the deepest chapters and the most independent.

title: Glossary and further reading
text: Glossary Terms are in alphabetical order. Italic words in an entry are terms to search for. Aliasing. Frequencies above half the sample rate folding back as false lower ones. Search: Nyquist frequency , anti-aliasing filter . See Computer audio . Anchor (SMuFL). A named point on a glyph, such as where a stem should attach to a notehead. Search: SMuFL metadata . Antialiasing (drawing). Smoothing the jagged edges of shapes by blending edge pixels. Qt: QPainter.RenderHint.Antialiasing . Attempt. One answer to a question, right or wrong. The log of attempts is the history; attempt_no is 1 for the first answer to a showing. See Data . Bit depth. How many bits store each audio sample. Alto uses 16. Search: quantisation , dynamic range . Bounding box (ink box). The smallest rectangle around a glyph’s shape; used to center a notehead. Search: glyph metrics . Brace. The curly bracket joining the two staves of a grand staff. Closure. A function that remembers variables from the function that made it. Search: lexical scope , late binding . Clef. The sign at the start of a staff saying which pitches its lines mean. Treble, bass, and the C clefs (alto, tenor, soprano, mezzo-soprano, baritone). Cooldown (scheduler). How long a question stays unlikely after being asked, long for easy questions and short for hard ones. Cold start. What to do about a question or a user with no history. CWMN. Common Western Music Notation, the notation Alto draws. Dataclass. A class that holds fields, with its methods written for you. @dataclass ; frozen=True makes it immutable. Decibel (dB). A logarithmic unit for amplitude ratios: 20 × log10(ratio) . Halving an amplitude is -6 dB. Desirable difficulties. Robert Bjork’s term for practice conditions that feel harder but make learning last. Search: interleaving . Device pixel ratio. How many physical pixels make one of Qt’s logical pixels on a high-resolution screen. Search: HiDPI . Diatonic index. octave * 7 + letter : a note’s position on the staff ladder, ignoring accidentals. Note.diatonic . Doctest. An example in a docstring that is run as a test. Search: doctest module . Easing. The shape of an animation’s speed over time. QEasingCurve . Search: Penner equations . Engraving. Preparing music for print; the craft that notation software imitates. Search: music engraving rules . Equal temperament. Dividing the octave into 12 equal semitones, each a frequency ratio of 2^(1/12). Event loop. The loop that waits for clicks, timers and repaint requests, and calls the code that handles them. QApplication.exec() . Fake (test). A small class that stands in for something real and records what is done to it. Search: test double . Fixture (pytest). A function that prepares what a test needs; a test asks for it by parameter name. Forgetting curve. The decay of memory over time without review. Search: Ebbinghaus . FSRS. The Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler, a modern memory-model scheduler; its model is DSR (difficulty, stability, retrievability). Glyph. The shape of one character or symbol in a font. In a music font, a notehead, a clef, a flag. Grand staff. A treble and a bass staff joined by a brace, used for piano. Interleaving. Mixing different kinds of problem in one practice session. Item key. A 20-character hash that identifies a question, so the same question is recognized when it returns. Question.item_key() . Keyword-only argument. A parameter that must be given by name, written after a bare * in the definition. Ledger line. A short extra line for a note above or below the staff. Leech. A card or question that is failed again and again. MIDI note number. A number for each pitch: middle C is 60, A4 is 69, each semitone adds 1. Model/view. Separating the data (the model) from the widget that shows it (the view). Qt: QAbstractTableModel , QTableView . Monkeypatch (pytest). A fixture that temporarily replaces an attribute or function for one test. Multisampling. Recording an instrument at many pitches and playing the nearest. Search: sampler , velocity layers . Nyquist frequency. Half the sample rate, the highest frequency that can be represented: 22,050 Hz at 44.1 kHz. Offscreen platform. Qt’s platform plugin that draws into memory instead of onto a screen, used by the tests. QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen . Overtone / partial. A frequency above the fundamental in a note’s sound; together they make the timbre. Painter ( QPainter ). The object that draws shapes, text and images onto a widget or image. Palette ( QPalette ). A widget’s table of named colors ( Window , Base , Text , Highlight …). PCM. Pulse-code modulation: audio stored as a list of sample values. WAV files carry PCM. Pitch shifting. Changing the pitch of a recording. Alto does it by resampling , which also changes the duration. Property animation. Animating a named property of a Qt object. QPropertyAnimation . Resampling. Changing the sample rate or reading samples at a different speed, by interpolating between neighbors. Retrieval practice / testing effect. Recalling an answer strengthens memory more than rereading it. Sample (audio). One measurement of a sound signal. Do not confuse with a recorded sample in the music-production sense: a recording of one note. Sample rate. Measurements per second; 44,100 for CD quality. Signal and slot. Qt’s way for an object to announce an event and others to respond. Signal , .connect , .emit . SM-2. The SuperMemo 2 algorithm: item intervals multiplied by an ease factor. Search: Wozniak . SMuFL. Standard Music Font Layout: names, code points and metadata for music fonts. Search: W3C Music Notation Community Group . Softmax. Choosing among options with probability proportional to exp(β × value) . Search: Boltzmann distribution , exploration-exploitation . Spacing effect. Spreading study over time produces better lasting memory than cramming. Staff space. The distance between two staff lines; the unit of measurement in engraving. Alto’s gap . Strain. Alto’s number, 0 to 6, for how much practice a question needs. Style sheet (QSS). Qt’s CSS-like language for appearance. Search: Qt Style Sheets reference . Timbre. The quality that distinguishes two instruments playing the same note; set by the mix of partials. Token (cancellation). A counter captured by a delayed callback so it can tell it has been superseded and do nothing. Type hint. An annotation saying what type a value should be; checked by Pyright. Search: PEP 484 . Voice (notation). An independent line of music on a staff. Alto’s staffs show single notes and simple chords and do not need voices. WAV / RIFF. A common audio file format: a small header followed by PCM samples.

text: Reading list

title: Glossary and further reading
text: Python and software craft Luciano Ramalho, Fluent Python , 2nd ed. (O’Reilly, 2022). Brett Slatkin, Effective Python , 2nd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2019). Brian Okken, Python Testing with pytest , 2nd ed. (Pragmatic Bookshelf, 2022). John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design (Yaknyam Press, 2018): on keeping modules deep and interfaces small, which is what Question and Exercise are. Martin Fowler, Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code , 2nd ed. (Addison-Wesley, 2018). Andrew Hunt and David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer , 20th anniversary ed.
