title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice Alto’s central idea is that practice time should go where it is needed: questions you miss or answer slowly come back sooner and more often, and questions you know well fade into the background. This chapter explains the learning science behind that, the family of algorithms people use for it, how ASRS schedules questions during practice, and how to change it without breaking it.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: Practice algorithms Under Settings → Practice → Question scheduling , each profile can choose ASRS, ARTS, SM-2, or FSRS. The Alto Spaced Repetition System (ASRS) is the default.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: ARTS Adaptive Response-Time-based Sequencing chooses the next question using your last first attempt and the number of other questions you have answered since. A miss can bring a question back after one intervening answer. A fast, correct answer usually gives you a longer gap. You can practice as long as you like. Alto applies the published ARTS priority equation to saved questions under the current exercise settings and a sample of freshly generated questions. It uses a 100-millisecond response-time reference to distinguish quick answers in music drills, a baseline priority of 1 for unseen questions, and a random choice among tied scores. Earlier first attempts in the same exercise count when you reopen the app or switch algorithms. Mettler, Massey, and Kellman, equation 1

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: Calendar practice Under Settings → Practice , New cards/day and Maximum reviews/day set the daily allowance for each exercise. The defaults are 10 new cards and 200 reviews. Both algorithms share these settings and the day’s usage. To change one exercise, open its settings with the sliders button and choose Daily Limits . Clear Use global for either limit to override it. Each limit has an Unlimited checkbox. For example, you can keep new cards at 10 per day and review every card that comes due. A zero pauses that kind of practice. Exercise tiles show new cards in blue, outstanding incorrect cards in red, and today’s available reviews in green. The red count includes missed cards under the current settings even when their retry time is in the future or the daily review limit has been reached. Showing a new card uses an introduction slot. An unanswered new card stays available in blue so you can finish it after leaving the exercise. Grading the first answer completes the introduction. Grading a subsequent review uses one review slot, including a miss. A miss ends that showing. While the missed card waits for its scheduled retry, Alto offers other eligible cards. If only the retry remains and a review slot is available, the open exercise waits for it and resumes automatically. The allowances reset at local midnight, and overdue cards keep their scheduled dates. Due questions come first. By default, Alto grades the first submission automatically. During the initial timing calibration, SM-2 uses grade 4 for a correct answer and grade 2 for a miss, with a one-minute retry after a miss. FSRS uses Good and Again with the Python library’s default learning steps. The first time a card moves between SM-2 and FSRS, the new scheduler inherits its due date and review progress. On later switches, each scheduler resumes its own schedule for that card. ARTS and ASRS practice leaves both calendar queues intact. SM-2 specification · Python FSRS During calibration, Next interval shows how long after a correct first answer the card will be due. The value appears at the lower right of the music, or on one line beneath the keyboard. A new SM-2 card shows 1 day , and a new FSRS card shows 10 min . After 40 timed, correct first answers in an exercise, automatic grading uses that profile’s rolling distribution. View the chart and adjust the cutoffs in Settings → Practice → Response-time grading… . Before you answer, the three possible intervals appear beside the music or in one row below the keyboard. A correct answer displays the assigned grade and interval. Response-time grading . To choose your own interval, enable Grade correct answers with Hard, Good, or Easy in Settings → Practice . After a correct answer, the interval appears above each grade button. Choose how difficult it was to recall the answer to schedule the review and move on. Response time ends when you answer the exercise. A wrong answer automatically earns Again and moves you to the next available card. Self-grading disables the exercise’s Next Question setting. Both algorithms use Anki’s default learning steps. On a new card, Hard repeats in 5 min 30 s, Good advances to 10 min, and Easy skips to a day-based review. SM-2 starts Easy around four days. FSRS calculates it from memory stability at 90% desired retention. Alto applies the displayed delay from the time you choose a grade and uses its own daily limits. Anki deck options For the range above each grade button and an example of how Alto spreads new cards across review days, see Self-grading a new card . Note Identification, Note Construction, and Notation Identification count their full catalogs. In Notation Identification, each selected symbol counts as one card for Answer Button and one for Click on Staff . Different excerpts and staff positions share the symbol’s review date within each question type. If you select only Vertical turn and identify it correctly on your first SM-2 attempt, its first review is due one day later. Other generators sample questions up to the remaining daily allowance. With unlimited new cards, their blue count shows the next batch of up to 10 new questions and refills as you practice. A saved question is eligible under its original settings, when the exercise can adapt it to the current settings, or when the current generator produces the same question. Changing settings preserves its identity and schedule.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: Why scheduling matters: three findings Cognitive psychology has measured these for well over a century. They are the reason such software exists. The forgetting curve. Hermann Ebbinghaus, memorising nonsense syllables in the 1880s, showed that memory decays quickly at first and then more slowly, roughly exponentially. Without review, most of a new item is gone in days. The spacing effect. The same amount of study produces better long-term memory if it is spread out over time than if it is crammed together. Each successful retrieval after a delay slows the next forgetting. That is the basis of spaced repetition : review an item just before you would forget it, and the gaps can grow. The testing effect (also retrieval practice ). Trying to recall an answer strengthens memory more than re-reading it. Answering a question is not just a measurement, it is the exercise. A related idea, Robert Bjork’s desirable difficulties , is that conditions that make practice feel harder (spacing, mixing topics, testing instead of rereading) often make learning last longer. Mixing different kinds of problem is called interleaving , and it is why Alto lets an exercise draw from several clefs, keys and note values at once.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: The families of scheduling algorithm All of them answer the same question: given what happened the last few times a person saw an item, when should it come back? Leitner boxes (1970s). Cards live in numbered boxes. A right answer moves a card up a box, which is reviewed less often; a wrong one sends it back to box 1. Simple, no arithmetic, and the origin of many apps. SM-2 (SuperMemo, 1987). Piotr Wozniak’s algorithm, still the basis of many programs. Each item has an ease factor EF (starting at 2.5). After a review graded q from 0 to 5, the next interval is 1 day, then 6 days, then the previous interval times EF ; EF itself moves up for easy reviews and down for hard ones, never below 1.3. A grade below 3 resets the item. Intervals grow geometrically, which matches the exponential forgetting curve. Half-life regression (Duolingo, 2016). Burr Settles and Brendan Meeder model the probability of recall as p = 2^(-Δ/h) , where Δ is the time since last seen and h is a half-life (the delay at which recall falls to half). The half-life is learned from data from many users with a regression on features such as how often the word was seen and missed. DSR models and FSRS (2020s). The Difficulty, Stability, Retrievability model treats memory as three numbers per item. Retrievability R is the probability of recall right now, a function of time and stability; stability S is how long until R falls to 90%; difficulty D is how hard the item is. After each review a formula updates S and D , with parameters fitted to review logs. FSRS (the Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler ) is the open-source version used by Anki. Rating systems and student models. Different in spirit: instead of scheduling, estimate a person’s ability and an item’s difficulty . Item response theory (IRT) and the Elo rating system do this; Bayesian knowledge tracing models the chance that a skill is “known” given a history of answers. Elo, adapted to education, is simple enough to code in a page. Bandits and sampling. If you treat “which question next?” as a choice among options with different payoffs, you are in the territory of the multi-armed bandit problem and the exploration versus exploitation trade-off. A softmax (or Boltzmann ) policy picks each option with probability proportional to exp(β × value) . Hold that thought.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: ASRS ASRS samples generated questions and prior attempts on each turn. It generates fresh questions. FRESH = 10 new Question s are made by the exercise for each pick. It adds stored ones. From the database come questions this profile has met before under the same settings : the 25 with the highest strain ( hardest ) plus 10 random ones ( random_extra ), from Database.replay_candidates . It gives each candidate a weight from the scheduler, and draws one at random in proportion to weight ( scheduler.choose , which is rng.choices(options, weights=weights) ). A question just asked ( avoid ) is excluded. That is a weighted sampler , not a calendar. There are no due dates, nothing is ever “overdue”, and the system degrades gracefully when you skip a week. The cost is that it has no explicit model of forgetting over long gaps. It uses recent time only to avoid repeating a question too soon.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: The strain Every question a profile has met has a number, its strain (the database column strain ; “how much practice it needs”), between 0 and STRAIN_MAX = 6 . A new question starts at NEW_STRAIN = 1.5 . After each attempt, update_strain changes it: if not correct : strain += WRONG_PENALTY # +1.5: every wrong attempt pushes it up elif attempt_no == 1 : strain += - CORRECT_REWARD + speed_term ( seconds , par_seconds = par_seconds ) # -0.5, plus a speed adjustment else : strain -= RETRY_REWARD # -0.2: right, but only after misses strain = min ( max ( strain , 0.0 ), STRAIN_MAX ) Speed matters. The first answer’s time is compared with the exercise’s par_seconds , a number each exercise sets for “how long a good first answer takes”. speed_term returns a bonus of up to -0.6 for answers at or below half of par, falling linearly to zero at par, then a penalty growing to +1.0 at four times par. For par_seconds = 3 : First answer took Speed term 1 s or less (≤ 0.5 × par) -0.60 1.5 s -0.60 3 s (par) 0.00 6 s +0.33 12 s or more (≥ 4 × par) +1.00 A worked history, with par_seconds = 3 : start at 1.5. A wrong answer in 4 s: 3.0. A right answer on the retry: 2.8. Then three quick right answers (1.5 s each, each -0.5 and -0.6): 1.7, 0.6, 0.0. The idea is that a question you know becomes unremarkable in about three confident answers, and a question you keep missing climbs toward the ceiling.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
section: From strain to the chance of being asked
text: From strain to the chance of being asked scheduler.weight turns strain into a number used for the draw: def weight ( strain , * , last_seen , now ): if strain is None : # never seen: a fixed middling weight return math . exp ( WEIGHT_SLOPE * NEW_STRAIN ) # exp(0.6 * 1.5) = 2.46 cooldown = BASE_COOLDOWN * 2 ** ( 3.0 - strain ) # seconds a question is "resting" recency = 1.0 - math . exp ( - max ( now - ( last_seen or 0.0 ), 0.0 ) / cooldown ) return math . exp ( WEIGHT_SLOPE * strain ) * max ( recency , MIN_RECENCY ) There are two factors. exp(0.6 × strain) is the softmax idea: a weight that grows exponentially with strain. Each extra point of strain multiplies the weight by e^0.6 ≈ 1.82 . A question at strain 6 is about 37 times as likely as one at strain 0. Recency keeps a question from coming back right away. It rises from 0 to 1 as time passes since the question was last seen, with a cooldown that is long for easy questions and short for hard ones: 960 s at strain 0, 120 s at strain 3, 15 s at strain 6. After 60 seconds, a strain-1.5 question has recovered only 16% of its weight; a strain-6 one, 98%. A floor MIN_RECENCY = 0.02 stops anything being impossible. Strain Weight when long unseen Cooldown 0 1.0 960 s 1.5 (new) 2.5 339 s 3 6.0 120 s 4.5 14.9 42 s 6 36.6 15 s Those two constants, WEIGHT_SLOPE = 0.6 and BASE_COOLDOWN = 120 , are the main dials. Raise the slope and practice concentrates harder on weak questions; lower it and it spreads out. Raise the cooldown and repeats are spaced further.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
section: Item identity and the settings signature
text: Item identity and the settings signature Two pieces of bookkeeping make the history meaningful. Both are easy to break. Question.item_key() is a 20-character hash of what is asked and where it is drawn , not of the note value or the order of the buttons. The same note on the same clef is the same item, whatever the order of the answer buttons. If you add a field to Question that changes what the question is , you must decide whether it belongs in the key. Changing the key changes every item’s identity, which orphans users’ history, so do it only deliberately. Exercise.settings_signature() identifies the settings that shape the questions. A stored question is only replayed while the signature of the exercise now matches the signature it was stored with. If a user turns off the bass clef, bass-clef items stop coming back, and they return when it is turned on again. An exercise that reads settings must override settings_signature or old questions would be replayed outside the user’s current settings.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: What is stored Each answer writes two things in one pass ( Learner.record ): a row in attempts (always: wrong answers included, with the time in milliseconds), and an update of the items row for the question (strain, times seen, times right first try, times wrong, total first-answer time, the signature, and the question itself as JSON so it can be replayed). See Data and persistence . The statistics page is computed from attempts : accuracy, median time, how many questions per day, the hardest questions ( strain ordered), and the review heatmap.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
section: Trying a change: simulate a student
text: Trying a change: simulate a student Do not tune this by feel. Change a constant, run a simulation, look at the numbers. A simulated learner needs only a small rule for “how likely is a right answer for this question”. The script below uses twenty fixed questions of falling difficulty, asks 400 questions, and reports how often each was asked and its final strain. It runs on an in-memory database and takes under a second. import random from collections import Counter from alto.exercises.base import Exercise , Question from alto.learning import Database , Learner class Twenty ( Exercise ): """Twenty fixed questions, "q0" to "q19".""" name = "Twenty" par_seconds = 3.0 def generate ( self , rng : random . Random ) -> Question : return Question ( f "q { rng . randrange ( 20 ) } " , choices = [ "right" , "wrong" ], answer = "right" ) skill = { f "q { n } " : 0.95 - 0.04 * n for n in range ( 20 ) } # chance of a right answer: q0 is easy, q19 is hard rng , now = random . Random ( 1 ), 1_000_000.0 db = Database () # in memory: nothing is saved learner = Learner ( db , profile = db . add_profile ( "Sim" )) exercise , asked = Twenty (), Counter () for _ in range ( 400 ): q = learner . pick ( exercise , rng = rng , now = now ) right = rng . random () < skill [ q . prompt ] seconds = rng . uniform ( 1.5 , 3.0 ) if right else rng . uniform ( 3.0 , 6.0 ) learner . record ( exercise , question = q , answer = "right" if right else "wrong" , correct = right , attempt_no = 1 , seconds = seconds , now = now , ) asked [ q . prompt ] += 1 now += seconds + 1.0 # the next question appears a second later Passing now= to pick and record is what lets a simulation run faster than real time. The run above gives, for a few of the questions: q0 asked 3 times, strain 0.0 (easy: nearly forgotten about) q5 asked 2 times, strain 0.0 q10 asked 12 times, strain 3.18 q15 asked 57 times, strain 5.05 (hard: asked most) q19 asked 56 times, strain 5.04 That is the intended behavior: the hard questions get about twenty times the attention of the easy ones, and the easy ones are still asked occasionally (new items, the random replays, and the floor on recency). Try halving WEIGHT_SLOPE and see how the spread flattens. A real evaluation would also model forgetting (a right-answer chance that falls with time since last seen) and look at long-run accuracy, as research on schedulers does.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
section: Design problems to know by name
text: Design problems to know by name Cold start. A new question has no history, so its weight is a guess. ASRS uses NEW_STRAIN for it. Leeches. An item that is failed again and again. It saturates at the strain ceiling and can crowd out everything else. Anki tags leeches and can suspend them; Alto does not, because strained questions are only more likely , and the recency term keeps them from repeating immediately. Ceiling and floor effects. Clipping strain to 0 and 6 loses information at the ends. That is a deliberate simplicity. Gaming. If the user always answers instantly, the speed bonus rewards them. The score counts only the first attempt. Non-stationarity. People improve and forget, so a model fitted once drifts. A scheduler that updates with every answer, as this one does, adapts for free. Response time as evidence. Using speed as well as correctness is common in research on fluency, and it is what makes a skill like sight-reading, where being right but slow is not yet mastery, trainable.

title: Spaced repetition and adaptive practice
text: Where to go from here If you wanted a true memory model, the next step would be to give each question a stability that grows with each successful retrieval and a retrievability that decays with time (the DSR family), and to schedule by “chance of recall now”. It suits fixed decks better than generated ones. For Alto’s generated questions, a better investment is probably in how new questions are chosen: adapting the range, clef and key to estimated ability, with an Elo-like rating of each setting.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Styling beyond QtWidgets Out of the box, Qt widgets look like whatever platform they run on: gray rectangles on Windows, rounded and translucent on macOS. Alto wants one consistent look with rounded corners, soft highlights and a light and a dark theme, and some pieces (the staff, the keyboard, the switches, the charts) that no standard widget provides. This chapter explains the layers Qt gives you for appearance, which one Alto uses for what, and the color and design ideas behind the choices.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Four layers of appearance From the most automatic to the most hands-on: The style ( QStyle ). The object that knows how to draw every standard widget: a button, a scroll bar, a check box. On each platform Qt picks the native one. Fusion is a built-in cross-platform style that looks the same everywhere. The palette ( QPalette ). A table of named colors ( roles ) that the style draws with: Window (the background), Base (the background of lists and text boxes), Text , Highlight (the selection color), Mid , Midlight , Dark , and so on. Each role has three states: active, inactive and disabled. Style sheets (QSS). A subset of CSS that overrides how standard widgets are drawn: borders, radii, backgrounds, padding. Custom painting. Overriding paintEvent and drawing the widget yourself with QPainter . Alto uses all four, each where it fits: Need Layer Where Light, dark or follow-the-system Palette (through the color scheme) alto/ui/theme.py Rounded buttons, check boxes, lists, menus, scroll bars Style sheet alto/ui/style.py Switches, theme cards, charts, the staff, the keyboard Custom painting settings_menu.py , app_settings.py , charts.py , staff.py , keyboard.py Monochrome icons that match the text color SVG, tinted and rendered alto/ui/icons.py

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
section: Themes: the color scheme and the palette
text: Themes: the color scheme and the palette Since Qt 6.8 you can tell Qt which color scheme to use: QGuiApplication.styleHints().setColorScheme(Qt.ColorScheme.Dark) . Qt then switches the palette. Qt.ColorScheme.Unknown means “follow the operating system”. apply_theme does exactly this, then builds the style sheet from the new palette: def apply_theme ( key : str ) -> None : QGuiApplication . styleHints (). setColorScheme ( _SCHEMES . get ( key , Qt . ColorScheme . Unknown ) ) app = QApplication . instance () app . setStyleSheet ( app_style ( app . palette ())) The chosen theme is saved ( ui/theme ) and applied again at start-up, before any window exists. The rule that makes theming work: take colors from the palette, never from a constant. A widget that paints with palette.color(QPalette.ColorRole.Text) is correct in both themes; one that paints with QColor("black") is correct in one. The staff is deliberately a white “paper” in both themes, because music reads best black on white; that is a design decision, not an oversight.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Style sheets, in practice Alto’s standard push buttons have a one-pixel border and share the ten-pixel corner radius used by its fields. In dark mode, exercise tile outlines are near black ( #181818 ) and other standard button outlines are graphite gray ( #505050 ). Hover tints the surface. Keyboard focus adds a second pixel to the outline and reduces the padding so the label stays in place. Pressed and checked buttons use the theme’s accent color. QPushButton { border : 1px solid < edge color > ; border-radius : 10px ; padding : 6px 12px ; } QPushButton :focus { border : 2px solid palette ( highlight ); padding : 5px 11px ; } Selectors. QPushButton matches the class and its subclasses; QListWidget#nav matches the one with setObjectName("nav") ; QToolButton[arrowButton="true"] matches a widget with that dynamic property ( widget.setProperty("arrowButton", True) ). If you set a property after the widget is shown, call widget.style().unpolish(widget) and .polish(widget) so the sheet is applied again. Pseudo-states ( :hover , :pressed , :checked , :disabled ) and sub-controls ( ::indicator , ::item , ::handle ) name the parts of a widget you can style separately. palette(highlight) reads a palette role, so a sheet can follow the theme without Python. The box model is the same as CSS: content, padding, border, margin. A widget that gets a style sheet is drawn by a different code path. Once you style a part of a widget, Qt stops using the platform style for it and you must style the rest, or it looks half done. Styling QCheckBox::indicator means styling its checked, hover and disabled states too, as style.py does. What QSS cannot do. It cannot animate (a :hover change is instant), cannot draw arbitrary shapes, and gradients are limited to qlineargradient and qradialgradient . For those, paint it yourself. Alto’s sheet is one Python string template in alto/ui/style.py , filled with str.format using colors computed from the current palette: return _TEMPLATE . format ( RADIUS = RADIUS , edge = dark , accent = accent_c . name (), nav_hover = blend_name ( window_c , b = text_c , t = 0.07 ), ...) Because .format treats { and } as fields, every brace that is really CSS is doubled in the template. If you add a rule and get a KeyError or IndexError , you forgot to double a brace. The sheet is rebuilt on every theme change, since the colors come from the palette.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Numeric fields Use a standard QSpinBox for an editable integer, as in Settings → Practice and the exercise’s Daily Limits submenu. The application stylesheet centers the value and gives the field the same rounded corners, heavier lower edge, and accent focus outline as Alto’s other fields. The two chevrons share a narrow column on the right. Qt handles stepping, typed input, and range limits. Place the label above the field, associate it with the field using label.setBuddy(field) , and give the field the same accessible name. Keep the control at its natural width. Check the widest allowed value, both step buttons, keyboard focus, and disabled text with the application stylesheet in light and dark themes.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Painting your own widgets When no sheet can do it, draw it. The Switch in settings_menu.py is a good small example: about thirty lines of paintEvent give a pill-shaped track whose color is a blend between the “off” and “on” palette colors, and a white knob that slides. track = blend ( off , b = on , t = self . _pos ) # _pos goes 0 -> 1 while the knob slides p . setBrush ( track ) p . drawRoundedRect ( self . rect (), self . H / 2 , self . H / 2 ) x = margin + r + self . _pos * ( self . W - 2 * ( margin + r )) p . drawEllipse ( QPointF ( x , self . H / 2 ), r , r ) Patterns to copy: State in numbers, drawing from numbers. The widget holds _pos , a float. Animation changes the number and calls update() . Painting reads the number. There is no separate “off look” and “on look”. blend(a, b=, t=) in alto/ui/colors.py mixes two colors linearly. It is the workhorse: hover tints, disabled states, the fade on a right or wrong answer. Read the palette inside paintEvent , not in __init__ , so a theme change shows up on the next repaint. sizeHint() must be right, or layouts will squash the widget. Keep drawing code free of side effects. paintEvent can be called at any time and as often as Qt likes.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Color: the ideas worth knowing sRGB and gamma. Screen colors are stored in sRGB, which is not linear in light. Mixing two sRGB colors with plain arithmetic, as blend does, gives a result a little darker in the middle than a physically correct mix. For UI tints that is fine and common. For anything that must be perceptually even (a heat map), use a designed palette. See Poynton in the reading list. Contrast. Text must be readable against its background. The WCAG guidelines define a contrast ratio from the relative luminance of two colors and ask for at least 4.5:1 for body text. When you add a color, check it in both themes. Do not rely on color alone. About one man in twelve cannot distinguish red from green. Alto marks right and wrong answers with green and red flashes, and shows the explanation as text as well. If you add a chart that needs red against green to be read, add a second cue (position, a label, a pattern) or pick a color-blind-safe pair such as blue and orange. Sequential palettes. The review heatmap uses one hue in steps of lightness, which reads as “more”. That is the right choice for ordered data. Cynthia Brewer’s ColorBrewer scheme names (sequential, diverging, qualitative) are the vocabulary. Alpha. A color with transparency ( setAlpha(110) ) is the cheapest way to dim something, as Switch does when disabled.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Icons alto/ui/icons.py holds icons as snippets of SVG with the word COLOR where the fill goes. svg_icon(inner, color=...) replaces it, renders the SVG with QSvgRenderer into a pixmap twice the size, sets the device pixel ratio to 2 so it is sharp on a high-resolution screen, and returns a QIcon . Pass the text color from the palette and the icon matches the theme. Because the color is baked into the pixmap when the icon is made, an icon does not change by itself when the theme changes. That is why changing the theme builds a fresh MainWindow ( rebuild() ): it is simpler than finding and refreshing every icon, and a theme change is rare.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Fonts A QFont names a family and a size. Prefer pixel size ( setPixelSize ) for drawing that must line up with other geometry, as the staff does, and point size for ordinary text. Fonts that ship with the program are loaded with QFontDatabase.addApplicationFont(path) , which returns an id you can turn into the family name; this is how the music fonts in alto/assets/fonts are used (see Rendering music notation ). Always give a fallback: if a font is missing on the machine, Qt substitutes one silently.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Visual design vocabulary A few terms, so you can search for the right thing: Elevation is the impression that a surface sits above another; Alto fakes it with the heavier lower border on buttons. QGraphicsDropShadowEffect makes real shadows but costs performance on every repaint. Affordance is what a control’s appearance says about what you can do with it. A raised button invites pressing. Design tokens are named values (a radius, a spacing, an accent color) used everywhere instead of literals. RADIUS in style.py is one; changing it changes every corner. Skeuomorphism and flat design are the two ends of a style spectrum. Alto sits in the middle: flat, with small cues. A spacing scale (multiples of 4 or 8 pixels) keeps layouts feeling regular.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: The docs site The website in docs/ has its own theme in docs/assets/css/site.css , written with CSS custom properties (variables such as --fg and --accent ) that are redefined for dark mode, both from the operating system ( prefers-color-scheme ) and from a toggle that sets data-theme on the page. The screenshots come in a light and a dark pair for the same reason. See For developers .

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
section: A checklist for a new themed widget
text: A checklist for a new themed widget Take every color from the palette or from blend of palette colors. Paint in paintEvent ; change state, then call update() . Set a correct sizeHint . Look at it in both themes, with the screenshot script or by running the app and switching. Add a test that grabs it ( widget.grab() ) and checks it is not blank, as tests/test_rendering.py does.

title: Styling beyond QtWidgets
text: Further reading The Qt documentation: “Qt Style Sheets” (including the Reference and the Examples, which show every widget), “QPalette”, “QStyle”, and “Styles and Style Aware Widgets”, at doc.qt.io. Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 , World Wide Web Consortium Recommendation, w3.org/TR/WCAG21: the “Contrast (Minimum)” criterion, 1.4.3, and “Use of Color”, 1.4.1. Charles Poynton, Digital Video and HD: Algorithms and Interfaces , 2nd ed. (Morgan Kaufmann, 2012): gamma, luminance and color spaces from the source. Cynthia A. Brewer, Designing Better Maps: A Guide for GIS Users (Esri Press, 2005): the thinking behind ColorBrewer. Edward R. Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information , 2nd ed. (Graphics Press, 2001): charts, ink and clutter. Donald A. Norman, The Design of Everyday Things , revised ed. (Basic Books, 2013): affordances and feedback. Ellen Lupton, Thinking with Type , 2nd ed. (Princeton Architectural Press, 2010): type for people who are not designers. Steve Krug, Don’t Make Me Think, Revisited (New Riders, 2014): usability in short chapters. Apple, Human Interface Guidelines , and Google, Material Design guidelines: two worked-out design systems to learn from.

title: Home
text: Learn music theory with Alto Study music theory in short lessons and practice what you learn with spaced repetition. Download Alto

title: Home
text: What you can practice Circle of Fifths Find relative keys and the chords that belong to a key. Scales Identify scales and modes by their patterns, or build them on the staff. Chords Tell triads and seventh chords apart and recognize inversions in arpeggios. Intervals Name the distance between two notes on a staff or a keyboard. Keyboard Identification Name highlighted piano keys and identify the intervals between them. Notation Identify written symbols, from noteheads and clefs to ornaments and playing techniques.

title: Home
text: Key Features Spaced repetition. ASRS and ARTS use your accuracy and response time to choose the next exercise question. SM-2 and FSRS schedule a due date for each review. Compare the four algorithms . MIDI keyboard input. On Linux, play answers on a USB MIDI keyboard or use the Virtual MIDI Piano Keyboard (VMPK) to practice notes, intervals, and scales. MIDI setup . Anki-compatible decks. Add music theory to your usual Anki reviews by exporting just the exercises you want, such as interval identification in bass clef. Anki export guide . Statistics and a database browser. Charts of accuracy, speed and volume, plus a calendar heatmap of a year of practice, filterable by exercise and timeframe, plus a table view of everything stored. Statistics . Notation and keyboards your way. Eleven notation styles, including Finale Maestro, Leland, Bravura and two handwritten jazz styles, and eleven keyboard looks from a modern piano to a French harpsichord. Settings . Plugins for more instruments. An instrument pack adds artwork, recordings, exercises, lessons and glossary entries in one ZIP: name the notes on a viola fingerboard, find the interval between two highlighted harpsichord keys, or label an instrument’s parts. Install one with a registration code or from a file under Tools → Plugins, and uninstall it without losing your practice history. Plugins . Local and private. Your history is one file on your computer. Your data . Free and open source under the MIT License. Statistics for a demo profile: how often you are right, how fast, and how much you practice. The review heatmap: every day you practiced, at a glance.

title: Home
text: Development Status Alto is in alpha. You can work through the lessons and practice with the exercises now, but their content and layout may change between releases. For the latest features and fixes, see the changelog . The roadmap lists current features and planned exercises. Download Alto Version 0.0.2  Alpha Free for Desktop Linux alto-0.0.2-linux-x86_64.tar.gz Unpack it, then run sh install.sh install . Download Windows alto-0.0.2-windows-x64-setup.exe Download macOS There is no installer yet. You can run Alto from its source code . Run from source Release notes · Older releases · Getting started

title: Lessons
text: Lessons Lessons are step-by-step walks through a topic for someone meeting it for the first time. Nothing about them is scored or recorded. Start with Pitches and Notes to connect a sound to a piano key and a written note. Its last step opens Keyboard Note Identification , Note Identification , Note Construction , or Notation Identification . Each exercise’s book button opens hints for that exercise and a link back to the lesson. Clef Basics then explains how to read different clefs. Intervals builds on staff reading to name the distance between two pitches. Scale Identification uses that notation to explore patterns of notes. Key Signatures teaches how to read and write their sharps and flats. The Circle of Fifths shows how keys and their signatures relate. When you open an exercise from a lesson, Back to lesson at the upper left of the exercise returns you to the step you left.

title: Lessons
text: Finding them The home page has a switch at the top, Exercises and Lessons . Choose Lessons to see a tile for each lesson, with the icon of the exercise that practices the same topic: the Circle of Fifths lesson has the circle of fifths icon. Alto remembers which side you were on. The cards change with the transition chosen under Settings… › Appearance › Transitions . Use Tiles to open the catalog for the selected section. During an exercise or lesson, the two icons switch the navigation list. Your current activity stays open until you choose another one. Once you have begun a lesson, a bar along the bottom of its tile shows how far through you are and the corner says Step N/M . Click it to open the lesson, and Leave lesson (or Esc ) to return to where you were. Start over goes back to the first step. The Circle of Fifths exercise also has a way in: open its reference pane with the book button, and press New to this? Take the full lesson at the top. The Clef Basics exercise has the same, with a table of the clefs under the button.

title: Lessons
text: The lesson list Inside a lesson, the list on the left shows the lessons, as the exercise list does in an exercise. The lesson that is open is in bold, with its steps listed under it and the one you are on highlighted. Click a step to go to it, or another lesson to open that. The button at the top left of the lesson hides and shows the list, and Alto remembers your choice.

title: Lessons
text: Inside a lesson A lesson is a series of steps. The title and progress are at the top and Back and Next are at the bottom. Back on the first step, and Finish on the last, leave the lesson. A step has some reading, and may have: A sound to hear. A button plays the notes being described, in the instrument chosen in the settings. A keyboard. Pitches and Notes starts with a bracket over two black keys and a C on the white key just to their left. The labels stay in place while the first two notes play and when you identify C’s neighbor. When you play a keyboard example, follow the keys as each note sounds. Chord tones light together. The original highlights return when playback stops. Staves. The clef lesson shows staves beside the reading, each with a clef, sometimes a note, and a line under it. In a small exercise the staff changes with the question. The circle of fifths. Click a key, or use the arrow keys, to see its key signature and its chords. Some steps have Down a fifth and Up a fifth buttons that walk around the circle for you. A small exercise. It cannot be failed. A wrong answer gets a hint, a second wrong answer shows the answer with its explanation, and a right answer is explained. Try again repeats a single question. In checks with multiple questions, Try another draws a question for the next attempt.

title: Lessons
text: Duration Open Lessons → Rhythm → Duration for a five-step introduction to counting sounds and silences. Read each rhythm on one line of noteheads, with a time signature at the left and a bar line at the end of each measure. Choose Show counts to see where each symbol falls. Each click marks the start of a written note. Keep tapping through a half note, a whole note, or a silent quarter rest and try a four-beat rhythm on your own. The final step opens Rythmic Equations to practice matching durations.

title: Lessons
text: Intervals Allow about 12–15 minutes for a first pass. Count letter names to find an interval’s number, then count half steps to determine its quality. The staff and keyboard illustrations use the pitches played by the listening buttons. The lesson compares C–E with C–E♭, introduces perfect intervals, and shows why C–F♯ and C–G♭ use the same two piano keys. A final check asks you to name an unfamiliar pair. The last step links to Interval Identification for reading two written notes, Keyboard Interval Identification for naming the interval between two piano keys, and Interval Construction for placing the second note on the staff. Each exercise has a book button with hints and a link to the lesson.

title: Lessons
text: Key Signatures Allow about 10–15 minutes. Start with two ways to write the same F♯. Listen to what happens when a natural cancels the signature, then read sharp and flat signatures to find major keys and their relative minors. Choose the staff you would write for A♭ major and try a fresh signature in treble or bass clef. The closing step links to Key Signature Identification , Key Signature Construction , and Order of Keys . Choose Order of Keys to place the individual sharps or flats in order. The book button in each exercise opens hints and a link back to the lesson.

title: Lessons
text: The Circle of Fifths lesson Eight steps for a beginner: A map of major keys. What a key is, and what a key signature is. A fifth. Counting five letter names, and hearing the interval. A small exercise: name the letter a fifth above. Fifths clockwise from C. Each step clockwise adds a sharp. Sharp keys on the circle. Find the key with a given number of sharps. Flat keys on the circle. Counterclockwise adds flats; where the two meet. Find the key with a given number of flats. Relative minors on the inner ring. Find the relative minor of a key. A key and its neighbors. The IV and V of a key. Find the key a fifth above or below another. Circle of fifths practice. A summary, and a button to practice in the Circle of Fifths exercise.

title: Lessons
text: The Clef Basics lesson Ten steps for a beginner: Pitch and the clef. The same place on the staff is a different note in the treble and bass clefs. The three clef symbols. Every clef is the G clef, the C clef or the F clef, put on a line. The G clef. The treble clef, and the French violin clef on the bottom line. The F clef. The bass clef on the fourth line, the subbass clef on the top line, and the baritone clef. The C clef and middle C. Soprano, mezzo-soprano, alto and tenor are the C clef on four lines, and each centers on middle C. The rarer clefs. French violin, subbass and the two ways to write the baritone clef. The clef symbol. A clef is drawn: is it the G, C or F clef? The clef’s line. A named clef: which line of a blank staff is it written on? The clef’s name. The two halves together, as in Clef Identification. Clef reading and placement. A summary, and a button to practice in the Clef Basics exercise.

title: Plugin API
text: Plugin API Alto’s plugin API is the contract between an instrument pack and the app. The author describes the instrument, its media, and its exercises in a UTF-8 JSON file named pack.json . Alto reads that file to draw the instrument, generate questions, check answers, and play feedback. You can build a pack with a text editor and your media files.

title: Plugin API
text: Minimum working pack Start with a folder containing pack.json and a picture named instrument.png . The example below assumes the picture shows a keyboard with a key at pixel [100, 80] . Choose a point on a key in your own picture, measured from its top-left corner. { "format" : 2 , "id" : "keyboard-parts" , "name" : "Keyboard Parts" , "instruments" : [ { "id" : "keyboard" , "name" : "Keyboard" , "image" : "instrument.png" } ], "exercises" : [ { "id" : "name-the-part" , "title" : "Parts of a Keyboard" , "type" : "image-choice" , "instrument" : "keyboard" , "questions" : [ { "prompt" : "Which part is marked?" , "point" : [ 100 , 80 ], "choices" : [ "Key" , "Case" ], "answer" : "Key" } ] } ] }

title: Plugin API
text: What Alto checks Manifest. Use the integer 2 for format , a nonblank pack name , and a pack id unique among installed packs. Include at least one instrument and one exercise. A pack ID such as keyboard-parts uses lowercase letters and digits, with single hyphens between words. Instruments and media. Each instrument needs its own ID, a name, and a readable PNG, WebP, or JPEG. Write paths relative to pack.json and include every file you reference. Recordings are optional. When you supply them, map each pitch to a mono 16-bit PCM WAV file. Exercises. Give each exercise a unique ID, a plain-text title, and the ID of an instrument in the same pack. For image-choice , each question needs a prompt, a point inside the picture, at least two distinct choices, and an answer that matches one choice exactly. For fingerboard-notes , calibrate at least two strings on the instrument and list the pitches to practice on each selected string. For keyboard-intervals , declare at least one keyboard on the instrument. Optional content. Alto also validates any lessons, glossary entries, and links you include. Use IDs from the same pack when linking these activities. An invalid entry prevents the whole pack from loading. To try the example, zip pack.json and instrument.png together so both appear at the root of the ZIP. Install it through Menu → Tools → Plugins… → Install plugin from file… and restart Alto. Open Instruments → Parts of a Keyboard and choose Key . Loading a pack locally requires no listing in the registered plugins table.

title: Plugin API
text: Plugin registration To request a listing in the registered plugins table , open an issue in Alto’s GitHub repository. In the issue, describe what your plugin does and include a link to its repository. Open a registration issue . Choose a plugin name and a Pack ID that are available in Alto’s registry. Names are compared without regard to capitalization or extra spaces, so “Viola Studio” and “viola studio” clash. Use the exact top-level id from pack.json as the Pack ID. It can contain lowercase letters and digits, with single hyphens between words. If either field belongs to another plugin, choose a different value before registration. If you change the Pack ID, update the manifest in your release ZIP as well.

title: Plugin API
text: Registry updates between releases Submit the registration form and check the Rights and licenses statement. The issue number is the proposed install code. For example, issue #1001 corresponds to code 1001 . A maintainer reviews the submission and applies the plugin-approved label. The Register plugin workflow checks the approved form and verifies the name, Pack ID, and code against current and historical registrations. It prepares a branch with the entry for docs/site-root/plugins.json . In Actions → Register plugin , open the run for the issue. Select Open registration pull request in the run summary, review the change, and select Create pull request . If the author corrects the form, remove and reapply the label after reviewing the edits. The workflow refreshes the same branch and any open pull request. A maintainer merges the reviewed change. After the docs deployment, the code appears in the registry and works in Alto. The same code and Pack ID carry forward across plugin releases. For repository setup, create the plugin-approved label. The workflow uses Contents: write to publish its registration branch. A maintainer opens the pull request with their own GitHub account. Earlier names and Pack IDs stay reserved to their original registration after a rename or removal. To check a proposed registry change locally, run python3 scripts/check_plugin_registry.py --base main from the repository root. A registry entry for issue #1001 could look like this. { "id" : "example-strings" , "code" : "1001" , "name" : "Example Strings" , "description" : "Practice naming notes on open strings." , "repository" : "https://github.com/example/strings" , "metadata" : "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/example/strings/main/alto-plugin.json" } The docs workflow publishes the registry at /alto/plugins.json . Each version of the Plugins page that supports the registry reads it when opened. After deployment, refresh the page to see a new registration. Each name opens a details page inside Alto’s docs.

title: Plugin API
section: Release ZIPs for installation and updates
text: Release ZIPs for installation and updates Attach the installable pack ZIP to the repository’s latest published GitHub release. Put pack.json at the root of the ZIP and set its id to the registered pack ID. If the release has several ZIP assets, name the pack asset <pack-id>.zip so Alto can select it. GitHub releases . In Menu → Tools → Plugins… , enter the code under Install plugin by code… . To update, select the installed ZIP and choose Update selected plugin . Alto looks up the registration, checks the latest release, and validates the new pack before replacing the installed ZIP. Existing ZIP installs with the registered pack ID can update the same way. Editable folders stay under the author’s control. A successful install or update offers a restart.

title: Plugin API
text: Plugin details and releases Alto’s plugin details page displays the README from the default branch of your registered GitHub repository. It also shows your registration code and a link to the repository. Update the README in your repository to revise what readers see in Alto’s docs. To keep the details page current, publish a JSON file in your plugin repository and include its raw HTTPS URL in your registration issue. Use a URL that follows your release branch so the same address serves each update. The file must be publicly readable by a browser on the Alto docs site. A raw GitHub file URL works for a public repository. If you host the file yourself, allow cross-origin reads from the docs site. { "about" : "Identify the four open strings by ear, then practice finding them on the fingerboard." , "version" : "1.2.0" , "compatible_alto" : "0.4.x" , "documentation" : "https://example.org/strings/guide/" , "download" : "https://example.org/strings/releases/1.2.0/strings.zip" } All five fields are optional. Use plain text for the description and versions, and absolute HTTPS URLs for the links. When you release a new plugin version, update this file along with the ZIP. Alto’s details page requests the file each time a reader opens it, so your release information can change between Alto releases. The registered description and repository link remain available if the file is missing or temporarily unavailable.

title: Plugin API
text: Manifest reference Field Meaning format The integer 2 selects this version of the pack API. Pack name Required. Enter a nonblank text string at the top level, such as "name": "Viola Instrument Pack" . Alto shows it during installation and removal. Pack id Unique among installed packs. Use lowercase letters, digits, and single hyphens between words. The same spelling rules apply to instrument and exercise IDs. instruments A nonempty list. Each instrument requires id , name , and image . Instrument IDs are unique within the pack. strings Required for fingerboard-notes . Two or more distinct open pitches in ascending order. Each entry requires open , nut , and bridge . Coordinates must lie inside the source image. Pitch spelling Uppercase A through G, optional # or b , then an octave from 0 through 8. Examples include C4 (middle C), F#4 , and Bb3 . correct_answer_animation Optional per instrument. Set file to a pack-relative animated GIF and anchor to image or string . A string anchor requires calibrated strings. views Optional per instrument. An object from a view name to a pack-relative picture, such as {"back": "images/viola-back.webp"} , for up to four extra pictures of the instrument. Each is a PNG, WebP, or JPEG of at most 16 megapixels, and it can have its own size. A picture question or lesson picture names one with view , and its point and focus are then in that picture’s pixels. Strings, the ruler, and the correct-answer animation always use the main image . positions Optional per instrument with strings. A list of up to 12 objects, each with a plain-text name of at most 12 characters and a whole number of half_steps above the open string, from 1 to 36, in ascending order. Alto labels the ruler above the neck with them. The ruler always shows a tick for each half step up to the octave. Without positions it shows only those ticks. The viola example lists 1st at 2, 2nd at 3, 3rd at 5, 4th at 7, 5th at 8, 6th at 10, and 7th at 12. Choose positions that match your instrument. keyboards Optional per instrument. A list of up to four keyboards that Alto draws itself, for exercises that highlight keys. Each needs a plain-text name (at most 40 characters, unique on the instrument) and lowest and highest , the natural keys at either end, such as E1 and F6 . Alto stacks the keyboards in the order you list them, top to bottom, so list an upper manual before a lower one. keyboard_style Optional per instrument with keyboards. How the drawn keys look. Any of white and black , each a list of two #rrggbb colors for the top and the bottom of a natural or a sharp key; white_edge , black_edge , case and cap (the cap over each sharp key), each one #rrggbb color; and the numbers narrow (how wide sharp keys are compared with a piano’s, 0.5 to 1.5), gap (pixels between natural keys, 0 to 4), round (how much the keys’ lower corners are rounded, 0 to 10) and length (how long a natural key is, in key widths, 2 to 6.5). Fields you leave out use Alto’s classic keyboard. Without keyboard_style , the keys are drawn in the learner’s own keyboard style. The harpsichord example draws ebony naturals and bone-capped sharps. lessons Optional list of up to six lessons for Alto’s Lessons page. See Lessons for the fields. Each lesson’s exercise must be an id in this pack’s exercises . kind Optional per instrument. Plain text of at most 30 characters that says what sort of instrument it is, such as harpsichord or viola . Alto uses it to group sounds of the same kind when a learner chooses the sound for an exercise. Without it, the instrument is grouped with no others. sustained Optional per instrument, true or false (default false ). Set it to true for bowed or blown sounds, so each note ends as the next begins. Leave it off for struck or plucked sounds, which ring on. samples and gain Optional per instrument. Exact recorded pitches play directly. Other notes use the nearest recording. Omitting samples uses the learner’s selected Alto sound. Gain sets the instrument’s playback level, greater than 0 and at most 1 (default 1). sound_info Optional per instrument, for the summary under Menu → Settings → Sound → Instruments . Use plain text, at most 800 characters each, in any of summary , source , source_url (an https link), performer , recorded , includes , terms , and note . Say “not stated” when you do not know the performer. Alto adds the pack name, the note range, and the size itself. The viola example credits TinySOL, its recording location and years, its CC BY 4.0 terms, and how the takes were prepared. Exercise description and prompt Optional. description is one to a few sentences of plain text, at most 400 characters, shown with the exercise. prompt is the question on each card of a fingerboard-notes exercise, at most 120 characters. Without them Alto uses short neutral wording that names the strings. Image-choice questions always carry their own prompt . Picture question view , marker_size , and focus Optional on each image-choice question. view names one of the instrument’s views ; leave it out for the main picture. marker_size is the dot’s diameter in picture pixels, from 6 to 200; leave it out for a large part. focus is [left, top, width, height] in picture pixels, at least 40 wide and tall and inside the picture, and it must contain the marked point . Alto shows only that region, so a small part such as a nut or a string is easy to see. Without focus the whole picture is shown. exercises A nonempty list. Each exercise requires a unique id , a plain-text title , a type , and an instrument ID from the same pack. Use notes for fingerboard-notes , questions for image-choice , and the fields described under Keyboard intervals for keyboard-intervals . Exercise icon and lessons Optional. icon is an SVG file for the exercise’s tile. lessons lists up to five lesson id s that teach it. See Linking lessons and exercises . glossary Optional list of up to 40 glossary entries. See Glossary entries . Exercise settings Optional on fingerboard-notes . An object with any of sound (a label of at most 30 characters), range (one clef name), accidentals and octave (each true ). See Settings for a note exercise . notes Each key is an open pitch from the selected instrument. Its list contains the notes to practice on that string, from open through one octave above it. The same pitch on two strings makes two distinct cards. questions One or more questions. Each has a plain-text prompt , a point in original image pixels from the top left, at least two distinct plain-text choices , and an answer exactly matching a choice. Optional note sets the pitch for correct-answer playback. Asset paths Relative to pack.json , using forward slashes. Keep all files inside the pack. Each referenced file can be up to 64 MiB, with 256 MiB total. Images can be up to 16 megapixels. You can change the pack’s display name. Keep the pack, instrument, and exercise IDs when updating existing content. Alto uses them to resolve assets and associate practice history with the same exercise. A new title or file location can use the same IDs.

title: Plugin API
text: Settings for a note exercise A fingerboard-notes exercise can offer its learners settings. Alto draws them in the same pane as its own exercises’ settings, remembers each learner’s choices, and applies them to the questions. You choose which of four controls appear by listing them under settings in the exercise: "settings" : { "sound" : "Viola sound" , "range" : "alto" , "accidentals" : true , "octave" : true } sound adds a row with the label you give (at most 30 characters) that opens a list of instruments. The exercise plays your instrument’s recordings until the learner picks another. The list shows the instruments that came with your plugin first, then other installed instruments of the same kind (other harpsichords for a harpsichord), then every other installed instrument, each group under its own heading. range adds a Range row for one clef, such as "alto" , where the learner moves the lowest and highest note asked. The selector never goes beyond the notes you list under notes , and Reset restores all of them. accidentals adds an Accidentals switch. On, Alto also asks each note between the ones you list on a string, written as a sharp and accepted as its flat, and offers sharps and flats as answers. octave adds an Octave switch. On, the answer includes the written octave, as in D4 , and Alto asks for the octave after the note name. List only the controls your exercise needs. Without settings , an exercise has none, and a picture exercise cannot have any. Alto keeps the learner’s practice history for the defaults: switches that start off, your own sound, and every listed note.

title: Plugin API
text: Lessons A pack can add lessons to Alto’s Lessons page. A plugin lesson works like Alto’s own: a short list of steps, each with a heading, a few paragraphs, and optionally a picture of your instrument, notes to hear, and a Knowledge check . Your lessons are listed after Alto’s, under the category you name, and the last step offers practice in one of your exercises. The viola example adds Parts of the Viola and Finding Notes on the Viola . "lessons" : [ { "id" : "finding-notes" , "title" : "Finding Notes on the Viola" , "about" : "Learn where the notes fall on each string." , "summary" : "Name the note at any spot on the strings." , "category" : "Viola" , "exercise" : "first-position" , "steps" : [ { "title" : "The open strings" , "picture" : { "instrument" : "bowed-viola" , "string" : "D4" , "note" : "D4" }, "hear" : [[ "C3" ], [ "G3" ], [ "D4" ], [ "A4" ]], "hear_label" : "Hear the four open strings" , "hear_instrument" : "bowed-viola" , "text" : [ "A string played without pressing it down is an **open string**." ], "task" : { "prompt" : "Which open string sounds the highest?" , "choices" : [ "C string" , "G string" , "D string" , "A string" ], "answer" : "A string" , "hint" : "Listen again." , "explanation" : "The A string is the highest." } } ] } ] Field Meaning Lesson id , title , about , summary , category Required except category . The title is at most 80 characters, about at most 300, summary at most 120, and category at most 40. A lesson with no category is listed under the pack’s name. A pack can have up to six lessons. Lesson exercise and related_exercises exercise is the id of one of this pack’s exercises, which the last step offers for practice. related_exercises optionally lists up to five other exercises from the pack. Lesson steps From 1 to 14 steps. Alto adds the practice buttons to the last one. Step title and text The heading, and 1 to 8 paragraphs of plain text of at most 700 characters. Wrap a term you are defining in double asterisks, such as **nut** , to show it in bold. Markup is not allowed. Step picture Optional. Give instrument , string , and note to show a note on a string, with Alto’s ruler and dot. Or give instrument and point , with the optional view , marker_size , focus , and marker , to mark a place on the picture as an exercise question does. Set marker to false to show the picture with no dot. Step hear , hear_label , hear_instrument Optional. hear is up to 12 chords, each a list of one to four note names, played by the Hear button. hear_instrument is the id of one of this pack’s instruments that has samples. Without it, Alto plays the learner’s own choice of sound. Step task Optional knowledge check, with a prompt , a hint for a wrong answer, an explanation , and either two to six choices with the answer that matches one exactly, or targets to click on the step’s picture (see below). A wrong answer gets the hint, a second wrong answer gets the answer, and nothing is scored. Lesson icon Optional. An SVG file for the lesson’s tile (see Icons ). Without it, the tile uses its primary exercise’s icon. Write lessons by the same rules as Alto’s own: teach one musical idea, aim for twenty minutes or less, define each new term in plain language where it first appears, and order your lessons from beginner to advanced. See Designing lessons and exercises .

title: Plugin API
text: Click the picture A knowledge check can ask the learner to click a place on the step’s picture instead of choosing a button. Give the task targets in place of choices and answer : "task" : { "prompt" : "Click one of the pegs." , "targets" : [ { "point" : [ 192 , 282 ], "radius" : 45 }, { "point" : [ 287 , 274 ], "radius" : 45 } ], "hint" : "The pegs are the dark knobs on either side of the pegbox." , "explanation" : "That is a peg." } Each target is a circle: its point and its radius are in the picture’s own pixels, in the view the step shows. A click inside any target is right. List up to four. The step’s picture must set marker to false , so the dot does not give the answer away. After a right answer, or the second wrong one, Alto marks the target.

title: Plugin API
text: Linking lessons and exercises A lesson names its exercises with exercise and related_exercises . An exercise can name its lessons from the other end with lessons , a list of up to five lesson id s: { "id" : "first-position" , "type" : "fingerboard-notes" , "lessons" : [ "finding-notes" , "parts-of-the-viola" ]} Alto shows both: the lesson’s last step offers each linked exercise as practice, and the exercise gets a Reference pane (the book button beside Help) with a button for each linked lesson, as Alto’s own exercises do. An exercise with no linked lesson has no Reference pane.

title: Plugin API
text: Icons for tiles Set an exercise or lesson’s icon to the path of an SVG file in the pack. Alto uses the same SVG for its tile and navigation row. Draw it as a single shape so it stays legible at the smaller navigation size. Alto renders it in the current theme’s text color. The root must be <svg viewBox="0 0 24 24"> , and the file at most 100 KB. Use only g , path , circle , ellipse , rect , line , polyline , and polygon , with geometry and paint attributes. Scripts, styles, images, links, and entity declarations are refused. Every color is replaced by the theme’s ink. Use fill="none" for a part that is not filled. A lesson with no icon uses its primary exercise’s. The viola’s icon is the outline of its own photograph, with its f-holes, fingerboard, and tailpiece cut out.

title: Plugin API
text: Glossary entries A pack can add terms to Alto’s Glossary . Entries are listed alphabetically with Alto’s own, and each links to the lessons and exercises that go with it, shown as tiles under the entry. List them under glossary : "glossary" : [ { "term" : "scroll" , "definition" : "The **scroll** is the curled, carved end of the viola." , "guide" : "Look at the far left of the picture." , "picture" : { "instrument" : "bowed-viola" , "point" : [ 100 , 385 ], "marker_size" : 80 , "focus" : [ 0 , 220 , 480 , 330 ]}, "caption" : "The scroll" , "exercises" : [ "viola-parts" ], "lessons" : [ "parts-of-the-viola" ] } ] Field Meaning term and definition Required. The term is at most 40 characters, listed as you write it. The definition is at most 500 characters of plain text, with **bold** for the term itself. guide Optional, at most 500 characters: how to recognize or use the term. picture and caption Optional. picture takes the same fields as a lesson picture, except a note on a string: instrument , point , view , marker_size , focus , and marker . caption is at most 120 characters and goes under it. An entry without a picture shows text alone. exercises and lessons Optional. Up to five id s each from this pack. The exercise tiles and the lesson tiles open that activity directly. A pack can have up to 40 entries. If two plugins supply the same term, Alto skips the second pack at startup and reports the conflict. A term that Alto already has is listed twice, the plugin’s with the plugin’s name after it.

title: Plugin API
text: Keyboard intervals A keyboard-intervals exercise highlights two keys on the instrument’s drawn keyboards and asks for the interval between them. The instrument must declare keyboards , and it can give them a keyboard_style . Alto draws the keyboards instead of the instrument’s picture, so no photograph or measurement is needed. It plays the lower and the higher note together, as a chord, on the plugin’s sound when the answer is right. { "id" : "intervals-on-two-manuals" , "title" : "Harpsichord Interval Identification" , "type" : "keyboard-intervals" , "instrument" : "flemish-harpsichord" , "keyboards" : [ "Lower manual" , "Upper manual" ], "lowest" : "E1" , "highest" : "F6" , "default_range" : [ "C3" , "C5" ], "intervals" : [ "m2" , "M2" , "m3" , "M3" , "P4" , "A4 / d5" , "P5" , "m6" , "M6" , "m7" , "M7" , "P8" ], "placements" : [ "same" , "across" ], "settings" : { "sound" : "Harpsichord sound" , "range" : true , "intervals" : true , "manuals" : true } } Field Meaning keyboards The names of the instrument’s keyboards to use. Without it, every keyboard is used. lowest and highest The widest range of keys the exercise has questions for, such as E1 and F6 . Both must be keys on the keyboards in use. Alto draws each keyboard over the range being asked, so a shorter range gives larger keys. default_range Optional. The lowest and highest key asked until the learner chooses another range, such as ["C3", "C5"] . It must lie within lowest and highest . Without it, the whole range is asked. settings Optional. What the learner can change: sound (the label of a row that opens the list of instruments to sound, as for other exercises), range ( true adds a Range page with a draggable keyboard and a lowest and highest key) intervals ( true adds a page of checkboxes for the intervals) and manuals ( true adds a page of checkboxes for the keyboards, so a learner can have both highlighted keys on the upper manual, on the lower manual, or on either). Intervals too wide for the chosen range cannot be checked, and the answer buttons follow the checked intervals. intervals The answers to offer, from m2 , M2 , m3 , M3 , P4 , A4 / d5 , P5 , m6 , M6 , m7 , M7 and P8 . Without it, all twelve are asked. Every listed interval is also an answer button. placements "same" puts both keys on one keyboard, and "across" puts one key on each of two keyboards. Without it, both are used. "across" needs two or more keyboards. Alto treats all the keyboards as playing the same pitches. prompt Optional. A plain-text question of at most 120 characters that replaces the default. Alto asks every combination of interval, lowest key, and placement once. A pack with two keyboards and a five-octave range therefore has thousands of cards, though Alto asks only those inside the chosen range and intervals, and remembers each card separately. Narrow lowest , highest , intervals , or placements for a smaller exercise. A lesson step or a glossary entry can highlight keys too. Give its picture the instrument , keys , and an optional span . keys is a list of one to four [keyboard name, pitch] pairs, such as [["Lower manual", "C4"], ["Upper manual", "A4"]] , and span is the lowest and highest key to draw, such as ["C3", "C5"] . Without span , each keyboard is drawn over its whole range. Write a sharp key with a sharp, as in C#4 .

title: Plugin API
text: Correct-answer animations An instrument can supply a transparent animated GIF. Draw the moving shape on a transparent background, export at least two frames, and include the GIF in the pack. Alto reads the frame timing from the GIF and draws the visible pixels in the correct-answer color. Export a looping GIF for motion that continues throughout a sustained note. The viola example uses "correct_answer_animation": {"file": "animations/string.gif", "anchor": "string"} . Its GIF shows a horizontal string with both ends fixed at the middle of the left and right edges. Alto rotates and scales it from the learner’s finger position to the bridge on the marked string. On an open string, the vibration starts at the nut. The same GIF works at every position and in the magnified view. Preview a correct E4 answer · Download the viola’s animation . For an overlay aligned to the entire picture, use "correct_answer_animation": {"file": "animations/keys.gif", "anchor": "image"} . Give the GIF the same proportions as the instrument picture and draw the moving parts in their corresponding positions. The image anchor is the default. A string-anchored effect applies only to fingerboard questions. Wait plays the animation and leaves the answered question on screen. After Animation advances after feedback. Immediately plays the answer audio and skips the overlay. Muting keeps the same timing. On a picture question without a note, an image overlay plays for the usual 600 ms of visual feedback.

title: Plugin API
text: Distribution and troubleshooting Select pack.json and its sibling asset folders and compress them into a ZIP. Opening the ZIP should show pack.json immediately. Include credits and permissions for the files you distribute. Test the resulting ZIP by moving your working folder outside the plugins folder, installing the ZIP, and restarting. A recipient needs only that ZIP and a build of Alto with instrument pack support. Symptom What to check Missing exercise tile Install the ZIP with Tools → Plugins… → Install plugin from file… and restart Alto. For an editable pack, check that its folder contains pack.json and restart after edits. Missing picture or recording Match the relative path, extension, and capitalization to the actual file inside the ZIP. Verify the file opens and that recordings are mono 16-bit PCM. Unknown instrument The exercise’s instrument must exactly match an id in this pack’s instruments list. Missing pack name Add a top-level name next to the pack id in pack.json . Existing format 2 packs also need this field. Duplicate ID Move the previous ZIP or extracted copy out of the plugins folder before installing an update. Give an independent pack a new pack ID. Dot on the wrong string Pair each string’s own nut and bridge points. Recalibrate after cropping, rotating, or resizing the source picture. Older JSON-only example Start with the example ZIP from the latest release of the viola plugin tutorial and copy your exercise titles and note lists into it. Add an instrument reference to every exercise.

title: Plugin API
text: Plugin removal Choose Menu → Tools → Plugins… , select the installed ZIP or pack folder in the list, and press Uninstall plugin . Confirm the question, and Alto moves the selected item to the system trash and restarts. Selecting an editable pack folder moves the entire folder, including your edits. After Alto restarts, the pack’s exercises disappear from the exercise list. Alto keeps each profile’s practice history. To reinstall a downloaded ZIP, press Install plugin from file… in the Plugins dialog again. To recover an editable folder, restore it from the system trash and restart Alto.

title: Plugin details
text: Plugin details All registered plugins Loading plugin details…

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: Harpsichord plugin tutorial Build a plugin for a keyboard instrument. You’ll draw a double harpsichord from a list of keyboards, ask learners to name the interval between two highlighted keys, let them choose their own range, intervals and manuals, and then add a question about the instrument’s parts, a lesson and a glossary entry. You’ll reuse the photographs and recordings from the example pack and write your own manifest. This tutorial builds on the viola plugin tutorial . A keyboard needs no calibration, because Alto draws the keys itself, so you’ll spend your time on the keyboards and the settings instead.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: Working folder Download the example harpsichord pack . Find the directory that contains Alto’s database, alto.db , and create a plugins folder there if needed. See database locations . Inside plugins , create a folder named my-keys and extract the ZIP directly into it. Keep CREDITS.txt with the media. Then delete everything you won’t use yet, so the folder looks like this: my-keys/ pack.json images/harpsichord-overview.webp sounds/C4.wav sounds/D4.wav sounds/E4.wav CREDITS.txt

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: An interval exercise Open pack.json in a plain-text editor and replace its contents with this manifest. { "format" : 2 , "id" : "my-keys" , "name" : "My Keys" , "instruments" : [ { "id" : "studio-harpsichord" , "name" : "Studio harpsichord" , "image" : "images/harpsichord-overview.webp" , "keyboards" : [ { "name" : "Upper manual" , "lowest" : "E1" , "highest" : "F6" }, { "name" : "Lower manual" , "lowest" : "E1" , "highest" : "F6" } ], "samples" : { "C4" : "sounds/C4.wav" , "D4" : "sounds/D4.wav" , "E4" : "sounds/E4.wav" }, "gain" : 0.9 , "kind" : "harpsichord" } ], "exercises" : [ { "id" : "intervals" , "title" : "Intervals on My Harpsichord" , "type" : "keyboard-intervals" , "instrument" : "studio-harpsichord" , "lowest" : "E1" , "highest" : "F6" , "default_range" : [ "C3" , "C5" ], "intervals" : [ "M2" , "M3" , "P5" ] } ] } Save and restart Alto. Open Intervals on My Harpsichord under Instruments . Alto draws both manuals, highlights two keys, and offers the three intervals as answer buttons. With the speaker on, a correct answer plays the two notes together, as a chord, on your recordings. In Instruments → Harpsichord Interval Identification, the complete pack uses two manuals to ask the learner to identify an interval. What each part does: keyboards lists the manuals, up to four. Each has a name, a lowest key and a highest key. Alto draws them stacked with the first one listed at the top, so list the upper manual first. The ends must be natural notes, because a keyboard can’t begin or end on a black key. Keys with the same letter and octave are the same pitch on every manual. lowest and highest on the exercise are the widest range the exercise has cards for. default_range is the range learners start with. It must fit inside the first pair. intervals chooses the answers from m2 , M2 , m3 , M3 , P4 , A4 / d5 , P5 , m6 , M6 , m7 , M7 and P8 . Leave it out to ask all twelve. samples pairs each recording with the pitch that was actually recorded. One recording is enough to start. Alto shifts it to reach the neighboring notes, so more recordings across the range keep the shift small. kind says what sort of instrument this is. You’ll use it later, when learners choose which instrument sounds. Alto asks every combination of interval, lowest key and placement once. A two-manual instrument with a five-octave range has thousands of cards, which is fine, because Alto only asks the cards inside the learner’s range.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: Choose where the keys sit An exercise can ask both keys on the same manual, one on each, or both. Add placements to the exercise to choose. The default is ["same", "across"] . "placements" : [ "same" ] With ["same"] , both highlighted keys are always on one manual. With ["across"] , one is on each. To restrict which manuals the exercise uses, add "keyboards": ["Lower manual"] to the exercise. Each name must match a keyboard on the instrument.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: Choose how the keyboards look Without keyboard_style , Alto draws the keys in the learner’s own keyboard style. The keyboard_style field on the instrument changes the look to match your instrument. Add it after keyboards . "keyboard_style" : { "white" : [ "#4a3b30" , "#241a14" ], "black" : [ "#4b3b30" , "#2a2019" ], "white_edge" : "#000000" , "black_edge" : "#000000" , "case" : "#120d09" , "cap" : "#eee3c8" , "narrow" : 0.95 , "gap" : 1.5 , "round" : 2 , "length" : 4.5 } Colors are #rrggbb . white and black are each a pair of colors, for the top and the bottom of a natural or a sharp key, such as ["#4a3b30", "#241a14"] . The numbers adjust the shape: Field Effect narrow How wide the sharp keys are compared with a piano’s, from 0.5 to 1.5. gap The pixels between natural keys, from 0 to 4. round How much the keys’ lower corners are rounded, from 0 to 10. length How long a natural key is, in key widths, from 2 to 6.5. white_edge , black_edge , case , cap The outline of each kind of key, the wood around the keys, and the cap over each sharp key. The harpsichord example uses dark natural keys with light sharps, which is how the Ruckers instrument it pictures was built. The long, narrow keys come from a length of 4.5. Change the numbers, save, restart and compare. Every field is optional, and you can leave out any you don’t want to change.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: Let learners choose Add a settings entry to the exercise to give learners controls. Each setting you list shows up in the exercise’s Settings panel. "settings" : { "sound" : "Harpsichord sound" , "range" : true , "intervals" : true , "manuals" : true } range adds a Range page with a small draggable keyboard, and a lowest and highest key. The big keyboards redraw while it’s dragged, and a new question comes when the learner pauses. intervals adds a page of checkboxes. An interval too wide for the chosen range can’t be checked, and the answer buttons follow the checked intervals. manuals adds a page with a checkbox for each manual. If only Upper manual is checked, both highlighted keys are always on the upper manual. If only the lower is checked, both are on the lower.
