If both are checked, the keys can also be one on each. sound adds a row, labeled with the text you give it, that opens a list of instruments to sound. The plugin’s own instruments are first, then other instruments of the same kind , then everything else that’s installed. That is why you set kind earlier. A learner with several harpsichord plugins sees the others in the middle group. The plugin’s own sound is used until the learner picks another. Each setting is saved for the exercise. The learner’s starting settings keep their practice history, and a changed range, interval choice or manual choice is tracked as its own set of cards.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
section: A picture question about the parts
text: A picture question about the parts A keyboard exercise draws its own keys, so it doesn’t need the photograph. You can still use the photograph in a second exercise. Add a comma after the first object in exercises and add this one. It marks a point on the original image and asks what part is there. { "id" : "parts" , "title" : "Parts of My Harpsichord" , "description" : "Name the parts of the harpsichord." , "type" : "image-choice" , "instrument" : "studio-harpsichord" , "questions" : [ { "prompt" : "Which part of the harpsichord is marked?" , "point" : [ 733 , 600 ], "choices" : [ "Lid" , "Nameboard" , "Apron" , "Cheek" ], "answer" : "Lid" , "marker_size" : 100 , "focus" : [ 250 , 60 , 1000 , 1000 ] } ] } point is measured in pixels from the top-left corner of the original image, which is 1500 × 2250 here. marker_size is the diameter of the ring. focus is a rectangle [x, y, width, height] that Alto zooms to, so small parts aren’t lost in a large picture. To ask about another picture of the instrument, add it under views on the instrument, for example "views": {"strings": "images/harpsichord-strings.webp"} , and add "view": "strings" to the question. In Instruments → Parts of the Harpsichord, choose the name of the part marked in blue.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: A lesson about intervals A lesson walks a learner through steps, each with a picture, some text, and an optional question. A step can highlight keys on the keyboards instead of a point on a photograph. Add lessons after exercises . "lessons" : [ { "id" : "half-and-whole" , "title" : "Half Steps and Whole Steps" , "about" : "Count the half steps between two keys on a double harpsichord." , "summary" : "Count the steps between two keys." , "category" : "Harpsichord" , "exercise" : "intervals" , "steps" : [ { "title" : "The half step" , "picture" : { "instrument" : "studio-harpsichord" , "keys" : [[ "Lower manual" , "C4" ], [ "Lower manual" , "C#4" ]], "span" : [ "C3" , "C5" ] }, "text" : [ "The distance from one key to the very next key, whatever its color, is a **half step**. C4 and the sharp key just above it, C#4, are a half step apart." ], "hear" : [[ "C4" ], [ "C#4" ]], "hear_label" : "Hear a half step" , "hear_instrument" : "studio-harpsichord" , "task" : { "prompt" : "How many half steps separate C4 and D4?" , "choices" : [ "1" , "2" , "3" ], "answer" : "2" , "hint" : "There is one key between them." , "explanation" : "C4 to C#4 is one half step, and C#4 to D4 is another." } } ] } ] keys lists up to four [keyboard, pitch] pairs to highlight. span is the range of keys to draw, so the lesson shows a few octaves instead of all five. hear lists the notes the button plays, one after another. hear_instrument chooses the instrument. Each recorded pitch plays its own recording, and others are shifted from the nearest one. exercise is the exercise the last step offers for practice. An exercise can also name its lessons with "lessons": ["half-and-whole"] . The example pack has two lessons: one about the parts of the instrument, and one that teaches the half step, whole step and each interval on the keys. In Lessons → Intervals on a Double Harpsichord, the half-step example places the highlighted keys next to each other on the lower manual.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: A glossary entry Glossary entries explain terms in the Glossary and link them to your exercises and lessons. Add glossary after lessons . "glossary" : [ { "term" : "double harpsichord" , "definition" : "A **double harpsichord** has two keyboards, one above the other. Each keyboard can play its own set of strings, so a player can change tone color by moving from one to the other." , "guide" : "Look at the front of the instrument. Two rows of keys mean it is a double." , "picture" : { "instrument" : "studio-harpsichord" , "marker" : false }, "caption" : "The two manuals of a double harpsichord" , "exercises" : [ "intervals" ], "lessons" : [ "half-and-whole" ] } ] Use lowercase for the term unless it is a proper noun. Keep the definition to one concise paragraph, and use guide for what to look or listen for.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: Pack installation To test the plugin you built, compress the contents of my-keys into my-keys.zip . Open the ZIP and check that pack.json is at its root. Move the editable folder outside Alto’s plugins folder so only one copy loads. Install the ZIP through Menu → Tools → Plugins… → Install plugin from file… and restart. Open both exercises under Instruments , open the lesson from Lessons , and look up your term in the Glossary. If the plugin doesn’t load, Tools → Plugins… lists the problem. Alto names the field that’s wrong, such as a keyboard that doesn’t exist on the instrument or a range outside the keys.

title: Harpsichord plugin tutorial
text: The complete harpsichord example The original download shows the same pieces working together. Install the original harpsichord.zip through the Plugins dialog and restart Alto. Open Instruments → Harpsichord Interval Identification , open Settings , and try Range , Intervals and Manuals . Choose Harpsichord sound to pick another instrument. The pack adds Parts of the Harpsichord , where learners name 16 marked parts across five photographs: the whole instrument, the keyboards, the strings and jacks, the bentside, and the spine. It also adds two lessons and 14 glossary entries. The manifest fields used here are described in the plugin API reference , including its Keyboard intervals section. The recordings are from the Versilian Community Sample Library’s Flemish harpsichord, the 8′ register, with one take for every whole tone from F♯1 to C6. They are released under CC0, so no credit is required, though the pack gives it. For Alto, each take was trimmed to the pluck, cut to 1.6 seconds, level-matched, faded out and converted to 32 kHz mono 16-bit WAV. The recordings are of a different instrument than the pictured one. VCSL on GitHub The photographs are of a double harpsichord built by Andreas Ruckers in Antwerp in 1636 and rebuilt in Paris by Pascal Taskin in 1787, from the Museum für Kunst und Gewerbe Hamburg. They were published under CC0 by Rainer Halama for Wiki Loves Music. The keyboards in the interval exercise are drawn by Alto, so they need no photograph. CREDITS.txt lists each file.

title: Plugins
text: Plugins An Alto plugin adds an instrument and practice material to the app. Each plugin is an instrument pack that pairs artwork with exercises. It can also include recordings, lessons, and glossary entries. For example, a learner can identify a note marked on a fingerboard, hear its pitch, or open a lesson about that instrument. Find the registration code in the table below. In Alto, choose Menu → Tools → Plugins… → Install plugin by code… and enter the code. Alto downloads the latest release from the registered repository. Restart Alto to use the plugin. To get a newer release later, select the installed plugin and choose Update selected plugin . You can also install a downloaded ZIP with Install plugin from file… . Installed exercises appear under Instruments . To build a plugin, start with the Plugin API to see what Alto requires. Then follow the viola plugin tutorial to build and test a playable exercise on a string instrument, or the harpsichord plugin tutorial to build one for a keyboard. Each tutorial lives in its own repository, viola-plugin-tutorial and harpsichord-plugin-tutorial , with the finished plugin as an editable folder and as a ZIP on its Releases page.

title: Plugins
text: Registered plugins To register your plugin, open an issue on Alto’s GitHub repository . In the issue, include your plugin’s name, its Pack ID from pack.json , a description, and a repository link. Confirm that you have the rights to distribute the plugin and its contents. Once the registration is approved and published, the issue number is your install code. Select a plugin’s name to see its details in Alto’s docs. Third-party plugins Third-party developers create and maintain the plugins listed below. You install, update, and use them at your own risk. Alto accepts no responsibility for their content, how they work, or any loss or damage they cause. Plugin Code Description Loading registered plugins…

title: Viola plugin tutorial
text: Viola plugin tutorial Build a viola plugin that asks the learner to name a note on the D string. You’ll reuse the artwork and recordings from the example pack, write your own manifest, and add a second exercise that asks learners to identify the bridge.

title: Viola plugin tutorial
text: Working folder Download the example viola pack . Find the directory that contains Alto’s database, alto.db , and create a plugins folder there if needed. See database locations . Inside plugins , create a folder named my-strings and extract the ZIP directly into it. Keep CREDITS.txt with the media. These are the files you’ll use for the first exercise. my-strings/ pack.json images/viola-front.webp animations/string.gif sounds/D4.wav sounds/E4.wav CREDITS.txt

title: Viola plugin tutorial
text: D-string exercise Open the extracted pack.json in a plain-text editor. Replace its contents with this working example. It uses the picture and the D4 and E4 recordings you just extracted. { "format" : 2 , "id" : "my-strings" , "name" : "My Strings" , "instruments" : [ { "id" : "studio-viola" , "name" : "Studio viola" , "image" : "images/viola-front.webp" , "sustained" : true , "strings" : [ { "open" : "C3" , "nut" : [ 399 , 414 ], "bridge" : [ 1517 , 446 ]}, { "open" : "G3" , "nut" : [ 399 , 391 ], "bridge" : [ 1517 , 412 ]}, { "open" : "D4" , "nut" : [ 399 , 371 ], "bridge" : [ 1517 , 373 ]}, { "open" : "A4" , "nut" : [ 399 , 353 ], "bridge" : [ 1517 , 337 ]} ], "correct_answer_animation" : { "file" : "animations/string.gif" , "anchor" : "string" }, "samples" : { "D4" : "sounds/D4.wav" , "E4" : "sounds/E4.wav" }, "gain" : 0.85 } ], "exercises" : [ { "id" : "d-string" , "title" : "First Finger on the Viola D String" , "type" : "fingerboard-notes" , "instrument" : "studio-viola" , "notes" : { "D4" : [ "E4" ]} } ] } Save and restart Alto. Open First Finger on the Viola D String . This one-note check always shows E4 at the second guide on the D string. With sound enabled, a correct answer plays sounds/E4.wav . Change ["E4"] to ["D4", "E4"] , save, and restart to practice both open D and E with their own recordings.

title: Viola plugin tutorial
text: Fingerboard calibration Picture. Put a straight-on photograph or drawing of your instrument in images/ . Show the whole playable length from nut to bridge. Set image to that file’s path. PNG, WebP, and JPEG are supported. Strings. Open the final image in an editor that displays the pointer’s pixel coordinates. On each string, record the point where it leaves the nut and the point where it meets the bridge. Enter each as [x, y] , measured from the top-left corner of the original image . List the strings from lowest open pitch to highest. Each string has its own two points, so a tapered neck or a diagonally framed picture works. Recordings. Put isolated, pitched recordings in sounds/ . Export each as mono, 16-bit PCM WAV . Identify the actual recorded pitch in samples . For instance, "G3": "sounds/plucked-g.wav" pairs that recording with G3. One recording is enough to start. Additional recordings across the range reduce how far Alto shifts a neighboring sample. Say where the recordings came from in sound_info , and keep their license and credits in the pack. Exercise. Give your instrument its own id . In an exercise, set instrument to that ID and choose the playable pitches under notes . For a pack with two instruments, add a second entry to instruments , with its own ID, picture, endpoints, and recordings. Each exercise selects one instrument. Several exercises can select the same one. Calibration check. Temporarily ask only for an open string and the note one octave above it, such as "G3": ["G3", "G4"] . The open-string marker should sit on the nut and the octave marker halfway to the bridge on that same string. If both are displaced, recheck the image’s original dimensions and your coordinates.

title: Viola plugin tutorial
section: A picture question about the bridge
text: A picture question about the bridge For a keyboard, wind instrument, or percussion instrument, supply an image and mark the location for each question directly. An instrument used only for picture questions can omit strings . A question about a part can be silent. To play a pitch when the learner answers correctly, add a note such as "C4" and include a recording under the instrument’s samples . To try this with the starter folder above, add a comma after the first object in exercises and add this second object. Save, restart, and open Parts of My Viola . The point marks the bridge on the original 2040 × 768 image. For your own instrument, use its ID, pick a point on your picture, and write the choices the learner should see. { "id" : "parts" , "title" : "Parts of My Viola" , "instrument" : "studio-viola" , "type" : "image-choice" , "questions" : [ { "prompt" : "Which part of the viola is marked?" , "point" : [ 1500 , 400 ], "choices" : [ "Scroll" , "Bridge" , "Tailpiece" ], "answer" : "Bridge" } ] } In Instruments → Parts of My Viola, the blue marker sits on the bridge where it supports the strings. Choose Bridge.

title: Viola plugin tutorial
text: Pack installation To test the plugin you built, compress the contents of my-strings into my-strings.zip . Open the ZIP and check that pack.json is at its root. Move the editable folder outside Alto’s plugins folder so only one copy of the pack will load. Install the ZIP through Menu → Tools → Plugins… → Install plugin from file… and restart. Open both of your exercises under Instruments and check the D-string playback and bridge marker.

title: Viola plugin tutorial
text: The complete viola example The original download shows how the same two exercise types work with four strings, two photographs, and a full set of samples. Install the original viola.zip through the Plugins dialog and restart Alto. Open Instruments → Viola Note Identification and turn on the exercise speaker. To listen to the installed recordings, open Menu → Settings → Sound , select Bowed viola , and press Hear it . Its source is Viola Instrument Pack , with 49 notes from C3 to C7. Choose Use this instrument to play these recordings in other exercises that use your selected sound. Settings → Sound lists Bowed viola alongside the built-in instruments. Select it to preview the recordings with Hear it. On a correct fingerboard answer, the marked string vibrates from the dot to the bridge while the note plays. The pack also adds Parts of the Viola , where learners name 30 marked parts: the scroll, pegbox, pegs, nut, fingerboard, each string, bridge, f-holes, tailpiece, fine tuner, bouts, corner, purfling, and top plate on the front, and the neck, button, back plate, and ribs on a second photograph of the back. Small parts are shown close up. The four open strings in the picture are C, G, D, and A from bottom to top. The nut is the ridge where the strings enter the black fingerboard. A dot there means to play the open string. A ruler above the neck shows where to look: each small tick raises the pitch by one half step, and each labeled tick marks a position that the pack names. The viola example names 1st to 7th position, where the first finger lands. A faint line leads from the dot to its tick. Here the dot is under the 1st position tick on the D string, two half steps above open D. Choose E . View the full-size viola artwork without the exercise markings , or the view of its back . The pack includes 49 bowed viola recordings from IRCAM’s TinySOL collection. Each semitone from C3 through C7 has its own one-second sample. The fingerboard exercise uses the recording for the marked pitch, including when that pitch appears on more than one string. TinySOL’s CC BY 4.0 license allows you to adapt and redistribute the audio with attribution. Keep CREDITS.txt with the recordings and describe any further edits. TinySOL recordings · CC BY 4.0 terms The artwork is a photograph of an 1893 viola by August Martin Gemünder, from the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Open Access collection (public domain). Both its front and its back were cut out from their studio backdrops and turned on their sides. The museum lists a 36.9 cm vibrating string length and a 67 cm overall length, and the picture matches its bout measurements. Museum record

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Spaced Repetition Choose a scheduling algorithm for your profile under Settings → Practice → Question scheduling . ASRS and ARTS let you practice for as long as you like. SM-2 and FSRS give each card a review date. With either of those, the exercise pauses when you are caught up. Another review can come due later the same day. Consider a single Note Identification question, F♯ in treble clef. A scheduler can choose whether to show F♯ on the next turn , or it can set a due date for its next review. Even schedulers that make the same kind of decision use different evidence. Scheduler What changes after an answer? How does F♯ return? ASRS Each attempt changes its strain. A weighted draw on each turn. Its weight recovers as seconds pass. ARTS The first answer sets how fast its priority grows. It returns when its priority ranks highest. Each intervening question raises that priority. SM-2 The first answer updates its run of successes and ease factor. Its review interval follows a sequence of day counts, with a short retry after a miss. FSRS The first answer updates its estimated memory stability and difficulty. After the learning steps, it gets a review date near the model’s 90% recall point.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Response-time grading In automatic SM-2 and FSRS practice, Alto compares a correct first answer with your previous answers to the same exercise. The fastest 15% earn Easy , the slowest 15% earn Hard , and the middle earns Good . A miss always earns Again . Each exercise has its own distribution, so time spent placing notes on a staff has no effect on the cutoff for identifying a keyboard note. Open Settings → Practice → Response-time grading… to see the distribution for an exercise and its cutoffs in seconds. Change the Easy and Hard percentages there. Good gets the remaining share. The percentages apply to this profile across exercises and both calendar schedulers. A zero disables that tail. Answers exactly at a cutoff earn Good. Alto starts with Good until there are 40 eligible answers. It recalculates the cutoffs from the most recent 100 timed, correct first answers before grading each new response. Previous practice in any mode counts. Retries and interrupted timings are excluded. A correct interrupted answer earns Good. After calibration, the intervals appear to the right of the music, with Easy at the top, Good in the middle, and Hard at the bottom. Keyboard exercises show Hard, Good, and Easy from left to right beneath the keys. After a correct answer, Alto shows the assigned grade and interval. Keyboard Note Identification and Keyboard Interval Identification each need 40 timed, correct first answers of their own. If you see three intervals under one keyboard and a single interval under the other, the second exercise is still collecting timings. The scheduler uses the same intervals as the corresponding grade buttons.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Self-grading a new card In Settings → Practice , select Grade correct answers with Hard, Good, or Easy . After a correct answer, Hard and Good keep a new card in its short learning steps. Easy skips those steps. SM-2 starts its first Easy review at 4 days. With Alto’s default FSRS settings, the starting estimate is about 8.3 days. Choose a grade to schedule the card at the interval above that button. First correct answer SM-2 FSRS Hard 5 min 30 s 5 min 30 s Good 10 min 10 min Easy 3–5 days 6–10 days Alto spreads reviews across nearby days so that cards learned together can come due on different days. This adjustment is called fuzzing . For example, two new FSRS cards can show 7 days and 9 days for Easy even though both start with the same estimate. If you reopen the same card before grading it, its preview stays the same.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: ASRS The Alto Spaced Repetition System (ASRS) is the default scheduler. For each turn, it generates a few questions and adds some you have answered before under the same exercise settings. It draws from that pool at random, giving more weight to questions you find difficult. A question you just answered gets less weight for a while. The better you know it, the longer that effect lasts.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Strain Each question has a score called strain , which says how much practice it needs. It starts at 1.5, stays between 0 and 6, and changes with each answer. Answer Change in strain Wrong Add 1.5 for each miss. Right on the first try Subtract 0.5, then adjust for speed. Right after a miss Subtract 0.2.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Response time For a correct first answer, ASRS compares the time you took with the exercise’s par time . At par there is no speed adjustment. At half the par time or faster, ASRS subtracts another 0.6. At four times par or slower, it adds 1.0. The adjustment changes gradually in between. A slow but correct answer can therefore make the question more likely to return. Par times by exercise Exercise Par time Note Identification, Keyboard Note Identification 3 s Key Signature Identification, Clef Basics, Notation Identification 5 s Interval Identification, Keyboard Interval Identification, Chord Quality, Note Construction, Key Signature Construction 6 s Circle of Fifths 7 s Scale Identification, Interval Construction 8 s Arpeggio Identification 9 s Order of Keys 12 s Scale Construction 25 s

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Probability of the next draw For a question with strain \(s\), ASRS sets a recovery time \(c\) in seconds. If \(t\) seconds have passed since the last answer, its weight \(w\) recovers according to \[c = 120 \cdot 2^{3-s}\] \[w = e^{0.6s}\max\left(0.02,\,1-e^{-t/c}\right).\] Higher strain gives a question both a higher eventual weight and a shorter recovery time. A fresh question gets a weight of \(e^{0.6\cdot 1.5}\approx 2.46\). To get the probability of drawing a question, divide its weight by the sum of all eligible weights. Suppose you miss F♯ once, moving its strain from 1.5 to 3, and leave it there. Later, the only two eligible candidates for a draw are F♯ and an unseen B. At strain 3 the recovery time is 120 seconds. After two minutes, F♯ has weight \(e^{1.8}(1-e^{-1})\approx 3.82\). Its chance of coming up next is \[\frac{3.82}{3.82+2.46}\approx 61\%.\] B can still win that draw. With the same two candidates, elapsed time alone changes the odds.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: ARTS Adaptive Response-Time-based Sequencing (ARTS) measures the gap between questions in turns. Its clock advances each time you give a first answer in this exercise. Retries during the same showing and time away from practice leave the clock where it was.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Priority per turn Let \(h\) be the number of intervening first answers since you last answered F♯, and \(T\) the time in milliseconds you took on that first attempt. Alto uses a 100 ms reference time. The natural logarithm, \(\ln\), makes a slower correct answer count more, with a diminishing increase for each extra millisecond. Mettler, Massey, and Kellman, equation 1 Last first answer Priority now Unseen \(1\) Incorrect \(2h\) Correct \(0.11h\ln\!\left(\frac{\max(T,101)}{100}\right)\) Alto compares eligible questions under the current exercise settings and selects the highest priority. It breaks ties at random.

title: Spaced Repetition
section: A fast and a slow identification
text: A fast and a slow identification Suppose F♯ and an unseen B are eligible. If you last identified F♯ in one second , after three other questions its score is \(0.11\cdot 3\ln(10)\approx 0.76\). B wins with 1. Had you taken four seconds , the same three questions would give F♯ a score of \(0.11\cdot 3\ln(40)\approx 1.22\), and F♯ would win. If you missed F♯, just one intervening answer would give it a score of 2. After a correct answer, response time sets the increase in priority per turn.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: SM-2 Alto’s SM-2 scheduler is based on Piotr Woźniak’s algorithm. Algorithm SM-2, © SuperMemo World, 1991. SuperMemo SuperMemo 2 (SM-2) keeps a count of successive successful reviews, the last interval in days, and an ease factor \(E\) for each card. A new card starts with \(E=2.5\). During calibration, Alto grades a correct first answer Good and a miss Again. Under Settings → Practice , select Grade correct answers with Hard, Good, or Easy to choose the grade yourself. Each button shows its interval above it. A wrong answer records Again and advances automatically. The exercise’s Next Question preference is disabled while self-grading is on. Original SM-2 specification

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Review intervals and ease First submission during calibration Change to the card Next review Good (grade 4) Add one success. Keep the current ease. 1 day for the first success and 6 days for the second. After that, \(I_{n}=\lceil I_{n-1}E\rceil\), the previous interval times the ease, rounded up to a whole day. Again (grade 2) Reset the success count and interval to zero. Set the ease to \(\max(1.3,E-0.32)\). 1 minute. The next showing starts a new review.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Self-graded SM-2 The buttons use Anki’s default learning steps. A new card shows 5 min 30 s for Hard and 10 min for Good. Easy skips both steps and schedules a review around 4 days later. At the second step, Hard repeats the ten-minute step and Good graduates the card with a one-day interval. Once a card graduates, Hard starts at 1.2 times the previous interval. Good multiplies the previous interval by the card’s ease, and Easy applies a further 1.3 multiplier. Good credits half the days overdue and Easy credits all of them. Hard lowers ease by 0.15, Easy raises it by 0.15, and Good preserves it. A miss lowers ease by 0.20 and starts a ten-minute relearning step. At that step Hard waits 15 minutes, Good schedules one day, and Easy schedules two days. Anki deck options

title: Spaced Repetition
section: Three reviews of F♯ during calibration
text: Three reviews of F♯ during calibration Identify a new F♯ correctly on day 0 and it is due on day 1. Get it right on day 1 and it is due on day 7. A third success on day 7 gives an interval of \(6\cdot 2.5=15\) days, so the next due date is day 22 . Each bar starts at a successful review and measures the gap to the next due date. Suppose instead that you miss F♯ on day 7. Its ease falls to 2.18 and Alto schedules a retry one minute later. Three successive correct reviews from there give gaps of 1, 6, and 14 days . The shorter third gap comes from the ceiling calculation \(\lceil 6\cdot 2.18\rceil=\lceil 13.08\rceil=14\).

title: Spaced Repetition
text: FSRS The Free Spaced Repetition Scheduler (FSRS) models the chance you can recall a card as time passes. Alto uses FSRS-6 with its default parameters. A correct first submission earns Good during calibration. With self-grading on, you can choose Hard , Good , or Easy after a correct answer. A miss always earns Again . For a new card, Good puts its next learning step ten minutes away and Again puts it one minute away. A miss on a card already in review starts a ten-minute relearning step. Python FSRS scheduler With self-grading, a new FSRS card starts with the same Hard and Good learning steps as SM-2. Easy graduates it directly using FSRS-6’s estimate of memory stability at 90% desired retention. On review cards, the three intervals use the same random adjustment and are ordered Hard, Good, Easy up to the maximum of 36,500 days. The interval printed above a button is the one Alto schedules. Anki review scheduling

title: Spaced Repetition
section: Estimated recall and the review date
text: Estimated recall and the review date FSRS tracks difficulty (\(D\), from 1 to 10) and stability (\(S\), measured in days). A stability of 8 days means the model expects a 90% chance of recall eight days after a review. Retrievability (\(R\)) is the predicted chance of recall after \(t\) whole days. With Alto’s default parameters the curve is approximately \[R(t)=\left(1+0.98035\,\frac{t}{S}\right)^{-0.1542}.\] The factor 0.98035 is chosen so that \(R(S)=0.90\). At the 90% target the base review interval therefore equals the updated stability in days. FSRS rounds it to whole days and may vary the scheduled day slightly to spread reviews out. Both cards start at 100% estimated recall. The more stable card takes longer to reach the review target.

title: Spaced Repetition
section: A successful review on day eight
text: A successful review on day eight Suppose your F♯ card has \(D=5\) and \(S=8\) days. On day eight its predicted recall is 0.90. You identify F♯ correctly. For a Good review at least a day after the previous one, the stability update has two parts. The factor \(k\) depends on the card’s current difficulty and stability. \[k = e^{1.8722}(11-D)S^{-0.1666}.\] \[S_{\mathrm{new}}=S\left[1+k\left(e^{0.796(1-R)}-1\right)\right].\] The quantity in square brackets is about 3.29 , giving a new stability of 26.29 days and a base interval of 26 days . The term involving \(R\) explains why timing matters. If you recall the same card earlier, \(R\) is higher and the gain in stability is smaller. A miss uses a separate stability update before relearning.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Review intervals for F♯ Suppose you see a new F♯ card five times in Note Identification. Each row shows your answer and the gap until the next showing . For ASRS and ARTS, assume you answer one other question every 10 seconds. After each of those answers, F♯ competes with one unseen card. For SM-2 and FSRS, assume you review F♯ whenever it is due and the exercise is still collecting its first 40 timed answers. Showing and answer ASRS (median gap) ARTS SM-2 FSRS (base interval) 1. Correct in 4 s 9 questions (90 s) 3 questions (30 s) 1 day 10 min 2. Correct in 1 s 19 questions (190 s) 4 questions (40 s) 6 days 2 days 3. Correct in 1 s 19 questions (190 s) 4 questions (40 s) 15 days 11 days 4. Miss (corrected on the same showing in ASRS and ARTS) 8 questions (80 s) 1 question (10 s) 1 min 10 min 5. Correct in 4 s 11 questions (110 s) 3 questions (30 s) 1 day 2 days After the first answer, ASRS draws F♯ again within nine intervening questions about half the time. ARTS picks it as soon as it outranks the unseen card, after three questions. On the fourth showing, ASRS counts both the miss and the correction. ARTS uses the first answer. In SM-2 and FSRS, the miss ends the showing. The fifth row is the scheduled retry. FSRS uses base intervals here. In practice, its small random adjustment to longer intervals can also change the dates of later reviews.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Daily limits For SM-2 and FSRS, exercise tiles show new cards in blue , missed cards awaiting a correct answer in red , and due reviews in green . Below the search bar, New , Learn , and Due show the totals for checked exercise tiles that match the search text. A missed card stays in the red count while it waits and when it becomes due. Another miss on that card still counts as one. Due reviews come first. The default allowance for each exercise is 10 new cards and 200 reviews per local day . Change those numbers in Settings → Practice , or open an exercise’s Daily Limits submenu and clear Use global to override either number for that exercise. Check Unlimited to remove the daily cap on new cards, reviews, or both. A limit of zero pauses that kind of practice. On the exercise screen, the counts appear at the top, immediately to the left of the score and streak, in blue / red / green order: new cards, outstanding incorrect cards, and due reviews. The underlined number identifies the current card’s queue. A retry that is due appears in both the red and green counts, with red underlined while you answer it. After calibration, the keyboard shows the next interval for each passing grade. After a miss, Alto sets the card aside and offers other eligible questions. If the missed card is the only review left within your daily limit, the exercise shows its return time and resumes automatically when it is due. You can leave the exercise open. Practice resumes when the missed card is due. The two algorithms share the day’s allowances and keep separate review dates. Opening a new card uses one introduction slot. If you leave before answering, you can return to that card without using another slot. The allowances reset at local midnight, and overdue reviews remain due. You can see the next review date for a specific card in the database browser .

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Switching schedulers When a card first moves between SM-2 and FSRS, it keeps its due date, full review interval, and learning or relearning step. A card on a 180-day interval with 20 days left will still be due in 20 days. After that first transfer, each scheduler resumes its own saved schedule for the card. For mature cards, FSRS estimates stability and difficulty from the SM-2 interval and ease, assuming 90% historical recall. In the other direction, SM-2 uses the full FSRS interval and starts ease at 2.5. FSRS conversion from SM-2 ARTS and ASRS record your answers in your practice history. Calendar due dates, new cards, missed cards awaiting review, and daily allowances are independent of that practice.

title: Spaced Repetition
text: Your profile Alto tracks individual questions, such as identifying F♯4 in treble clef in D major. Changing the order of the answer buttons still counts as practice on the same question. Every submission is saved under your profile. A question that takes three tries leaves three entries, each with your answer, whether it was correct, and how long it took. Switching algorithms keeps that history. You can switch profiles in the menu (☰) and see your accuracy and response times in Statistics .

title: Release notes
text: Release notes All notable changes to Alto, newest first. The format follows Keep a Changelog , and Alto uses semantic versioning . Each release’s downloads are on its GitHub release.

title: Release notes
text: Unreleased Changes that are in the development docs and not in a release yet.

title: Release notes
text: Added A new Duration lesson under Rhythm introduces quarter, half, and whole notes and quarter rests with counted listening examples. Rhythm examples in lessons and the glossary show a time signature, upward stems, bar lines, and optional counts on staffless notation paper. Rythmic Equations lets you choose both the arithmetic signs and the number of operators (zero to three) independently on each side of the equals sign. Its Answer Type checkboxes let you practice missing symbols, missing numbers, or both. Turn on Parentheses to practice grouped calculations. Settings → Sound now has separate Instruments and Metronome pages. Hear four beats of High pip, Low pip, or Pencil click and watch a smooth spectrum curve rise and fall with each click. The Duration lesson and rhythm glossary examples use the selected click for note onsets and meter accents, with silence for rests. The tie example pairs the metronome with a sustained instrument note. Third-party instrument packs can supply artwork, recordings, correct-answer animations, and exercises in one ZIP. Tools → Plugins lists the installed plugins and installs one from a downloaded ZIP or uninstalls it while keeping practice history. Packs can also add their own lessons, extra views of an instrument such as its back, settings for a note exercise (a sound override, a range, accidentals, and the octave), tile icons, glossary entries, links between exercises and lessons, and knowledge checks answered by clicking the picture. The viola plugin tutorial includes a downloadable example with fingerboard and instrument anatomy exercises and two lessons. Instruments can also declare keyboards, which Alto draws in a look the plugin chooses, and a keyboard interval exercise highlights two keys on them, with a range selector, a choice of intervals, and a choice of manuals. A plugin exercise’s sound setting opens a list of instruments to sound instead of switching the plugin’s sound on or off. It lists the plugin’s own instruments first, then other instruments of the same kind, then the rest. The harpsichord example pack, with a Flemish harpsichord sound, shows a double harpsichord, asks the interval between two highlighted keys, names its parts, and adds two lessons and glossary entries. Alto can zoom. Ctrl + + , Ctrl + - and Ctrl with the mouse wheel make the text, controls, notation, keyboard and icons larger or smaller together, from 50% to 300%, and Ctrl + 0 goes back to 100%. The zoom is remembered. The glossary explains intervals: interval, harmonic interval, melodic interval, unison, simple intervals, compound intervals, perfect, major and minor. A harmonic interval’s example stacks its two notes and plays them together. Interval Identification has an Inversions switch for naming the inversion of a written interval. After a right answer, the staff shows and plays the inversion. Interval Identification has a Consonance switch for telling whether an interval is consonant or dissonant. Perfect unisons, fourths, fifths and octaves, and major and minor thirds and sixths, count as consonant, as do their compound forms. With Inversions on too, it asks about the inversion. Lesson keyboards highlight each note as it sounds and show chord tones together during playback. The Pitches and Notes lesson labels C and brackets its neighboring pair of black keys before asking learners to name the next white key.

title: Release notes
text: Changed The Windows installer now uses the Microsoft Visual C++ Runtime installed on Windows. If Windows lacks it or has an older version, the installer downloads Microsoft’s installer for it from Microsoft, checks Microsoft’s signature, and runs it; Windows asks for administrator permission and Microsoft’s window asks to accept Microsoft’s license. This happens once, also when Alto updates itself. Alto now needs Windows 10 or later. On Windows, the installer asks once to accept the terms for the Microsoft code in Alto’s program files, also when Alto updates itself: an update that has not been accepted yet asks before it changes anything, and canceling keeps the version already installed. The release builds have added checks that strengthen license compliance, and the downloads include the license notices of the third-party components they contain, in the licenses folder. Alto no longer depends on NumPy, which makes the installed program about 35–40 MB smaller on Linux and Windows. Sound previews are mixed as quickly as before, and the staff’s click map is built about four times faster. Notes made by pitch shifting or synthesis are now kept and reused instead of being made again each time they play, and the current instrument’s missing notes are made while Alto is idle after it opens, so even their first play is quick. Previews of plugin instruments are kept too, until the plugin’s recordings change.

title: Release notes
text: Fixed Keyboard Note Identification now saves its own Note names choice. Switching to Caret in Note Identification leaves the keyboard exercise’s answers unchanged. The Exercises and Lessons toolbar buttons now open their respective catalogs when the glossary is open. Single-question lesson knowledge checks say Try again after a wrong answer. Checks with multiple questions keep Try another . Lesson tiles, search, navigation, menus, and exercise controls now update their icons and colors when the desktop switches between light and dark mode while Alto is set to System. Light mode uses a gray window with white tiles and a pale gray search bar, including when following a light desktop.

title: Release notes
text: 0.0.2 Released 2026-11-19. GitHub release

title: Release notes
text: Added Profiles can use ASRS, ARTS, SM-2, or FSRS. With SM-2 and FSRS, set daily limits, see new, learning, and due counts, and optionally grade correct answers Hard, Good, or Easy. Switching between the two carries over the card schedule. Filter the exercise grid by category or turn on Shuffle to move between the selected exercises after an answer. The database browser shows when a question is due. Statistics can group question counts by hour, day, week, or month. The glossary covers enharmonic pitches, transposition, the circle of fifths, minor scales, and relative and parallel keys. The Next Question setting lets each exercise advance immediately, advance after playback and animation, or wait for Next . Help → About shows Alto’s version and alpha status. Help → Report an issue opens the GitHub issue tracker. Alto checks for new releases daily and offers upgrades from the main grid. Learners can update, defer the reminder for 24 hours, or skip a release. Automatic checks can be turned off in Settings → Updates. Interval Construction asks learners to place a second note above or below a given note on the staff. Automatic SM-2 and FSRS grades use each learner’s recent response times for the exercise. After calibration, each card shows the Hard, Good, and Easy review intervals before the learner answers. Practice settings include adjustable percentiles and a chart of the times used. The Anki Exporter in the Tools menu saves selected exercises as decks in one Anki package. You can preview cards, filter each deck, and include review schedules from an SM-2 or FSRS profile. Order of Keys asks learners to write a named key signature one sharp or flat at a time on a blank staff. Learners can choose clefs, scales, key signatures, and how many accidentals are already written. Every exercise with answer choices now offers Limited and All button layouts. Each exercise remembers its own selection. Interval Identification has per-clef pitch ranges, staff keys, display choices, an interval checklist, a Quality menu for practicing the interval number, quality, or both, and Limited or All answer buttons. A Key Signatures lesson teaches how to read and write major and minor key signatures and links to the key signature exercises. An Intervals lesson uses staff and keyboard examples to teach interval numbers and qualities, with links to staff and keyboard identification and staff construction. Answer cards opened from Database or Statistics show graphs of response time and cumulative first-try accuracy for the question. Double-clicking a row in Questions that need practice opens the saved question and its answer. A beginner lesson on pitches and notes links to three note exercises, with reference hints and a return path to the lesson. Notation Identification lets learners name a highlighted marking or find a named component on the staff. Hovering previews a component before answering, and learners can choose which notation terms to practice. Eight public-domain piano excerpts from Schubert and Schumann put 34 of those terms in musical context. Keyboard Interval Identification with configurable keyboard and interval ranges, compound intervals, and Limited, All, or Compact answer buttons. Compact answers use a quality letter and an interval number. A searchable glossary in the top toolbar, with notation examples, playback, and related exercise and lesson tiles. An interactive Scale Identification reference and lesson, with scale comparisons and note highlighting. An optional octave answer in Note Identification, saved window geometry, and Restore defaults in Settings. Scale degrees as a note-name group for Note Identification, Keyboard Note Identification and Note Construction, with caret notation (1̂–7̂), function names (Tonic, Supertonic, and so on), altered degrees and explicit major-key context. Note-name previews have visible text labels.

title: Release notes
text: Changed Alto upgrades the practice database the first time you open this version. Before upgrading, close Alto and copy alto.db to a backup folder to keep a copy of your previous history. Push buttons have a rounded hairline border, a tinted hover state, and a keyboard focus ring. In dark mode, exercise tile outlines are near black and other standard button outlines are graphite gray. Lesson questions and their feedback appear together in a “Knowledge check” callout. Lesson samples and instrument previews play at the same volume as the corresponding exercise notes. Playable staff examples in lessons, the glossary, and saved answer cards highlight each note or chord as it sounds. Lesson staves keep clefs, signatures, and notes together as the pane widens. Longer examples wrap with their clef and signature. The documentation homepage groups practice into six topic cards that switch between light- and dark-theme screenshots. Keyboard exercise icons use seven realistically proportioned white keys; the interval icon adds a span bracket. Exercise button-group labels appear above their buttons, and theme rebuilds preserve the exercise settings page. Code, documentation, and interface text use American English; saved color-scheme settings remain compatible. Appearance settings use a hierarchical sidebar and grouped overview. Data pages share the toolbar Back button, and active toolbar icons use the theme accent color. Scale Identification replaces Scale Spelling, keeping its icon. Identify an ascending scale on a staff, with selectable clefs, scale types, and independent staff and scale key signatures. Navigation is grouped on the left of the top bar, with Statistics and Browse database on the right. Exercises / Lessons changes the sidebar without leaving the active activity. Separate pane and grid buttons toggle the list or return to tiles while retaining the question, answer selection and lesson step. Search filters tiles and lists, and a back button resumes the active exercise or lesson. Before starting an activity, the workspace prompts you to select one.

title: Release notes
text: Fixed The documentation homepage shows dark app screenshots in dark mode, and its Keyboard Identification icon matches the other blue topic icons. Scale Identification plays with even rhythm on the first correct answer, highlights each note as it sounds, and waits for the scale to finish before advancing. Switching themes in Settings is faster, and Settings opens more quickly.

title: Release notes
text: 0.0.1 Released 2026-11-15. GitHub release

title: Release notes
text: Added A new exercise, Clef Basics: a blank staff and the name of a clef. Choose the G, C or F clef symbol with three buttons, the mouse wheel or a right click, and put it where it makes that clef: the C clef on the second line is the mezzo-soprano clef. It can be tried on lines, spaces and three ledger lines each way. Its settings are Question Type, Clef Construction or Clef Identification (a clef is drawn on a staff and you press the button with its name), and Clefs, which chooses which clefs are asked for, including the French violin and subbass clefs. The baritone clef is accepted as the F clef on the middle line or the C clef on the top line. A Clef Basics lesson, in ten short steps with small exercises: what a clef does, the G, C and F clef, the line each puts its symbol on, and how to tell them apart. The Clef Basics exercise has a reference pane, opened with the book button, with a table of the clefs and a button that opens the lesson. The documentation has a version for each release and one for the development version, with a dropdown in the top bar to switch between them. A page of an older release says so and links to the latest. The documentation home page has a Download Alto button under the first paragraph, and a download section in place of “Get started”. Its main button names the visitor’s system and goes to the right file, with the other systems listed below it. The documentation has a Release notes page, made from this changelog, under About in the sidebar and linked from the home page. The circle of fifths has a Colors setting with fourteen color schemes, and a Create your own that saves schemes of your own. It applies to the exercise, the lessons and the reference.

title: Release notes
text: Changed The notation-font previews in Settings use the DSCH motif (D, E♭, C, B) in treble clef. Instrument previews play the same DSCH motif as the notation-font previews. Exercise and lesson icons use consistent musical glyphs and follow the theme color. In Key Signature Construction a number on the fork lights up as the mouse passes over it, the circle can be dragged along the fork, and the mouse wheel works over the staff and the Answer button too. The documentation sidebar sorts the pages under headings that open and close, with the developer guide and the API reference as single rows that open their pages, long pages have an “On this page” list that follows your reading, and every page ends with links to the previous and next pages. The home page leaves checking a download and updating to the Getting started page, which now explains both. The circle of fifths is colored from cyan through blue to indigo by key signature, instead of every color of the rainbow. The circle of fifths opens, and redraws when its window is resized, several times faster. Lessons that show it open faster too.

title: Release notes
text: Fixed Instrument previews keep an even rhythm on first playback by rendering the phrase as one audio clip. Changing the theme in the settings no longer sends you back to the exercises home page, or makes the window disappear and grow back from a dot. The window stays where it is, showing the exercise, lesson step or page you were on.

title: Release notes
text: 0.0.0 Released 2026-11-15. GitHub release The first release.

title: Release notes
text: Added Exercises Eleven exercises in four categories: Notation: Note Identification, Keyboard Note Identification and Note Construction. Intervals: Interval identification. Scales and keys: Key Signature Identification, Key Signature Construction, Scale spelling, Scale Construction and the Circle of Fifths. Chords: Chord quality and Arpeggio identification. Seven clefs, in every exercise that has a clef setting: treble, bass, alto, tenor, soprano, mezzo-soprano and baritone. Every exercise can be answered from the keyboard alone. Settings for the exercises, remembered between sessions. Learning Questions you miss, or take a long time over, come back more often; ones you answer quickly and correctly fade into the background. Profiles, each with its own history, kept in one local database file. Lessons: a beginner lesson on the circle of fifths in eight steps, with small unscored exercises, and an Exercises Lessons switch on the home page. A book button opens an interactive circle of fifths in a pane beside the exercise. Statistics Charts of accuracy, speed and volume, filterable by exercise and timeframe. A calendar heatmap of the last twelve months of practice. Click a bar, point, exercise or day to see the answers behind it. A database browser for everything stored. Look and sound 26 color themes, including light, dark and following the desktop, and a form to make your own. 11 notation styles (music fonts), 12 keyboard looks, and 30 transitions between the exercise and lesson cards, including none. The Salamander Grand Piano as the default piano, and recordings of a marimba, vibraphone, flute, horn and viola, chosen in Settings. The recordings and fonts are used under their own licenses, listed in THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md . Your data Export backup… and Import backup… in the menu. A backup is one .altobackup file holding every profile, every answer and every setting. Importing replaces everything, and a safety copy of what was there is saved first. Installing and updating scripts/alto-install.sh installs Alto from GitHub into its own environment, adds it to the application menu, updates it and removes it. Uninstalling keeps your data unless --purge is given. Check for updates… in the menu: says whether a newer release is available, offers to install it with its progress shown, and restarts Alto when you press OK. A packaged copy (the Linux download installed with install.sh , or the Windows installer) downloads the release, checks its signature and checksum, and then closes, installs it and opens again. Releases are signed, and Alto installs nothing whose signature does not verify. Settings → Updates shows the version you have, and a choice to follow the main branch instead of releases, for the latest changes before they are released. A Linux download: a .tar.gz with its own Python and Qt, so nothing else needs to be installed. sh install.sh install installs it for you alone, with an entry in the application menu, and sh install.sh uninstall removes it and keeps your data unless --purge is given. Installing a newer download over it updates it. A Windows installer: Alto for one user with no administrator prompt, an entry in the Start menu and in Settings → Apps, and an uninstaller that asks whether to also remove your practice history and settings. Running a newer installer updates it. The installer is not signed, so Windows may warn about an unknown publisher the first time. Both downloads are built and tested on GitHub when a version is tagged, and published with checksums. alto --version prints the version. ALTO_HOME keeps a copy of Alto apart, with its own history and settings, and scripts/dev.sh runs a clone that way. Documentation A documentation site, a developer guide, an API reference generated from the docstrings, and ARCHITECTURE.md .

title: Roadmap
text: Roadmap

title: Roadmap
text: Alpha phase Alto is in alpha. Complete means the feature is available in the current development version. Planned marks the proposed development sequence. Under consideration marks a candidate for future work. Chord construction and staff-to-keyboard practice are next. Ear training and rhythm come next. Both provide the groundwork for melodic dictation and harmonic analysis.

title: Roadmap
text: Notation and pitch Feature What the learner does Status Note identification and construction Name a written note or place a named pitch in the requested octave and clef. Complete Clefs Identify a clef or place its symbol on the correct staff line. Complete Notation symbols Identify a highlighted symbol in a short excerpt, or find a named symbol on the staff. Complete Accidental scope Work out which pitch sounds after a cancellation or a barline. Under consideration Enharmonic spelling Respell a pitch to fit a specified key or harmonic role. Under consideration

title: Roadmap
text: Intervals and instruments Feature What the learner does Status Staff intervals Identify written seconds through fifteenths, shown together or in ascending or descending order. Complete Keyboard notes and intervals Name a highlighted piano key or identify the interval between two highlighted keys. Complete Interval construction Place the second note a named interval above or below the first. Feedback distinguishes an incorrect staff position from an incorrect accidental. Complete Staff-to-keyboard practice Select the piano key for a written note, then play scales and select chord tones on the keyboard. Planned Transposition Rewrite a phrase in a new key or convert a transposing instrument’s part to concert pitch. Planned Interval inversion and reduction Invert a minor sixth or reduce a major tenth to its simple interval. Under consideration Instrument ranges and fingerboards Find an out-of-range note in a part or locate a pitch on a fretboard in a given tuning. Under consideration MIDI performance Play a written phrase on a connected keyboard. Under consideration

title: Roadmap
text: Scales and tonality Feature What the learner does Status Scale identification and construction Identify the key or mode of a written scale, or build the scale on the staff. Complete Key signatures Identify and construct signatures and fill in missing sharps or flats in order. Complete Written scale degrees Read a note as a scale degree or place a requested degree on the staff in a given key. Complete Relative keys Find the relative major or minor on the circle of fifths. Complete Parallel keys Compare scales that share a tonic but have different key signatures. Under consideration Other scale families Build and compare pentatonic, blues, whole-tone, and octatonic scales. Under consideration

title: Roadmap
text: Ear training Feature What the learner does Status Intervals by ear Name an interval after hearing its notes in succession or together. Replay the example and see the notation after answering. Planned Chords by ear Identify root-position triads by sound, then identify seventh chords and inversions. Planned Tonal scale degrees Hear a key established, then identify the scale degree of a new pitch. Planned Pitch recall Reproduce a sequence of two or three pitches. Planned Scales and tonal centers by ear Identify a heard scale or find the tonic of a short phrase. Under consideration Singing and intonation Sing a requested degree, continue a phrase, or judge a pitch against a reference. Under consideration Tuning and acoustics Match frequency ratios, identify harmonic partials, or listen for beats between pitches. Under consideration

title: Roadmap
text: Rhythm and meter Feature What the learner does Status Durations, rests, dots, and ties Complete a measure or replace tied notes with an equivalent duration. Planned Meter and grouping Subdivide beats and correct the beaming or rest grouping in simple and compound meters. Planned Tuplets Fill a beat with a triplet or another specified division. Planned Rhythm reading and imitation Tap a steady pulse, a written rhythm, or a pattern heard after a count-in. Calibrated timing distinguishes missing or extra taps from tempo drift. Planned Rhythm dictation Match a heard rhythm to written examples, then enter the pattern in the given meter. Planned Syncopation and groove Locate a displaced accent or distinguish straight and swung subdivisions by ear. Under consideration Additive meter, polyrhythm, and rhythmic cycles Group a measure of 7/8, align three pulses against two, or identify the return of a taught cycle. Under consideration

title: Roadmap
text: Chords and functional harmony Feature What the learner does Status Chord quality Identify root-position triads and seventh chords on the staff. Complete Arpeggio inversions Name the chord type and inversion from its notes written in succession. Complete Roman numerals on the circle of fifths Name the highlighted chord by Roman numeral in a major key. Complete Chord construction Spell a named triad or seventh chord by placing its notes on the staff. Planned Block-chord inversions Identify the root, bass, and inversion when the chord tones are written together. Planned Diatonic function and minor-key harmony Label or build chords in a major or minor key, including chords that use a raised degree in minor. Planned Cadences and progressions Identify a cadence or analyze a short progression across different voicings. Planned Harmonic rhythm Mark where the harmony changes within a phrase. Under consideration Chromatic harmony and modulation Resolve an applied dominant, identify a borrowed or altered chord, or locate a pivot between keys. Under consideration Jazz and popular harmony Read lead-sheet symbols, identify guide tones, build voicings, and analyze blues progressions or repeating chord patterns. Under consideration

title: Roadmap
text: Melody, counterpoint, and form Feature What the learner does Status Melodic dictation Write a heard phrase, with separate feedback on pitch and rhythm. Planned Two-voice dictation Transcribe two independent lines from the same excerpt. Under consideration Contour and motif Trace a melody’s shape, find a recurring motif, or transform it by inversion, retrograde, or augmentation. Under consideration Nonchord tones and voice leading Identify a passing tone or suspension, or correct parallel fifths, voice crossing, or an unresolved tendency tone. Under consideration Counterpoint and four-part writing Add a line to a given melody or realize a figured bass in four voices. Under consideration Phrase structure and form Distinguish a period from a sentence or mark the sections of a piece. Under consideration Texture and orchestration Identify a texture in an excerpt or choose a playable instrumental doubling. Under consideration Post-tonal theory Find a pitch-class set’s prime form or identify a transformation of a twelve-tone row. Under consideration Modal traditions Identify a characteristic phrase or mode segment from examples within a specific tradition. Under consideration Composition and improvisation Write or play a short response that meets a given musical constraint. Under consideration

title: Roadmap
text: Lessons and practice Feature What the learner does Status Guided lessons Study pitches and notes, clefs, intervals, scales, key signatures, and the circle of fifths, then open related exercises. Complete Spaced repetition and statistics Review questions under the selected scheduler and inspect accuracy, response times, and individual answers in a local profile. Complete Response-time grading Inspect response times by exercise and adjust the percentiles used for automatic SM-2 and FSRS grades. Complete Mixed practice Combine an earlier prerequisite, a current topic, and a passage that uses both in one suggested session. Planned

title: Roadmap
text: App features Feature What the learner does Status Anki-compatible deck export Export filtered exercise questions and optional review schedules for practice in Anki. Complete Instrument packs Install third-party artwork, samples, and exercises for identifying fingerboard notes or marked instrument parts from one ZIP. Plugins · Viola plugin tutorial . Complete Instrument plugins Add an instrument with its own sound and play it using an interactive on-screen version of the instrument. Planned Exercise and lesson plugins Install custom exercises and lessons and use them alongside Alto’s built-in material. Planned Glossary plugins Install a plugin that adds new terms to the glossary, with definitions, interactive examples, and links to related lessons and exercises. Planned

title: Roadmap
text: Beta phase Alto is developed with the help of artificial intelligence. The main goal for beta is to replace prose generated by large language models with human-written text throughout the app and its documentation. Lessons, exercise prompts, and feedback should sound like a teacher explaining an idea to a student. The editorial review will also check definitions, musical examples, and answers for accuracy and correct errors where needed. A second goal is to refactor the codebase so it is easier to read, test, and maintain. That work includes simplifying complicated code, removing duplication, and using tests to verify behavior as the implementation changes.

title: Settings
text: Settings There are two kinds of settings. App settings apply everywhere. Exercise settings belong to one exercise.

title: Settings
text: App settings Open them from the menu (☰) with Settings… or Ctrl + Alt + S . The dialog does not block the window: you can keep it open and use the exercises, and opening it again brings the same one forward. A new theme is applied to the window when you close the settings. Categories are listed on the left, and the selected one’s settings appear on the right. Restore defaults… resets app and exercise preferences after confirmation. It removes custom themes and keyboard colors and keeps your profiles and practice history.

title: Settings
text: Appearance Expand Appearance in the left sidebar to choose Theme , Notation style , Keyboard style , or Transitions . Theme. The themes are in a list on the left. The right side is the theme’s card: its name, three pictures of the window one above another. Beside the Light and Dark pictures are squares of that version’s colors, and the window, accent and ink colors written out as hexadecimal codes. The pictures are Light , Dark and System . The System picture is cut through on a slant, light on one side and dark on the other, because that version is light when your operating system is set to light and dark when it is set to dark, and changes with it. Choosing a theme in the list uses it at once, in whichever of Light, Dark and System you chose last, so you can go down the list and see each theme in the version you prefer. Clicking a picture changes the version. The picture in use is outlined, and its theme is bold in the list. The first theme, Default , is the desktop’s own colors. Then there is Studio , with cool grays and a clear blue, and twenty-four more: Parchment, Slate Blue, Sage, Harbor, Lavender Hush, Rosewater, Marigold, Pine, Indigo Ink, Graphite, Terracotta, Mint, Sky, Plum, Sand, Teal, Copper, Charcoal and Gold, Cherry, Moss, Arctic, Dusk, Lime Shock and Ember. Your own themes. The top of the theme list is My themes , with a row ＋ New theme… . Choosing it opens an editor in place of the card. Save (filled in the accent color), Cancel and, for a theme already saved, Delete theme are at the top right of the editor, where they stay in view while the colors below them scroll. Give the theme a name, then choose a color for each part of its Light version and its Dark version : the window, panels, text, quiet text, outlines, accent and the track behind a switch. Click a color to open the color picker: the pointer becomes a hand over a color, a ring appears around it, and the code beside it turns bold and dark. A small picture of each version follows the colors as you change them. A new theme starts as a copy of Studio, and choosing another theme in the Start from list takes that theme’s colors at once, for both versions. Save keeps the theme and uses it, in the version you last chose. Your themes are kept with your other settings, so they are there next time, and they are part of a backup. A theme of your own appears in the list with the same three pictures as any other, and its card has a Change colors… button for the editor, from which you can also Delete theme after it asks. Notation style. The music font used to draw clefs, notes and accidentals. Each choice shows a preview. Your choice applies to every staff in the app, including the small pictures in the settings panels. The default is Finale Maestro. Style Character Finale Maestro The look of Finale. Leland MuseScore 4’s font. Light and modern, modeled on SCORE. Bravura The reference font of the SMuFL standard, which Dorico uses by default. Noto Music Google’s engraved look. Sebastian A classic engraved face with generous proportions. Leipzig The default of Verovio. Crisp and compact. Eugene Inspired by hand-engraved Parisian scores of the early 1900s. Golden Age A heavy, old-fashioned plate-engraved look. Petaluma A handwritten look, as in jazz real books. MuseJazz A brush-pen hand, like MuseScore’s jazz template. Finale Broadway A bold copyist’s hand, as in Broadway scores. Under the styles, Baritone clef chooses how that clef is written. It is the same staff and the same notes either way (the bottom line is B2 and the top line is C4): F clef, on the middle line is the default. It looks like a bass clef moved up, with its dots on either side of the middle line. C clef, on the top line looks like an alto clef moved up, with its center on the top line. The choice applies to every baritone staff in the app and its pictures, in whichever music font you have chosen. Keyboard style. How the piano keyboard looks in the keyboard exercise and in the range picker. Each choice is a card with a small picture of the keys. Your choice applies to every keyboard in the app. The default is Classic, the standard Alto look. Style Character Classic White keys in a dark case. Modern piano A current upright or grand, with red felt under the fallboard. Antique ivory Naturals aged to a warm yellow, in a rosewood case. Harpsichord, Italian Boxwood naturals and dark sharps in a cypress case. Harpsichord, French Reversed colors: ebony naturals with bone-topped sharps. Baroque pipe organ Bone and ebony keys in an oak case, under a row of stop knobs. Tonewheel organ Plastic keys in a walnut case, with the lowest octave reversed. Flat and minimal No case and no gradients. Reads well at small sizes. Engraving Ink on paper, like a plate in an old method book. Color by note One hue per semitone, so every C has the same color. Midnight neon Dark keys with a cyan glow and magenta sharps. High contrast Pure black and white with heavy outlines and a yellow dot on every C. The colors are typical of the materials, not measurements of one instrument. Build your own. Below the cards, each part of the keyboard has a row: Naturals , Sharps , Case , Felt strip and Sharp caps . Click a part’s swatch to open the color picker, or click one of the round chips for a color named after a material: Acrylic white, Mother-of-pearl, Ivory, Bone, Boxwood, Maple, Cypress, Oak, Walnut, Rosewood, Ebonized pearwood, Ebony, Black acrylic, Aluminum, Brass, Red felt, Green baize and Blue felt. Hover a chip to see its name. The case, felt and caps can be left out with the ✕ chip. Changing any part switches to the Custom style, and your colors are remembered. The double whole note is always drawn in its square form, whichever font you choose. All the fonts are bundled with Alto except Noto Music, which is read from your system. Transitions. How the home page changes when you switch between the exercises and the lessons. The choices are in a list on the left, and a preview on the right plays the one you pick, once, on a mock of the home page with the app’s own cards and the Exercises | Lessons switch, so you can see it before you leave the settings. The Exercises | Lessons switch in the preview works, so you can press it to try the transition, in both directions, as often as you like. Replay starts again from the exercises. (Only the first lesson is real; the other three lesson cards in the preview are marked Example, so that the transition has more than one card to move.) No transition changes the cards at once. Next comes Cascade , the default, where the new cards arrive one after another. There are twenty-nine in all, and they fall into a few families: Fades and dissolves: Fade in, Crossfade, Slow dissolve, Blur, Focus pull. Slides: Slide sideways, Slide up, Rise, Stream. Growing and shrinking: Zoom, Zoom out, Shrink and grow, Elastic, Burst, Ripple, Gather, Unfold. Spins and turns: Flip, Flip over, Spin, Swing, Whirl. Reveals: Wipe, Curtain. One card after another: Cascade, Wave, Fall in, Scatter, Drop and pop. The choice applies the next time you flip the switch.

title: Settings
text: Sound

title: Settings
text: Instruments Choose the instrument used for notes and for the correct-answer chime. The instruments are listed in a box on the left: piano, flute, French horn, viola, marimba and vibraphone. The one in use is in bold and checked. Choose any of them to see a summary on the right of what its sound is made from: where the recordings come from, who played them, and when and how they were recorded; which articulation and dynamic were used, such as blown without vibrato at fortissimo or struck with yarn mallets; how many notes are recorded, their range, and whether every semitone is covered (notes in between are shifted from a neighbor); how much space they take, and the terms they are available under. The viola can be played two ways, so it has one entry. Its page describes the Arco (bowed) and Pizzicato (plucked) recordings together, and has a row of buttons for each, such as Use this instrument (Arco) . The list says which one is in use, such as “Viola (Pizzicato)”. Press Use this instrument , or double-click the entry in the list, to switch to it. Press Hear it beside it to listen to a short arpeggio first without choosing it, even while sound is muted. Sound can also be muted with the speaker button in any exercise. The flute, French horn and arco viola, which are blown or bowed, end each note as the next one begins, as a player would. So does the piano, which is played without the pedal: each note is damped as the next key goes down, so a scale does not blur together. Other struck and plucked instruments, such as the marimba and pizzicato viola, ring on. An instrument whose recordings are not installed in your copy of Alto is shown in italics and cannot be chosen, because it would only play as the synthesized piano.

title: Settings
text: Metronome Select High pip , Low pip , or Pencil click in the list to read about its sound. Press Preview to hear four clicks at 120 BPM, even when exercise audio is muted. The spectrum curve rises with each click and settles between beats. Lower frequencies appear on the left and higher frequencies on the right. Press Use this sound or double-click the list entry to save it. A check mark identifies the sound in use. High pip is the default. The Duration lesson and rhythm glossary examples play this click at each written onset. In meter examples, louder clicks mark accents and softer clicks mark subdivisions. The tie example pairs the clicks with the selected instrument so you can hear the held note.

title: Settings
text: Updates Automatically check for new releases daily is on by default. When a new release is available and the main grid is active, Alto asks whether you want to update. Yes starts the update or opens the download page, depending on how you installed Alto. No lets Alto offer the same version again after 24 hours. Don’t remind me again skips this version. Alto will still notify you when a newer version is available. To revisit a skipped release, choose Tools → Check for updates… . To stop automatic prompts for all releases, turn off Automatically check for new releases daily . Follow the main branch switches manual checks to the latest commit for copies installed with the install script. Automatic release checks pause on that channel. Packaged copies always follow releases. See Getting started .

title: Settings
text: Practice Select a scheduler for the current profile. With SM-2 or FSRS , you can set daily limits and choose whether to grade correct answers yourself. Open Response-time grading… to adjust the automatic Hard and Easy percentages and inspect the times for each exercise. Response-time grading . This profile can start ten new cards per exercise each day and review every card that comes due.

title: Settings
text: Exercise settings Open the sliders button at the top right of an exercise to see its options. It opens a pane on the right. Each row summarizes its setting with a small picture, and clicking a row opens that setting’s page. See Exercises for what each option does. Changing a setting starts a new question right away, and the settings are remembered the next time you open Alto.

title: Settings
text: Where settings are stored Settings are kept by Qt in your user configuration (for example ~/.config/alto/alto.conf on Linux), separate from your practice history. See Your data .

title: Shortcuts
text: Shortcuts

title: Shortcuts
text: Keyboard For keyboard practice in Notation Identification, select Question Type → Answer Button . When you choose an exercise from the list, the keyboard goes to it, so its keys work at once. Tab and Shift + Tab move between the buttons, and Space presses the one that has the focus. Hover over any button to see its key.

title: Shortcuts
text: Choosing an answer Keys What it does 1 to 9 Press the matching answer button, counting from the left. Available when an exercise has nine answers or fewer. C D E F G A B Keyboard Note Identification and Circle of Fifths: the natural note or key of that name. A minor key is typed as the major key of its letter. Shift +a letter, Ctrl +a letter Keyboard Note Identification and Circle of Fifths: the sharp ( Shift ) or the flat ( Ctrl ) of that note or key. 1 to 6 Circle of Fifths, Roman numerals: I, ii, iii, IV, V and vi. For a key with two names (such as B and C♭) press the key of each name. 1 to 9 Keyboard Note Identification with the octave asked: the octave, typed as its number. A S D F Arpeggio Identification: the inversion, which is the second row of buttons. The chord type is on 1 to 4 . With scale-degree answers, digits name the degrees. In a bank with more than nine choices, add Shift for a sharp or Ctrl for a flat; add Alt as well for a double sharp or double flat. The octave row uses A , S , D , F and so on, as shown on its buttons.

title: Shortcuts
section: Staff placement in Note, Interval, and Scale Construction
text: Staff placement in Note, Interval, and Scale Construction Clicking the staff is never needed. A pale note, the caret , shows the note that would be placed, and the line under the staff says what comes next, in words that a screen reader can read. Keys Button What it does ↑ / ↓ Higher / Lower Move the note one line or space up or down. The first press starts from the middle line of the staff. Page Up / Page Down Octave ↑ / Octave ↓ Move the note an octave up or down. A to G   Jump to the nearest note with that name, above or below. ← / →   Step backwards or forwards through no sign, ♯, ♭ and ♮ (♮ only when the staff has a key signature). + - 0 ♯ ♭ ♮ Choose a sharp, a flat or a natural for the next note. Return Place note Place the note at the caret. Backspace Undo Scale Construction: take back the last note or step. Interval Construction also accepts Ctrl + - for a double flat and Ctrl + + for a double sharp. Once all the notes of a scale are placed, and the Steps setting is on, the same keys mark the steps: Keys Button What it does W / H W / H Choose a whole or a half step. ↑ ↓ ← →   Switch between whole and half. Return Mark step Mark the step and move on to the next pair of notes. When everything is placed, Return presses Answer . Return always does the next thing: it places a note or marks a step while there is something to place, and answers once there is not.

title: Shortcuts
section: Building a key signature (Key Signature Construction)
text: Building a key signature (Key Signature Construction) Keys What it does ↑ or → One more sharp (or one fewer flat). ↓ or ← One more flat (or one fewer sharp). Home Back to the natural sign: no sharps or flats. Return Answer.

title: Shortcuts
section: Placing a clef (Clef Basics, Clef Construction)
text: Placing a clef (Clef Basics, Clef Construction) Keys What it does ← or → Choose the G, C or F clef before or after this one. ↑ or ↓ Move it up or down a line or space. Return Answer: place it where it is.

title: Shortcuts
